item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-27
item.description:
• NFS2ROOT: Linux nfsd pre-auth heap overflow, root shell claimed; limit TCP 2049, Ubuntu and RHEL 9/10 not fixed. CVE-2026-99362 is an unauthenticated heap overflow in the Linux kernel NFS server (nfsd) over NFSv4.1 or 4.2, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 in the CVE record, that OpenSec says it turned into a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049. It is fixed upstream in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (later also 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193 and 6.6.163), but on 2026-11-27 Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel; the exploit is private and no exploitation is reported. →
  • SoftwareOK Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers carried a Python RAT; check hashes, reinstalling may not remove it. AhnLab ASEC reports that Q-Dir 12.83.0.0 to 12.85.0.0 and DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 installers distributed from SoftwareOK's official site were tampered with and install a Python remote-access tool that compares running processes with 1,206 security-product names. ASEC says copies updated through the update function may be affected, has not found how the files were replaced, and the vendor's pages carry no notice as of 2026-11-27. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01NFS2ROOT: Linux nfsd pre-auth heap overflow, root shell claimed; limit TCP 2049, Ubuntu and RHEL 9/10 not fixed. CVE-2026-99362 is an unauthenticated heap overflow in the Linux kernel NFS server (nfsd) over NFSv4.1 or 4.2, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 in the CVE record, that OpenSec says it turned into a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049. It is fixed upstream in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (later also 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193 and 6.6.163), but on 2026-11-27 Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel; the exploit is private and no exploitation is reported. →
  2. 02SoftwareOK Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers carried a Python RAT; check hashes, reinstalling may not remove it. AhnLab ASEC reports that Q-Dir 12.83.0.0 to 12.85.0.0 and DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 installers distributed from SoftwareOK's official site were tampered with and install a Python remote-access tool that compares running processes with 1,206 security-product names. ASEC says copies updated through the update function may be affected, has not found how the files were replaced, and the vendor's pages carry no notice as of 2026-11-27. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 1Trending vulnerabilities 1Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 15

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

SoftwareOK: Q-Dir 12.83 to 12.85 and DesktopOK 12.82 and 12.85 installers from the vendor's official site carried a Python remote-access tool, ASEC says the update function may have been affected too, and reinstalling may not remove it

AhnLab's ASEC reports that Q-Dir 12.83.0.0, 12.84.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 and DesktopOK 12.82.0.0 and 12.85.0.0 were replaced with tampered installers on SoftwareOK's official distribution path, and that the SHA-256 of some files downloaded from the official site did not match the value posted on its download page. ASEC says the evidence indicates malicious files were also generated during the update process of installed copies, a point it later hedges (users of the update function "may have been affected"), and that it has not identified how the files were replaced (ASEC, 2026-11-25).

The tampered installer embeds the genuine, correctly signed Q-Dir or DesktopOK executable and runs it from the public user folder so the program appears to work. It then downloads the legitimate 7-Zip console extractor and a package holding a Python runtime and a remote-access tool, unpacks it under a Microsoft-looking folder in ProgramData and persists through a scheduled task, named to look like Edge, that runs the windowless Python interpreter. The tool runs shell commands and Python code, transfers files, takes screenshots and collects system information, and it compares running processes with a list of 1,206 security-product process names and sends the matches to its server. ASEC does not describe the server protocol, names no malware family or actor, and reads Chinese-language comments in the code only as a hint (ASEC, 2026-11-25).

ASEC gives no distribution window. SoftwareOK's release pages date Q-Dir 12.83 to 4 November, 12.84 to 13 November and 12.85 to 21 November (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-21) and DesktopOK 12.82 to 28 October and 12.85 to 19 November (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-26), which bounds only when the listed versions could first have reached users, and its Q-Dir download page carries no notice about tampering as of 2026-11-27 (SoftwareOK, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
Any Windows endpoint on which the listed versions were installed or updated since 2026-10-28; ASEC adds that other versions installed or updated while the tampered files were distributed may be affected. The installed program is the genuine signed one, so a signature check on it passes; the check that finds the tampering is the installer's SHA-256 against the vendor page.
Detection
Software-inventory telemetry for the listed versions; in scheduled-task creation and process-creation telemetry, a task running a bundled Python interpreter from under ProgramData and an extractor tool started by an installer; and egress from that interpreter. After removal ASEC says to look for the Python environment, scheduled tasks, related files and external connections.
Defender takeaway
Treat every host that ran an affected installer or updater as compromised: isolate it, remove the tool and rotate the credentials used on it, because ASEC says uninstalling and reinstalling the utility may not remove the remote-access tool.
incident27 Nov 04:41Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: AhnLab ASEC · SoftwareOK

02Trending vulnerabilities1 item

NOTABLECVE-2026-99362NATOB2

NFS2ROOT, CVE-2026-99362, Linux kernel NFS server (nfsd): an unauthenticated heap overflow over NFSv4.1 or 4.2 that OpenSec says it turned into a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049 (CVSS 3.1 9.8); fixed upstream in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1, Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel on 2026-11-27, exploit private, no exploitation reported

CVE-2026-99362 is a heap out-of-bounds write in the Linux kernel's NFS server: nfsd4_sequence() narrows the reply buffer to the session's cached-reply limit before it accepts the slot sequence id, a client can negotiate that limit down so every slot has a zero-length buffer, and the server then caches a whole reply into a buffer with no room; the flaw has been present since Linux 3.16 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-11-19). The announcement lists fixes in 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-11-19); ENISA's record, last updated on 2026-11-23, adds 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193 and 6.6.163 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23).

OpenSec, which reported it, says an unauthenticated client reaches a root shell with one TCP connection to port 2049 over NFSv4.1 or 4.2, shows this in its own recording and says its exploit stays private (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). watchTowr reports no exploitation in the wild as of 2026-11-26 (watchTowr, 2026-11-26), and the fix with its root-cause text has been public on the linux-nfs list since 2026-08-17 (linux-nfs, 2026-08-17).

Distribution status as read on 2026-11-27: Debian trixie and the 6.12 backport kernel for bookworm are fixed, bookworm's default 6.1 kernel is not (Debian, 2026-11-27); Red Hat fixed RHEL 8 on 2026-11-26 (RHSA-2026:103817) while RHEL 9 and 10 are listed as affected with no fix (Red Hat, 2026-11-26); Ubuntu shows no fixed kernel on any release from 16.04 to 26.10 (Ubuntu, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
A host that serves NFS. Red Hat says default RHEL does not run nfsd, which limits the attack surface to systems configured to export NFSv4.1 or 4.2 shares (Red Hat, 2026-11-26). OpenSec's test is nfsd loaded, /proc/fs/nfsd/versions showing +4.1 or +4.2 and a listener on port 2049 on a non-loopback address, with a kernel older than the fixed one and no distribution backport (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). No source says whether an empty export list or client-address restrictions reduce the reach.
Detection
OpenSec says the traffic is valid NFS with no network signature and names kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, oopses with nfsd4, svc or call_usermodehelper frames, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server and bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source; no vendor confirms these (OpenSec, 2026-11-25). On a server that was reachable while unpatched, the kernel-worker-spawned shell is the compromise check.
Defender takeaway
On NFS servers, restrict TCP 2049 to trusted networks, the step OpenSec, watchTowr and Red Hat all name, or stop nfs-server where it is not needed (Red Hat, 2026-11-26); turning off NFSv4.1 and 4.2 is the researchers' mitigation and no vendor endorses it. Then install the first distribution kernel that lists the CVE and reboot. A host that does not run nfsd is outside the exposure the sources describe.

Sources: Linux kernel CVE team · OpenSec · watchTowr · ENISA EUVD · Red Hat · Red Hat Security Data API · Debian Security Tracker · Ubuntu · linux-nfs mailing list

03Updates to prior coverage9 items

HIGHCVE-2026-46300exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-46300, Linux kernel: local privilege escalation via xfrm ESP-in-TCP ("Fragnesia"), listed by CISA as exploited and chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to reach root, PoC public

First published 2026-05-15 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:59 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyupdated_at

Palo Alto's bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 (2026-11-24) says exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against internet-exposed management interfaces, the vendor's own statement beside CISA's listing and Dream Research's account, and lists a first fixed PAN-OS build for the flaw in every train that is later than the PHP2Shell hotfix.

Palo Alto Networks published bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 on 2026-11-24, titled "OSS CVEs Fixed in PAN-OS", whose exploitation-status block reads "Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet" (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24). That is the vendor's own statement of exploitation of this flaw, next to CISA's listing and Dream Research's account. The bulletin says "The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability through an internet-exposed management interface, and we are not aware of any other exploitation method" (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

It lists a first fixed PAN-OS build for this flaw in every train, later than the hotfix that fixes PHP2Shell (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24; Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-29). Its FAQ says a device running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the PHP2Shell advisory is protected, still recommends upgrading to a fixed release at the next maintenance interval where management access is restricted, and recommends upgrading immediately and restricting access where the management interface is internet-reachable (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24). The bulletin says nothing on Panorama, Prisma Access or Cloud NGFW for this flaw.

Sources: Wiz Research, 2026-05-13 · Help Net Security, 2026-05-14 · Red Hat (RHSB-2026-003) · Red Hat Product Security · Aikido Security · FIRST.org EPSS API · Microsoft Security Blog · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog · Dream Research · Dream Research (report updated 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (threat brief, updated 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory CVE-2026-109618, updated 2026-10-29)
NOTABLECVE-2026-115731 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-115731, Puppet Enterprise before 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1: deserialization of a crafted agent report gives code execution as the Puppet service user to any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate, and unauthenticated where the CA autosigns; CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.4)

First published 2026-11-18 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsourcing_notesourcesevidenceactionsbodyupdated_at

Huntback's decoy captured the exploit chain for CVE-2026-115731 on 2026-11-19, two days after the KEV listing: a certificate request, a fetch of the signed certificate that tests for autosigning, and a report upload carrying a type definition, which it reads as a check for vulnerable servers. The hunt signal is a PUT to the certificate-request path from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within seconds, then a PUT to the report path.

Huntback, a research firm that runs decoy servers, captured the whole exploit chain on one Puppet Server decoy on the morning of 2026-11-19, in 1.47 seconds from one address (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The chain is a bare certificate request for a generated node name, which a CA that asks for a shared secret or other proof would refuse, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later without polling, which answers 200 only where the CA signs automatically, and a report upload whose wrapper is ordinary and whose event carries a type definition with a Ruby method annotation (Huntback, 2026-11-20). Huntback reads it as a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy signed the certificate, accepted the report with a 200 and returned no marker, and the same address had tried exploits for four other products in the previous ten days (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A scout from a different address had probed the status service and the CA paths about two and a half hours earlier without asking for a certificate. Huntback's advice is to list the signed certificates (puppetserver ca list --all) and account for every name, to refuse at a reverse proxy any report containing RubyMethod, since no agent sends a type definition in a report, and to keep TCP 8140 closed to networks that are not agents'; none of this is vendor guidance (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The capture is a single source and Huntback names no actor or victim.

Sources: Puppet (Perforce) PE 2026.0.1 release notes · CISA · ENISA EUVD (carries the CNA record) · OpenVox project advisory · Neodyme · Red Hat Product Security · Vox Pupuli · oss-security (OpenVox release notice) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-116493) · OpenVox (GHSA-q4hm-33rc-572g) · NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub · SecurityWeek · The Hacker News · Huntback
HIGHCVE-2026-132825updatedNATOA2

Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14: seven memory-safety flaws in the regexp engine and string case conversion, three rated Critical by the project, with proofs of concept for code execution; Veria Labs says Rails and classic Sinatra are exposed by default and announces a public Rails exploit for 25 November 2026 (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 3.1 7.4)

First published 2026-11-20 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryaffected_productsentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6, 3.21.11, 3.20.13 and 3.19.17 (2026-11-22) carry the Ruby fix and GitLab's 2026-11-25 release backports it to five older branches, so Veria Labs' table, unchanged since 2026-11-21, is stale; Veria's announced Rails exploit was not found released on 2026-11-27, and a co-discoverer says a plain Rails app is exploitable.

GitHub's release notes list the Ruby update as a critical fix in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.21.11 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.20.13 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) and 3.19.17 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), all dated 2026-11-22, with application-level mitigations where an update was not immediately possible; they name no Ruby version or CVE. GitLab's release of 2026-11-25 backports the Ruby fix, a bump to Ruby 3.3.14 and 3.4.13, to 19.3.10, 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12 and 18.11.15, which it calls an exception to its maintenance policy (GitLab, 2026-11-25).

Veria Labs' Rails proof of concept was announced for 2026-11-25 or later; its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation show no release as of 2026-11-27, which does not show that no exploit exists. Sanft writes that Rack's multipart method override and a field charset reach the vulnerable case conversion in a plain Rails application, and that OpenAI sent the Ruby maintainers working exploit proofs for the case-conversion and an integer-overflow flaw on 2026-11-07; the second flaw is limited to Rack 3.2.1 and earlier (Durendal, 2026-11-19).

Sources: Ruby project · Ruby project (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5) · NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub · Veria Labs · watchTowr · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-129481) · GitLab · GitLab (19.6.2) · GitHub Enterprise Server release notes · Durendal (Moritz Sanft)
HIGHCVE-2026-102489 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs

First published 2026-10-02 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.

DIVD published the forensic report on its September breach on 2026-11-25 (DIVD CSIRT blog, 2026-11-25), written by Merlon Security with NVISO's analysis of the Google Workspace side. It says the attacker likely used ARTEX, on the basis of 990 scripts and 3,259 output files, scripts commented in an LLM style, an API token named artex- plus a number and a Zammad administrator account named artex.ops, ARTEX strings in an e-mail subject and the numeric job IDs that ARTEX's intents use; it names no actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The chain at behaviour level: the attacker probed the perimeter from 07:40 UTC on 2026-09-21; an administrator logged in to Zammad at 18:53 and the WebSocket flaw yielded that session cookie 1.3 seconds later; the replayed session wrote a file through the package-upload endpoint at 19:06 and a malicious Ruby mail template as an override of a mailer view at 19:27, which a user-creation request rendered, giving code execution as the zammad user at 19:27:58. Command and control ran through a Zammad API endpoint, with files staged in the web-served directory and fetched back through the egress proxy because direct outbound traffic was blocked. Root followed through the second flaw: a service that runs as root read configuration from a directory the zammad account owned, and a dropped file plus a kill of the web worker, which the supervisor restarted, gave root by 19:46 and left a setuid copy of bash (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

From the Zammad host, in the same web-application VLAN as Jira and Confluence, the attacker sniffed passively from 21:19 and from about 01:37 on 2026-09-22 ran ARP-poisoning scripts, reaching a man-in-the-middle position between Confluence and its PostgreSQL database at 02:27. The link was unencrypted, so it read the database protocol, learned the schema from captured traffic and injected its own SQL into live connections, writing a remember-me session token of its choosing for an administrator into Confluence's token table and presenting it at 08:49; Jira followed through its OAuth tables and a replay of remember-me tokens at 14:08. The report says TLS on the database links would have stopped the injection, asks for deny-by-default micro-segmentation inside the VLAN and says a containerised Zammad would have prevented the root step (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Persistence was a new Zammad administrator account and API tokens, a root-run systemd loop with Restart=always and cron entries that run text files dropped in the web-served directory, and an edit of Zammad's Google sign-in initializer that switched the access type to offline and added the Gmail scope, which captured nothing because no user signed in while it was live. Credentials taken included the hosting provider's mailbox password in cleartext, OAuth tokens for the two shared mailboxes, the database password, an Elastic credential and Jira's OAuth consumer private key and password hashes. NVISO says the content of the two shared mailboxes up to the credential and session resets must be considered potentially compromised, and that tokens were re-issued after the network isolation, so network isolation alone does not revoke cloud OAuth access (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The alert fired at 19:43 UTC on 2026-09-21. A volunteer first looked at it at 03:04 on 09-22, 7 h 21 min later; the CISO was informed at 15:06, 19 h 23 min after the alert; and isolation completed at 23:24, 27 h 41 min after it (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Contradiction: DIVD's case page says "it took us 19 hours to initiate our first response on 22 September 2026" (DIVD, 2026-11-25), while the report says "The first response to these alerts was observed on Sep 22nd 2026 at 03:04 UTC", 7 h 21 min after the alert, and puts the CISO notification at 15:06 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). The case page's own metrics table lists a mean time to acknowledge of 07:20:51 ("Time between first alert and SOC pickup") and a mean time to respond of 19:16:51 ("Time between first attack and formal response"), the same 7 h 21 min the report gives for the first look and about the 19 hours of the prose, so the two documents use "first response" for different intervals (DIVD, 2026-11-25). The report counts about 39 hours of actor interaction in the cloud, to 08:33 on 2026-09-23 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Sources: NCSC-NL · DIVD CSIRT (case DIVD-2026-00015) · DIVD CSIRT (case DIVD-2026-00014) · DIVD CSIRT (public statements on the hack) · DIVD CSIRT (CVE record) · Zammad GmbH (vendor statement) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog · DIVD log-check script · Zammad GmbH (security advisory) · Zammad GmbH (release notes) · Zammad GmbH (GitHub security advisory) · Zammad GmbH (GitHub advisory records) · Horizon3.ai · DIVD CSIRT (data investigation overview) · DIVD CSIRT (case file, updated 2026-11-18) · Zammad (release 7.2.3) · DIVD CSIRT (forensics report) · DIVD CSIRT (blog) · DIVD CSIRT (case file, last modified 2026-11-25)
HIGHCVE-2026-123007 +10updatedNATOA1

NGINX nginx2root: five unauthenticated memory-corruption flaws (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 in HTTP/2, CVE-2026-121810 in HTTP/3, CVE-2026-123634 in the resolver, CVE-2026-113425 in the mail proxy) can lead to code execution as the worker process; fixed in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 and NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1, Rapid7 proof of concept public, no exploitation reported (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

First published 2026-11-19 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:55 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryaffected_productsentitiescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

nginx 1.31.10 and 1.30.8 (2026-11-23) and NGINX Plus 37.3.1.1 and 37.0.9.1 fix a further flaw, CPU exhaustion when ssl_early_data is on (CVE-2026-132779), so the update target moves; Veeam lists its 13.1 Software and Infrastructure Appliances as affected by the two HTTP/2 flaws with a fix through Veeam Updater since 2026-11-25, and GitLab's Linux package carries nginx 1.31.9.

nginx 1.31.10 and 1.30.8, both dated 2026-11-23, carry one security fix: when ssl_early_data is configured a client might cause excessive CPU usage (CVE-2026-132779) (nginx.org, 2026-11-23; nginx.org, 2026-11-23). nginx.org lists it as affecting 1.21.4 to 1.31.9 (nginx.org, 2026-11-27), so 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix the memory-corruption flaws but not this one; NGINX Plus 37.3.1.1 and 37.0.9.1 of the same day are security releases whose only fix is this flaw, and the 18 November Plus builds do not carry it (F5 NGINX Plus release notes, 2026-11-23). F5's own advisory and a score were not readable, and no source states whether R33 to R36 are affected.

Veeam's KB4976 lists Veeam Software Appliance 13.1 and Veeam Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 as affected by CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, because their nginx has HTTP/2 enabled on a listener that proxies requests to a backend; the other three flaws do not apply (Veeam, 2026-11-25). A fix has been in the Veeam repository since 2026-11-25, Veeam Updater checks every 12 hours and installs mandatory updates automatically on the nearest Sunday at 14:00, and until it is installed Veeam says to restrict TCP 443 on the appliances to trusted networks, because HTTP/2 cannot be disabled on them (Veeam, 2026-11-25). GitLab's Linux package and Docker images carry nginx 1.31.9 from 19.6.2, 19.5.9 and 19.4.11, and its page does not say whether they set ssl_early_data (GitLab, 2026-11-25). KB4976 also lists the Veeam Plug-In for AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure appliances as affected (install all available security updates through Veeam Updater) and Veeam Backup for Salesforce 3.2.1, which is affected by the same two HTTP/2 flaws (install the operating system vendor's update or disable HTTP/2); Veeam manages its Data Cloud services and asks for no customer action (Veeam, 2026-11-25).

Sources: nginx.org security advisories · Rapid7 · Wiz Research · Xint · Rapid7 proof-of-concept repository · CERT-EU · NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub · NCSC-NL · CERT.at · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT · Cisco PSIRT (cisco-sa-nginx-nov-2026-e8jska2s) · Siemens ProductCERT (SSA-935812) · Fortinet PSIRT (FG-IR-26-279) · Ubuntu security notices (USN-9159-1) · Synology (security advisory SA-26:20) · Unit 42 · nginx.org changes · nginx.org changes (1.30 branch) · nginx.org security advisories (as read 2026-11-27) · F5 NGINX Plus release notes · Veeam (KB4976, last modified 2026-11-25) · GitLab
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

First published 2026-10-22 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:54 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyupdated_at

Wiz shows that ARTEX writes a numeric intent ID from a per-installation counter it does not reset by default, and Cairn a per-project one, into AWS and Azure resource names, session names and comments, a pivot for hunting and linking activity; Wiz ties ARTEX-Harvester to more than a dozen organisations, Huntback's exposed console shows a Global Administrator takeover at a South Korean university, and DIVD's forensic report finds the same numbering in its own breach.

Wiz Research shows how ARTEX and Cairn leak their intent numbering into victim logs. ARTEX draws intents, facts, findings, hints and digests from one counter per installation that is never reset by default, so intent numbers climb across runs and targets and consecutive ones are rare, and it puts the number in its working directory, its session name and its prompt; Cairn formats zero-padded counters per object type and resets them for every project (Wiz, 2026-11-25). The numbers surface wherever an API takes a name or comment: AWS role session names, SSM command comments, KMS key descriptions and aliases, security-group rule descriptions, Azure run-command, VM and app-registration names, and the error message of a denied call (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Wiz uses them to link activity across rotating residential-proxy addresses and victims, to separate installations and to read scope from a jump far larger than the activity in one victim's logs, and cautions that hits are tool markers and pacing clues, not operator fingerprints: unrelated installations collide in the same ranges and operators reset or parallelise (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Google's report of 2026-10-31 had already seen incremental numeric markers in ARTEX file names, account names, passwords and e-mail subjects without being able to explain them (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31).

Wiz's account of ARTEX-Harvester ties it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organisations between late October and mid-November, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, the cross-victim intent counter and proxy-pool overlap, and warns that activity labelled ARTEX comes from multiple unrelated operators; these two posts do not mention Storm-0940 (Wiz, 2026-11-23).

Huntback reads an exposed ARTEX console whose workspace holds a South Korean university, where the numbering also leaks onto the victim, with a local administrator account named after an intent number. Single sign-on accepted a stored password hash as the password, a Microsoft 365 password-reset bridge ignored the old password, and a password-grant token, which involves no browser and no second factor, carried Global Administrator from 18:47:53 UTC on 2026-11-16; student-style accounts were then created and licensed and a further account was made Global Administrator (Huntback, 2026-11-24). Huntback says a Conditional Access policy requiring multi-factor authentication for every user and blocking legacy and non-interactive password sign-ins would have stopped the token request, names no actor, and says its detection queries were not run against a live workspace (Huntback, 2026-11-24).

DIVD's forensic report on its own September breach says the attacker was likely using ARTEX and that ARTEX's intents are numeric job IDs included in all input and output (DIVD, 2026-11-24).

Sources: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Expel · CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations · Recorded Future Insikt Group · Wiz Research · BleepingComputer · Yonhap News Agency · Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant · Check Point Research · CERT-EU · Netzwoche (Gohack26 report) · FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (FLASH-2026-1113-001) · European Commission (midday briefing transcript) · POLITICO Brussels Playbook · Cyber Security News · The Record · Macau Business · Nextgov · Wiz Research (intent IDs) · Wiz Research (ARTEX-Harvester) · Huntback · DIVD CSIRT (forensics report by Merlon Security, v1.5)
HIGHCVE-2026-109618 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release below its train's hotfix through the management web interface, and Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces; all twenty hotfixes are out

First published 2026-10-22 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:53 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryupdated_atcvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Palo Alto's bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 (2026-11-24, labelled Informational) says exploitation of the kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against internet-exposed management interfaces, which makes the vendor itself a source for the second half of the chain Dream Research described, and lists a later hotfix in every train that fixes the kernel flaw as well as the PHP flaws.

Palo Alto Networks published bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 on 2026-11-24 at 23:10 UTC (its timeline's initial-publication entry; the page header reads 2026-11-25), titled "OSS CVEs Fixed in PAN-OS" and labelled Informational with a zero CVSS block; its exploitation-status block reads "Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet" (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-46300 is the Linux kernel flaw Dream Research chained with PHP2Shell, so the vendor now itself states exploitation of the second half of the chain that Dream Research described; CISA's catalog has listed the kernel flaw as exploited since 2026-10-28 (CISA KEV, 2026-11-25). The bulletin's FAQ says all observed exploitation targeted devices with an internet-exposed management interface, that a device on a fixed PAN-OS listed in the PHP2Shell advisory is protected, and that "The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability through an internet-exposed management interface, and we are not aware of any other exploitation method"; it still recommends upgrading to a fixed release at the next maintenance interval where management access is restricted, and upgrading immediately and restricting access where the management interface or a dataplane interface with a management profile is internet-reachable (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

The bulletin lists the first fixed build for the kernel flaw per train, two to four hotfixes after the PHP2Shell build: 12.2.4-h3; 12.1.4-h15, 12.1.7-h15, 12.1.10-h6; 11.2.4-h25, 11.2.7-h25, 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, 11.2.16-h3; 11.1.4-h40, 11.1.6-h42, 11.1.7-h14, 11.1.10-h38, 11.1.13-h18, 11.1.16-h6; 10.2.7-h41, 10.2.10-h45, 10.2.13-h29, 10.2.16-h14, 10.2.18-h15. It has no workaround section and no affected-product table and says nothing on Panorama, Prisma Access or Cloud NGFW for this flaw; its mitigation is restricting management access to trusted internal addresses (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

Sources: Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, Impact of Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP on Palo Alto Networks Products) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, revised 2026-10-23) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, revised 2026-10-24) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, revised 2026-10-25) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory record with revision history) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, revised 2026-10-27) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory record with revision history, 2026-10-27) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.26) · Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (threat brief, revised 2026-10-25) · PHP (security advisory) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, as read on 2026-10-28) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, Internet Archive copy of 2026-10-27 17:10 UTC) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.27) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.11.25) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory record with revision history, as read on 2026-10-28) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, as read on 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory record with revision history, as read on 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory, as read on 2026-10-30) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (advisory record with revision history, as read on 2026-10-30) · Dream Research (report on the chained PHP2Shell and Fragnesia exploit against PAN-OS, updated 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (threat brief, updated 2026-10-29) · Palo Alto Networks PSIRT (bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015)
HIGHCVE-2026-133323 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA2

Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier, MISA-2026-0012: an unauthenticated blind command injection in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component (CVSS 3.1 10.0) and four more flaws there, one an XML injection that can run commands (9.0); CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133303 lead the five assigned CVE ids, patch KB000129195, Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory and CISA lists all five as exploited since 2026-11-25

First published 2026-11-18 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:52 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

Accenture APEX Labs reports that the AWV flaws were exploited before Mitel's advisory and patch: web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, root within about 30 minutes, directory credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration and used against a domain controller, local logs edited, and a second organisation's server talking to the same actor since 2026-11-09. A patched server cannot be assumed clean.

Accenture APEX Labs reports that the MISA-2026-0012 flaws were exploited before Mitel published its advisory and patch. At one victim organisation it places web-shell activity before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, with high confidence, when it was still 15 November in every time zone from UTC−12 to UTC+1 and Mitel dated its advisory 16 November (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Counted from the first observed request, the actor checked the version, bypassed authentication within a minute, had two uploads accepted at 9 minutes, ran its first web-shell command as the web service account at 12 minutes, reached root between 15 and 30 minutes with system logs reset as a side effect, and at 32 minutes used the credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration to authenticate to a domain controller over LDAPS; it then filtered web-shell requests out of the local web, error and admin logs and, 20 to 23 hours in, dumped databases on a backup server and a database server and uploaded the archives over many short HTTPS sessions (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). APEX withholds how root was obtained and does not say which of the five flaws were used.

A second organisation's MiCollab server, on a 10.0-series release exposed to this advisory and to the July one, has held a persistent HTTPS channel to the same actor server since 2026-11-09, and APEX has not determined how it was compromised. APEX assesses that AI-assisted tooling operating on the actor's server drove parts of the intrusion, an inference from sampled traffic to two commercial AI API services that it says cannot show exactly how they were used, and it names no group (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Mitel's advisory is unchanged at revision 2.0 and makes no exploitation statement; BSI's revision of 2026-11-25 rates it critical and says active exploitation was reported (BSI, 2026-11-25).

Sources: Mitel (MISA-2026-0012) · Mitel (MISA-2026-0006) · CERT-FR (CERTFR-2026-AVI-1547) · BSI CERT-Bund (WID-SEC-2026-4608) · BSI CERT-Bund (WID-SEC-W-2026-4608, CSAF record revision 2) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-130382) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-130376) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-130372) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-130381) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-130384) · CISA · CISA KEV catalogue · Accenture APEX Labs
HIGHCVE-2026-103406 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-103406, Juniper Session Smart Conductor before 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3: an unauthenticated OS command injection as root through a crafted salt minion ID in the AutomatedProvisioner (CVSS 3.1 9.8) is exploited: Juniper says at least one malicious exploitation was reported to it, BSI reported exploitation and CISA listed it on 2026-11-25

First published 2026-11-26 · open finding →

Update27 Nov 2026 04:51 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-inteltitlesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

Juniper updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24 to say at least one malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 was reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it, and NCSC Switzerland rates the flaw actively exploited, names the provisioning service as the entry point and advises keeping the management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted segments and auditing the fleet list for router names the team did not create.

Juniper updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24, before CISA's listing, to say "At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT" and to urge customers to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime mitigate; the bulletin page itself could not be read, so the wording is SecurityWeek's quotation (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26). NCSC Switzerland's post of 2026-11-26 rates the flaw actively exploited and says the router ID a joining device supplies is passed unsanitised into a shell command during provisioning key setup, so that root on the Conductor exposes every managed router and its provisioning keys; it relays that Juniper lists no official workaround and advises keeping the Conductor's management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments and auditing the fleet list for router names the team did not create (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). Neither source names an actor, a victim or a count of compromised systems.

Sources: CISA · CISA KEV catalogue · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-112215) · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-112212) · BSI CERT-Bund (WID-SEC-W-2026-4234) · SecurityWeek · NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub

04Action items15 items

  • Copy the application and network logs of every self-hosted Zammad instance, then upgrade it to Zammad 7.2.3, the critical security update of 2026-11-11 that supersedes 7.2.2, and add the Remote-User header-clearing line next to X-Forwarded-User in its nginx or Apache2 configuration (the Docker images apply it automatically); a 6.5 instance that cannot be upgraded yet gets the 6.5.5 emergency fix from Zammad's new 6.5 package repository, and an older instance that cannot be upgraded goes offline.
    FindingCVE-2026-102489 +1→
  • On every instance that was internet-reachable on 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 since 2026-09-21, run DIVD's log-check script, and treat a hit, or any DEB or RPM host where code ran as the zammad account, as compromised, rotating every credential its database held (mail-channel passwords, OAuth client secrets and refresh tokens, API tokens) and revoking cloud OAuth tokens as well as isolating the host, because DIVD's forensic report shows the attacker read those tables and network isolation does not revoke tokens.
    FindingCVE-2026-102489 +1→
  • Upgrade every Juniper Session Smart Conductor, and every Session Smart Router that CISA's record and NCSC.ch also list, to 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3 (by branch) and, until then, keep its management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments, because Juniper has had at least one malicious exploitation reported to it.
    FindingCVE-2026-103406 +1→
  • Update the Ruby interpreter to 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14 on every application host, worker, CI runner and container image that runs Rails, Sinatra or other Ruby code that handles untrusted text, rebuild the images and restart the workers, because updating a gem does not fix the interpreter, Rails is exposed in its default configuration and Veria Labs' Rails exploit, announced for 25 November 2026, may be released at any time.
    FindingCVE-2026-132825→
  • Upgrade every self-managed GitLab to 19.6.1, 19.5.8 or 19.4.10 or later, or on an older branch to 19.3.10, 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12 or 18.11.15 (a self-compiled installation rebuilds Ruby 3.3.14 or 3.4.13 instead), because GitLab ships the Ruby fix as critical patch releases and Veria Labs' Rails exploit is announced.
    FindingCVE-2026-132825→
  • Upgrade every GitHub Enterprise Server appliance to 3.22.6, 3.21.11, 3.20.13 or 3.19.17, because GitHub's release of 2026-11-22 carries the Ruby fix and Rails-class exploit proofs exist.
    FindingCVE-2026-132825→
  • Update every internet-facing nginx to 1.31.10 or 1.30.8 (NGINX Plus to 37.3.1.1 or 37.0.9.1) and restart the process, because a reload does not replace the running executable, 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 leave the ssl_early_data CPU-exhaustion flaw open and five unauthenticated flaws reach code execution as the worker with Rapid7's proof of concept for one of them public.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • On every Veeam Software Appliance and Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 install the Veeam Updater package now instead of waiting for the automatic Sunday 14:00 install, and limit TCP 443 to trusted networks until then, because Veeam lists both as affected by the two HTTP/2 flaws and HTTP/2 cannot be disabled on them.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • Update Synology DSM 7.4 to 7.4.1-90080-2 or above, DSM 7.3 to 7.3.2-86009-6, DSM 7.2.2 to 7.2.2-72806-11, DSM 7.2.1 to 7.2.1-69057-14, DSM 7.1 to 7.1.1-42962-10, BeeStation OS 1.5 to 1.5.6-68000 and APM 2.0, 1.2, 1.1 and 1.0 to 2.0.2-88107 (Synology recommends 7.3.2-86009-6 or above on DSM 7.2.x), and on DSM Enterprise 1.0, where the fix is still listed as ongoing, turn HTTP/2 off under Control Panel, Network, Connectivity, because CVE-2026-123007 affects DSM with HTTP/2 enabled.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • On every MiCollab on 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier whose AWV component was reachable from outside, including through a MiVoice Border Gateway web proxy, take a forensic image first, then apply Mitel's patch KB000129195 (after moving to 10.3.0.18 where needed) and restrict external access to the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component, then reset the LDAP connector account and any Kerberoastable service accounts and rotate administrator, SIP trunk and file-share credentials, because APEX Labs found exploitation before Mitel's advisory, root within about 30 minutes and directory credentials taken from the LDAP configuration.
    FindingCVE-2026-133323 +4→
  • Take the management interface of every PA-Series and VM-Series firewall and Panorama off the internet now by restricting it to a jump box or trusted internal addresses, because Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces, and install the hotfix PAN-SA-2026-0015 lists for your maintenance release (12.2.4-h3; 12.1.4-h15, 12.1.7-h15, 12.1.10-h6; 11.2.4-h25, 11.2.7-h25, 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, 11.2.16-h3; 11.1.4-h40, 11.1.6-h42, 11.1.7-h14, 11.1.10-h38, 11.1.13-h18, 11.1.16-h6; 10.2.7-h41, 10.2.10-h45, 10.2.13-h29, 10.2.16-h14, 10.2.18-h15), which includes the PHP2Shell fix and fixes the kernel flaw as well.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +2→
  • Rotate the directory bind account, HA replication keys, certificate private keys and device authentication keys of every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama that was reachable from the internet while unpatched and shows a PHP web shell or a tunnel, because the chain Dream Research recovered harvested exactly those from rooted firewalls, and the hotfix does not remove a web shell or tunnel already in place.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +2→
  • On every Linux host that serves NFS (nfsd loaded, NFSv4.1 or 4.2 on, TCP 2049 listening on a non-loopback address), limit TCP 2049 to the storage network now, where clients do not need NFSv4.1 and 4.2 set vers4.1=n and vers4.2=n in /etc/nfs.conf and restart nfs-server, then install the first kernel your distribution ships for CVE-2026-99362 and reboot, because Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10 list no fixed kernel on 2026-11-27 and OpenSec says one unauthenticated connection reaches a root shell.
    FindingCVE-2026-99362→
  • Inventory every Windows endpoint that installed or updated Q-Dir or DesktopOK since 2026-10-28, compare each installer's SHA-256 with the value on SoftwareOK's download page, and isolate any host with a bundled Python interpreter under ProgramData or a scheduled task that runs one, treating its credentials as stolen, because ASEC says simply uninstalling and reinstalling the program may not remove a Python RAT already installed.
    FindingSoftwareOK Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers carried a…→
  • Upgrade every Puppet Enterprise server to 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 or 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core to 9.1.3 or 8.22.2, OpenVox Agent to 9.3.0 or 8.32.0 and OpenVox Server to 9.2.0 or 8.18.0; open-source Puppet gets no fix) and, until the upgrade is in, stop the CA from autosigning certificate requests without strong verification and audit the certificates it issued for names nobody enrolled or that collide with an existing node name, because CISA lists the deserialization flaw as exploited, any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate reaches code execution on the server and a colliding name authenticates as another host.
    FindingCVE-2026-115731 +1→
Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-27T0355Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 2 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

  • Coverage window: standard, gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-26T0356Z-intel, window 26 h; no catch-up. Open backlog rows: none. KEV sweep: catalogue 2026.11.25 has no addition in the window (kev-window.txt), no RANSOMWARE rows. Closed-source drops: none.
  • New entries (2): NFS2ROOT CVE-2026-99362 (notable; the PD-11(b) own-mechanics limb: one-connection path to root on a kernel service, public fix text, distribution kernels unfixed on Ubuntu and RHEL 9 and 10; exploit private, no exploitation) and the SoftwareOK Q-Dir and DesktopOK tampered installers (notable; single source, ASEC; the update-path claim is ASEC's own hedge).
  • Changelog records (9, all update): Fragnesia (PAN-SA-2026-0015: the vendor's own statement of exploitation and later fixed builds, added after verifier iteration 1), Mitel MiCollab (Accenture APEX Labs: exploitation before the advisory; BSI's revised rating), PAN-OS (PAN-SA-2026-0015: vendor-confirmed exploitation of the kernel flaw and later hotfixes), nginx (new CPU-exhaustion fix, Veeam appliances, GitLab), Ruby (GitHub Enterprise Server and GitLab backports, Veria exploit not found), Juniper (vendor-confirmed exploitation, NCSC.ch advice), ARTEX (intent-ID numbering hunt pivot, Wiz, Huntback), Zammad (DIVD forensic report) and the Puppet entry (Huntback decoy capture, retyped from improvement after verifier iteration 1 because it is a new in-the-wild observation).
  • Contradiction: DIVD's "19 hours" and the forensic report's first look at 7 h 21 min after the alert measure different things (formal response, volunteer's first look); the Zammad entry's 2026-11-27 update section quotes both statements in a Contradiction paragraph and gives the report's containment time. The Veria Labs table lists GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 as unfixed while GitHub's release notes of 2026-11-22 carry the Ruby fix; the Ruby entry reports both. The kernel CVE announcement lists four fixed branches and the updated record eight; the NFS2ROOT entry says which.
  • borderline-drop: Basel-Stadt data-protection commissioner's directive on the canton's cloud VPN and web proxy (S2, S4), the previous fire (2026-11-26T0356Z-intel) judged the same item a privacy ruling on one canton's project with no obligation change for the constituency and no defender-side consequence; the primary is dated 2026-11-18/19, outside the window, and only trade-press relays are new, so it stays dropped; an entry written during this fire was deleted before commit.
  • borderline-drop: Planet IC municipal hosting provider (S4), no vector, actor, technique, product or Swiss party; only outages are stated for the municipal sites, and a generic supplier check rests on inference; incident floor.
  • borderline-drop: SpecterOps GitHub branch protection and Entra federated credentials (S3), lab scenario with a graph-derived claim, a vendor pitch, no detection content and a Microsoft preview feature underneath.
  • borderline-drop: Cacti Core 1.2.31 "4HTTP2ROOT" (S1), single watchTowr source, the guest account must be enabled, no CVE or fix to track, no exploitation; NoisyTCP CVE-2026-99288 (S1), remote kernel panic only, disclosed 2026-11-15, distribution patch cycle; OTRS OSA-2026-19 CVE-2026-93584 (S1), needs the optional Survey component, no exploitation or proof of concept; GPGME CVE-2026-129975 (S3), dropped by the previous fire for the same reasons, still no exploitation or public proof of concept; Exim 4.100.2 EXIM-Security-2026-11-82.1 (S3), vendor-rated Medium, no CVE id, no proof of concept.
  • borderline-drop: BSI warning on agentic offensive frameworks (S2), corroborates covered ground (BACS entry of 2026-11-25, the ARTEX entry), no new technique or action; FIFA data theft (S2, S4) and Planzer shipment-data theft (S2, S4), private Swiss organisations, no access vector or behaviour (FIFA's impersonation claim rests on anonymous sources), the same call as Erowa and Gleis D; CIA, ODNI and NGA intrusion (S4), anonymous sourcing, no vector or actor, dropped by the previous fire; Tokyo "Akachan First" voucher codes (S4), Japan, no Swiss nexus, cause not established; Numa agent against a Ukrainian municipal platform (S3), out of nexus, single source, the lesson is already in the BabidiGhost entry.
  • Single-source: SoftwareOK (ASEC; single-source, B2); the Mitel update (Accenture APEX Labs, one victim's incident-response evidence, flaws not mapped); the Puppet decoy capture (Huntback). Reduced confidence: none beyond these.
  • Candidate sources: opensec-blog and accenture-apex-labs added (each the primary for a published item). Not added: dragos-blog, otrs-security-advisories, steigerlegal-ch, dnip-ch, nordkurier-mv, hacksnack-ch, because no published item rests on them (dnip-ch rests on anonymous sources).
  • Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records attempted (S1 14, S2 7). Rotation slices excluded 17 records that a fire of the previous two days had attempted (S4's breaches pool was exhausted by it, so S4 ran five records and spent the rest on discovery).
  • Coverage gaps: juniper-support-portal (script-rendered shell, bulletin unread); f5-k-articles (shell, no score for CVE-2026-132779); databreaches-net (article bodies 403, feed only); lab52 (no post since 2026-10-05); znuny advisories ZSA-2026-17 to -43 (HTTP 500); NYT and Reuters pages (challenge shells); Linbell release PDFs (403). baselland-ch served its 2026-11-18 release through extract this fire although its record says 403.
  • Recipe notes for the next audit: watchtowr's labs feed under-collects, extract https://watchtowr.com/intelligence/ lists the FAQ and rapid-reaction pages newest first (NFS2ROOT and the Cacti item came only from there); bsi-rss returns raw XML; Netzwoche bodies read through url --direct; standard-mode WebSearch returned only 2018 FIFA coverage for the 2026-11-26 incident, extended mode found the in-window articles.
  • Entry-size debt left for the audit: the Zammad entry's main analysis is 1,030 words (limit 550, 1,068 before this fire), the PAN-OS entry 541 and the Mitel entry 538 after trims; the Zammad entry needs a rewrite to the bound. The summary fields of the ARTEX, nginx, Zammad, PAN-OS and Mitel entries have also grown past the one-to-three-sentence contract through successive fires' records; trimming them is left for the audit as improvement records. The Puppet release-notes citation date of 2026-11-12 predates this run and the page says only "Released November 2026"; left for the audit.
  • Source health: 345 of 345 records probed, 341 relevant. UNSOLVED: sans-isc (the container's egress now receives SANS's Access Restricted page and the feed path returns the home page to every transport, so a transport block; user-agent rotation against it was declined) and bfv-verfassungsschutz-de (the intermittent in-container TLS drop recorded on 2026-10-31); both stay, with notes, and neither is demoted.
  • Watchlist: none configured.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-26
item.description:
• Juniper Session Smart Conductor: unauthenticated root command injection exploited; upgrade to 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3. CISA added CVE-2026-103406 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25, after BSI revised its advisory to say the flaw is being exploited. ENISA's record, which carries Juniper's own description, calls it an OS command injection in the AutomatedProvisioner of Session Smart Conductor that lets a remote attacker run commands as root through a crafted salt minion ID (CVSS 3.1 9.8, no privileges or user interaction), with the affected ranges ending at 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3. Juniper's bulletin JSA112183 was updated on 2026-11-24 to say at least one malicious exploitation was reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it (the bulletin page itself could not be read); no source names an actor, victim or scale. →
  • 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected. 1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that an attacker who had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account pushed malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers: names, email addresses, identifiers, public keys, protocol parameters and tokens embedded in some emailed invitation, provisioning and account-recovery links. The attacker also copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed. 1Password says vault contents, vault keys and recovery keys were not affected and the exposed tokens need an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which it lengthened; it does not say how the account was compromised or how many customers are affected. →
  • SEPPmail 15.1.2 fixes unauthenticated GINA account takeover (9.3) and ten more flaws; update the gateway. SEPPmail's patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 fixes eleven flaws in Secure E-Mail Gateway versions before 15.1.2, led by CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over. Two more rows score 9.2 (a security-question recovery session accepted by the password-change workflows, and a hard-coded fallback secret for Large File Transfer attachments) and an unauthenticated request could reset a registered account's password without the security question. SEPPmail names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch is affected. →

TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01Juniper Session Smart Conductor: unauthenticated root command injection exploited; upgrade to 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3. CISA added CVE-2026-103406 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25, after BSI revised its advisory to say the flaw is being exploited. ENISA's record, which carries Juniper's own description, calls it an OS command injection in the AutomatedProvisioner of Session Smart Conductor that lets a remote attacker run commands as root through a crafted salt minion ID (CVSS 3.1 9.8, no privileges or user interaction), with the affected ranges ending at 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3. Juniper's bulletin JSA112183 was updated on 2026-11-24 to say at least one malicious exploitation was reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it (the bulletin page itself could not be read); no source names an actor, victim or scale. →
  2. 021Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected. 1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that an attacker who had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account pushed malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers: names, email addresses, identifiers, public keys, protocol parameters and tokens embedded in some emailed invitation, provisioning and account-recovery links. The attacker also copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed. 1Password says vault contents, vault keys and recovery keys were not affected and the exposed tokens need an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which it lengthened; it does not say how the account was compromised or how many customers are affected. →
  3. 03SEPPmail 15.1.2 fixes unauthenticated GINA account takeover (9.3) and ten more flaws; update the gateway. SEPPmail's patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 fixes eleven flaws in Secure E-Mail Gateway versions before 15.1.2, led by CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over. Two more rows score 9.2 (a security-question recovery session accepted by the password-change workflows, and a hard-coded fallback secret for Large File Transfer attachments) and an unauthenticated request could reset a registered account's password without the security question. SEPPmail names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch is affected. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 1Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 1Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 9

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

1Password: an attacker used an employee's corporate GitHub account to push malicious code to backend services that downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers, and copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system; vaults were not affected

1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that on 2026-11-19 it began investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account (1Password, 2026-11-25). The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about customers; the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed (1Password, 2026-11-25). It says the actor had stolen a token and that vault contents, the keys that protect them, account recovery keys and its apps and browser extensions were not affected (1Password, 2026-11-25).

The records taken for a subset of users, whose size is not stated, are names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, tokens embedded in certain emailed invitation, SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning, and account-recovery links, and non-secret internal metadata (1Password, 2026-11-25). Those tokens complete an invitation or recovery only together with an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which 1Password has lengthened from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters, and it says it found no evidence of account takeover with the exposed tokens; its advice to customers is caution about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery, that it will never ask for the account password or Secret Key, keeping both safe, and reporting suspicious messages to its support address (1Password, 2026-11-25). BleepingComputer adds that the harvested name and email list is useful for such phishing (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
Any organisation with 1Password accounts, since users' names, sign-in addresses and identifiers were in the copied records, and especially one using SCIM provisioning or account recovery, because tokens in those emailed links were among the data; 1Password says it notified a small number of users with pending invitations or recoveries directly (1Password, 2026-11-25).
Detection
In the identity provider's and 1Password's administrator audit records, invitation, provisioning and account-recovery events since about 2026-11-19 that no administrator or user requested; in mail-gateway logs, inbound mail that imitates 1Password invitations or recovery messages with real tenant or user details; and user reports of recovery codes nobody asked for. These checks are analysis from the data classes the post lists, which publishes no indicator.

Triage: a legitimate invitation or recovery message follows an administrator's or user's own action; one that arrives without it is the signal.

Defender takeaway
1Password's own advice covers phishing caution, never sharing the password or Secret Key and reporting suspicious messages, and BleepingComputer says it is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25); the action is to warn users about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery and to watch for unrequested provisioning events. For your own pipelines the mechanism is one employee source-control identity that could push to backend services and reach CI/CD, so require review on the deploy path and alert on pushes and workflow changes made with employee tokens.
incident26 Nov 05:04Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: 1Password · BleepingComputer

02Trending vulnerabilities2 items

NOTABLECVE-2026-130637 +10NATOA2

SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2: an unauthenticated template injection on the GINA login page can read and take over any GINA account (CVE-2026-130637, vendor score 9.3) and ten more flaws are fixed in the 2026-11-24 patch release; no exploitation or workaround stated

SEPPmail's revision history lists patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 with eleven security fixes, each marked as affecting versions before 15.1.2 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The worst is CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over, and the fix stops expanding request values as template placeholders. Two further rows score 9.2: CVE-2026-124840, where a session created by answering the security question was also accepted by the registration and settings workflows, so an attacker who knows the security answer could replace the password, and CVE-2026-124843, where a hard-coded fallback secret was used if the appliance's key material could not be loaded, which could let encrypted Large File Transfer attachments be decrypted outside the appliance (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

The remaining rows are CVE-2026-124844 (8.7), unauthenticated GINA uploads that were never removed and could fill the disk; CVE-2026-124838 (8.5), a configuration-service socket open to every local user; CVE-2026-124842 (8.3), an unauthenticated GINA request that reset the password of a registered account without the security question; CVE-2026-124839 (7.7), a crafted GINA account address that reached a shell command in a maintenance script at start, with elevated privileges; and four rows at 6.9 to 6.3 covering unescaped LDAP filter values (CVE-2026-124841, CVE-2026-124836), a crafted DKIM signature that injects forged Authentication-Results later covered by the gateway's ARC seal (CVE-2026-124837) and a GINA domain lookup that falls back to the default domain settings (CVE-2026-124845) (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch, whose last release is 15.0.7, is affected.

Exposure
A SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2 whose GINA web interface is reachable from outside; the revision history says release 15.1.0 added support for restricting the file types that external communication partners can upload through GINA, which shows external recipients use it (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page does not state the CVSS vector of any score.
Detection
In GINA web access logs, login-page requests whose parameters carry template placeholder syntax, unauthenticated password-reset requests for accounts that are already registered, calls to the registration and settings workflows that follow a security-question recovery, and bursts of unauthenticated uploads; in the gateway's audit log, GINA password changes without the usual recovery sequence. The fixes do not undo an account already taken over, so review GINA password-change and sign-in history for the period before the update. These checks follow from the mechanisms the vendor names; the page publishes no indicator.

Triage: an unauthenticated password reset on a GINA account that is not yet registered is legitimate, since the fix keeps it for unregistered accounts only; the same request taking effect on an already registered account without the security-question step is the abuse (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

Defender takeaway
Update every gateway on 15.1 to 15.1.2 and, for gateways on the 15.0 branch, ask SEPPmail whether these flaws apply, since the page does not say; where GINA is internet-facing, give the update priority within the regular cycle, because the template injection and the unauthenticated reset need no login, and review GINA account changes made before the update.

Builds on: 2026-11-05/seppmail-gateway-15-1-1-unauth-root-rce-and-file-access

vulnerability26 Nov 05:04Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: SEPPmail revision history
HIGHCVE-2026-103406 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-103406, Juniper Session Smart Conductor before 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3: an unauthenticated OS command injection as root through a crafted salt minion ID in the AutomatedProvisioner (CVSS 3.1 9.8) is exploited: Juniper says at least one malicious exploitation was reported to it, BSI reported exploitation and CISA listed it on 2026-11-25

CISA added CVE-2026-103406 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 (CISA, 2026-11-25); the catalogue record says a remote attacker could execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID and names both Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router (CISA KEV catalogue, 2026-11-25). BSI had revised its advisory on 2026-11-24 (23:00 UTC) with the summary "CVE-2026-103406 is being exploited" (translated from German), without stating its basis (BSI, 2026-11-24). Juniper itself updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24 to say that at least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to its security response team, as SecurityWeek quotes it (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26), and NCSC Switzerland rates the flaw actively exploited (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). No source names an actor, a victim or the number of compromised systems, and the only first-exploitation date, ENISA's exploited-since field of 2026-11-25, follows the catalogue listing (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28).

ENISA's record, which carries Juniper's description, narrows the flaw to the AutomatedProvisioner of Session Smart Conductor: an improper neutralization of special elements lets a remote attacker execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 with network access, no privileges and no user interaction (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28). The affected ranges are Conductor before 7.0.5, from 7.1.0 before 7.1.7 and from 7.2.0 before 7.2.3, so 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 are the first fixed releases (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28). The record references Juniper's bulletin JSA112183, which could not be read, and its CVE record was published on 2026-10-28. The same release fixes CVE-2026-103409 in the Session Smart Router, an unauthenticated flaw scored 9.8 that can be exploited only before the device is onboarded to Mist or a Conductor (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A Session Smart Conductor on a release below 7.0.5, 7.1.7 or 7.2.3 that a network attacker can reach; NCSC Switzerland names network access to the Conductor's provisioning service (the AutomatedProvisioner) as the prerequisite, with no authentication or user interaction, and no source gives the port or says whether it is on by default (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). CISA's catalogue record and NCSC.ch also name Session Smart Router, and SecurityWeek lists 7.2.3, 7.1.7 and 7.0.5 for both products (CISA KEV catalogue, 2026-11-25; SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26), so read the running release on each Conductor and each Router and compare it with the three fixed releases.
Detection
Process-creation events showing a shell or interpreter started as root by the Conductor's provisioning or salt services, minion or router registration events whose ID contains shell metacharacters or command-substitution syntax, and the Conductor's audit and configuration-change records; these follow from the mechanism ENISA relays, and no source publishes an indicator. Upgrading does not remove an attacker who is already in, so a Conductor that was reachable before the upgrade needs a check for accounts, router registrations and configuration pushed from it that nobody made; NCSC Switzerland's check is the fleet list, for router names the team did not create (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade every Conductor to a fixed release now rather than at the next cycle, since Juniper, CISA and BSI report exploitation of an unauthenticated root command injection; until then, NCSC Switzerland advises keeping the Conductor's management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26), because the flaw needs only network access.
Update27 Nov 2026 04:51 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-inteltitlesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

Juniper updated its bulletin JSA112183 on 2026-11-24, before CISA's listing, to say "At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT" and to urge customers to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime mitigate; the bulletin page itself could not be read, so the wording is SecurityWeek's quotation (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-26). NCSC Switzerland's post of 2026-11-26 rates the flaw actively exploited and says the router ID a joining device supplies is passed unsanitised into a shell command during provisioning key setup, so that root on the Conductor exposes every managed router and its provisioning keys; it relays that Juniper lists no official workaround and advises keeping the Conductor's management and provisioning interfaces off untrusted network segments and auditing the fleet list for router names the team did not create (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-26). Neither source names an actor, a victim or a count of compromised systems.

03Research, reports & policy1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

Okta Threat Intelligence: AI agents register on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations with disposable addresses from the mail.tm service, whose single rotating mailbox domain makes blocklists very likely stop matching within weeks; ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode each picked it at run time

Okta Threat Intelligence reports that since June 2026, and at scale through October and November, AI agents have registered accounts with disposable email addresses on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations that allow public self-service registration, activity Okta calls almost certainly malicious and that customers often reported alongside attacks on their applications (Okta, 2026-11-23). The addresses mostly belong to the mail.tm family, a free receive-only service whose API needs no account or key and lets a script create a mailbox, obtain a token and poll for one-time codes (Okta, 2026-11-23). In tests by the P0 Labs team of Permiso, which Okta acquired on 2026-08-26 (Okta, 2026-07-30), the ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode frameworks each picked mail.tm at run time, and in a data set containing attacker tooling mail.tm appeared on 80 percent of the attacker hosts where disposable email was found (Okta, 2026-11-23).

mail.tm exposes only one active mailbox domain at a time and replaces it periodically, so a blocklist built from earlier domains will very likely stop matching within weeks; Okta's Auth0 telemetry shows sign-ups tracking the domain the API currently returns, and the attackers' domain changed around 2026-10-30 when the API response did. Agents also used mailinator, guerrillamail and emailnator, and at one target an agent moved to another provider when blocked, which Okta reads as agents treating disposable mail as an interchangeable capability. Okta says the use always occurred within a short window of other agentic reconnaissance and intrusion attempts against the same entities (Okta, 2026-11-23). Bot detection and CAPTCHA generally stopped the October mail.tm sign-ups before email verification, but Okta warns agents can solve challenges and commonly register by calling the Auth0 Authentication API directly, which can skip protections applied in Universal Login (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
An Auth0 tenant or Okta organization that allows public self-service registration. For workforce users Okta says self-service registration is a prerequisite for many of the attacks it describes and should be disabled or restricted (Okta, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In identity-provider registration telemetry, sign-up events whose email domain belongs to a disposable provider's currently active mailbox domain, kept current by polling the provider's public domain endpoint instead of a static list, as Okta advises (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Triage: the discriminator Okta supports is context: a disposable-domain sign-up read alongside other agentic reconnaissance or intrusion attempts against the same entities, not the domain alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Defender takeaway
On Auth0, block sign-ups through the API while allowing Universal Login and block disposable domains with Actions; on Okta Workforce Identity, disable or restrict self-service registration. Treat a disposable-domain sign-up as a prompt to look for other agentic activity against the same estate, since Okta says it gives a heads-up to look for successful intrusion attempts, and do not rely on CAPTCHA alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Builds on: 2026-10-22/artex-storm-0940-agentic-llm-pentest-spraying-oauth-abuse · 2026-11-15/artex-aws-cloudwatch-log-secret-hunting-cognito-self-signup · 2026-11-14/cyberstrikeai-aws-cloudtrail-intrusion-one-source-ip · 2026-11-18/barracuda-cloud-intrusion-vendor-held-key-artex-consistent · 2026-11-25/unit42-agentic-ai-attackers-web-shell-footholds
