Palo Alto Networks lists PAN-OS and Panorama with HTTP/2 enabled as affected, Veeam lists its 13.1 Software and Infrastructure Appliances (fixed through Veeam Updater), Cisco lists Catalyst Center, Identity Services Engine 3.5, Nexus 3000 and 9000 in standalone NX-OS mode, UCS Director and about 20 other products with fixes dated November 2026 to March 2027 or still to be determined, Siemens and Synology list products with fixes pending or none, and Fortinet confirms FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiMail, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiADC, FortiWeb and FortiSIEM not impacted while 29 product names, FortiAuthenticator among them, remain under investigation. →
  3. 03Cyderes: 'tcherber' VPN toolkit for FortiGate and SonicWall, credential file mixing default and real logins, LDAP sweep. Cyderes' Howler Cell recovered a Go toolkit that wraps OpenConnect for FortiGate and NetExtender for SonicWall, a credential file of more than 500 FortiGate entries mixing default guest, admin and test logins with organisation-specific passwords, and VPN connection logs showing sustained root-level tunnels into multiple victim environments in May and June 2026. Once the tunnel is up the orchestrator maps internal routes and enumerates Active Directory over LDAP, while port scanning, SMB reconnaissance and credential validation are manual tools. Cyderes assesses a Russian-speaking initial access broker and malware-as-a-service seller and names no victim, vulnerability or firmware version. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 2Trending vulnerabilities 4Updates to prior coverage 8Action items 18

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures2 items

NOTABLENATOB2

tcherber: Cyderes finds an access broker's Go toolkit with VPN clients for FortiGate and SonicWall that, once a tunnel is up, maps internal routes and sweeps Active Directory over LDAP; a credential file mixes default guest, admin and test logins with organisation-specific passwords (more than 500 FortiGate entries) and connection logs show root-level tunnels into multiple victims in May and June 2026

Cyderes' Howler Cell identified a database holding more than 500 FortiGate VPN credential entries and VPN connection records showing successful root-level tunnels into multiple victim environments during May and June 2026 (Cyderes, 2026-11-17). The recovered Go toolkit wraps OpenConnect with --protocol=fortinet for FortiGate, with a 30-second reconnect loop that keeps the tunnel up, and NetExtender for SonicWall, whose wrapper probes seven login URL paths and ten page patterns to find the authentication domain (Cyderes, 2026-11-17). The credential file mixes default guest, admin and test logins with organisation-specific passwords, which Cyderes reads as both brute-force harvesting and credential-dump sourcing; the broker's forum advert claims the access came from brute-forcing and an "exploit toolkit", which Cyderes relays without confirming (Cyderes, 2026-11-17).

The orchestrator launches the FortiGate client in the background with a 20-second stabilization delay, maps internal subnets and gateways from the established tunnel, and runs an LDAP module that enumerates users, groups, domain structure and domain controllers; port scanning, SMB reconnaissance and credential validation sit in separate tools that the operator runs by hand (Cyderes, 2026-11-17). Cyderes assesses a Russian-speaking operator working as both an initial access broker and a malware-as-a-service provider, with operations ongoing as of September 2026, and notes that the handle comes from a build-path username that one machine or several could share (Cyderes, 2026-11-17). VMRay independently links the same build path to Zer0day Stealer and ENIGMA Locker and calls the same developer the likely author of an HVNC remote-control sample, without mentioning VPN access brokerage (VMRay, 2026-09-01).

Exposure
A FortiGate or SonicWall VPN gateway reachable from the internet that accepts a VPN account with a default or guessed password, or a password that appears in a credential dump; Cyderes names no vulnerability or firmware version and does not discuss multi-factor authentication (Cyderes, 2026-11-17).
Detection
VPN gateway logs for successful logins by default-named accounts and for repeated reconnect attempts from one source about every 30 seconds, the interval of the FortiGate client's retry loop; after the tunnel is up, route parsing and a broad LDAP enumeration of users, groups and domain controllers from an address in the VPN pool follow from the toolkit's orchestrator (Cyderes, 2026-11-17).
Defender takeaway
Audit VPN credentials on FortiGate and SonicWall appliances, which is Cyderes' own recommendation, and treat default-named accounts and dumped passwords as the entry the toolkit relies on (Cyderes, 2026-11-17).
threat19 Nov 05:22Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Cyderes Howler Cell · VMRay Labs
NOTABLENATOB2

CyberPower PowerPanel Business as a SYSTEM script channel on a domain controller: Symantec traces ntds.dit extraction with ntdsutil ifm and esentutl /vss and a side-loaded implant to scripts that the UPS-management service ppbed.exe runs as SYSTEM; Symantec does not say how the console was reached and no actor is named

Symantec analysed an intrusion in which the attacker used CyberPower PowerPanel Business (PPB), software that manages UPS devices, as the execution channel on a Windows domain controller (Symantec, 2026-11-18). Scripts placed in the product's extcmd folder and staged first under temp\profile\extcmd, are run by the PPB service ppbed.exe as SYSTEM, so the commands of the chain have ppbed.exe as their ancestor and the lineage runs ppbed.exe, cmd.exe, powershell.exe and then the implant (Symantec, 2026-11-18). The attacker pushed the scripts to the PPB web service endpoint /local/rest/v1/file/upload on TCP port 3052, worked hands-on, iterating scripts until ntds.dit was exported with ntdsutil ifm and esentutl /vss, and then side-loaded the implant, an old trusted executable paired with an unknown DLL in a user-profile path (Symantec, 2026-11-18). The channel is a documented product function: CyberPower describes user-programmable command executions for event actions (CyberPower, 2026-11-19), and Symantec notes the attacker did not use power events to trigger them (Symantec, 2026-11-18).

Symantec does not say how the attacker reached the console; public advisories or stolen administrator credentials could give that access, and it names no actor, victim sector or product version (Symantec, 2026-11-18). CISA's 2024 advisory lists PowerPanel Business 4.9.0 and prior as affected by weaknesses fixed in version 4.10.1 or later, which Symantec does not cite (CISA, 2024-05-02).

Exposure
Every host that runs PPB, a domain controller above all, whose web service on TCP 3052 a hostile network or a compromised administrator account can reach; Symantec says to audit the extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd paths of every PPB host against the product defaults (Symantec, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Process-creation lineage with ppbed.exe as the ancestor of cmd.exe or powershell.exe, every script staged under extcmd, whatever its name, certutil downloads and decodes, curl downloads and powershell -ep bypass loading .NET code in memory, inbound requests to TCP 3052 from addresses that do not administer the UPS, and on a domain controller ntdsutil, esentutl and new shadow copies; an unexpected DLL next to a trusted binary in a user-profile path marks the side-loaded implant (Symantec, 2026-11-18).

Triage: the activity looks like a power-management product launching cmd.exe, which defenders may dismiss as a routine power-related recovery process; scripts or event-to-command assignments that no administrator configured, children that are not shutdown or notification routines (which follows from the mechanism) and the absence of a preceding power event separate it from benign use (Symantec, 2026-11-18).

Defender takeaway
Treat PPB hosts as privileged execution surfaces: restrict TCP port 3052 to named administrator hosts, change the default administrator password and keep PPB patched, since CISA names 4.10.1 as the fixed build for its 2024 advisory (Symantec, 2026-11-18; CISA, 2024-05-02); where the techniques Symantec lists are found, assume Active Directory credentials are exposed and plan a krbtgt reset and wider credential rotation (Symantec, 2026-11-18).
threat19 Nov 05:20Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Symantec Threat Intelligence · CISA (ICSA-24-123-01) · CyberPower (PowerPanel Business product page)

02Trending vulnerabilities4 items

HIGHCVE-2026-90817exploitedNATOB1

CVE-2026-90817, REDCap 13.3.0 up to 16.0.48 LTS, 17.3.9 LTS and 17.4.3 Standard: an unauthenticated chain from a public survey request through the Data Import controller to code execution on the server, exploited as of 2026-10-07 for cryptocurrency mining and listed by CISA; fixed in 16.0.49 LTS, 17.3.10 LTS and 17.4.4 Standard (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Securifera, which found the flaw, describes a chain of five faults in REDCap, the research-data platform from Vanderbilt University. The public survey handler checks the passthrough value in two forms, so a double-encoded value reaches the root index.php dispatcher while the route restriction is skipped; the project user-rights object is built before the respondent identity exists, so the public context receives the Data Import privilege and the POST CSRF check is skipped because NOAUTH is defined; the Data Import commit path trusts the posted file name as a local path or PHP stream; the byte-order-mark cleanup writes changed bytes back to the same stream, which turns a CSV cleanup into an arbitrary overwrite; and a compiled-template cache file is then rendered as PHP through a route that works without a login (Securifera, 2026-09-27). An attacker needs only a valid survey hash, with no account, project membership, session cookie, role or CSRF token (Securifera, 2026-09-27); Securifera's repository publishes a proof of concept (Securifera repository, 2026-10-01).

Unit 42's note of 2026-10-07 reports active exploitation: an unauthenticated POST to a public survey URL stages a transient Blade-template web shell under the temp cache, run by php-fpm with the web server's permissions, which executes a Base64 bash cradle entirely in memory and pipes a payload disguised as a JPEG into bash (Unit 42, 2026-10-07). The chain deploys Monero miners, run with randomized syslog-themed process names, with at least four live workers; persistence is a modified crontab, an RSA public key appended to the authorized_keys of every accessible profile and an edited ~/.profile, and the attackers unset HISTFILE and purge the bash history (Unit 42, 2026-10-07). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-18).

Google's GTIG reported in June 2026 that the PRC-nexus cluster UNC6508 had exploited internet-facing REDCap servers of North American academic and medical organisations (Google GTIG, 2026-06-15). REDCap 13.3.0 through 16.0.48 LTS, 17.3.9 LTS and 17.4.3 Standard are vulnerable (Pentest-Tools, 2026-10-23); the CVE record names 16.0.49 LTS, 17.3.10 LTS and 17.4.4 Standard as the upgrade targets (OpenCVE, 2026-09-20).

Exposure
Any REDCap server from 13.3.0 to the builds above that serves a public survey; the attack needs a valid survey hash (Securifera, 2026-09-27).
Detection
Web access logs for POSTs to public survey URLs with a double percent-encoded passthrough and a Data Import route (Unit 42, 2026-10-07) and, where a WAF or proxy logs request bodies, a php:// stream in the file-name field (Securifera, 2026-09-27); transient Blade-template files under the web temp cache, a web-server worker or php-fpm spawning bash, and miner processes started under syslog-style names (Unit 42, 2026-10-07). Securifera's proof of concept deletes its injected cache so that REDCap regenerates a clean copy, so a clean cache does not prove the server was not hit (Securifera, 2026-09-27).

Triage: the survey flow is supposed to allow only the PDF route (PdfController:index), so a public survey request that reaches the Data Import controller or carries a stream wrapper in the file-name field is not benign (Securifera, 2026-09-27).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade now and check crontabs, authorized_keys, ~/.profile and processes on any server that was reachable on an older build, because an upgrade removes none of the persistence Unit 42 lists (Unit 42, 2026-10-07).

Builds on: 2026-06-16/prc-unc6508-ran-year-plus-espionage-through-internet-facing

vulnerability19 Nov 05:14Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Securifera (discoverer) · Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (timely threat intel) · CISA · Securifera proof-of-concept repository · OpenCVE (carries the CNA record text) · Pentest-Tools · Google GTIG
HIGHCVE-2026-123007 +10updatedNATOA1

NGINX nginx2root: five unauthenticated memory-corruption flaws (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 in HTTP/2, CVE-2026-121810 in HTTP/3, CVE-2026-123634 in the resolver, CVE-2026-113425 in the mail proxy) can lead to code execution as the worker process; fixed in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 and NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1, Rapid7 proof of concept public, no exploitation reported (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

F5 and the nginx project published the nginx2root fixes (nginx.org, 2026-11-18); CERT-EU counts five vulnerabilities, all able to lead to unauthenticated code execution with the privileges of the NGINX worker process (CERT-EU, 2026-11-18). CVE-2026-123007 is an HTTP/2 flow-control overflow: cancelling queued response data makes nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response (Rapid7, 2026-11-18), and Wiz demonstrated code execution on nginx serving ordinary static files (Wiz Research, 2026-11-18).

Rapid7 published a working proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007 against nginx 1.31.8; the exploit needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic and likely fails with concurrent clients (Rapid7, 2026-11-18; Rapid7 repository, 2026-11-18). CERT-EU reports no exploitation in the wild and NCSC.ch rates exploitation unknown with a proof of concept available (CERT-EU, 2026-11-18; NCSC.ch, 2026-11-18).

The memory-corruption fixes are in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 (nginx.org, 2026-11-18); nginx 1.31.10 and 1.30.8 of 2026-11-23 add a fix for CPU exhaustion when ssl_early_data is on (CVE-2026-132779, affecting 1.21.4 to 1.31.9 per nginx.org, 2026-11-27), as do NGINX Plus 37.3.1.1 and 37.0.9.1 (nginx.org, 2026-11-23; nginx.org, 2026-11-23; F5 NGINX Plus release notes, 2026-11-23). CERT.at lists NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 as fixing four of the five (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-113425); it also says 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1 already carry the fix for CVE-2026-123633 but stay affected by CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-121810, and NGINX Plus R33 to R36 have no update (translated from German) (CERT.at, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
An nginx build from the first affected release of each flaw (1.9.5, 1.19.7, 0.6.18, 1.25.0 and 0.5.33) up to 1.31.8 whose configuration uses the feature: an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 listener, the resolver with variable proxy_pass destinations plus mirror or SSI, or the mail proxy with auth_http (nginx.org, 2026-11-18; Xint, 2026-11-18). A distribution backport can fix a flaw without changing the version nginx -v reports (Xint, 2026-11-18). Veeam Software Appliance and Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 are affected by the two HTTP/2 flaws and cannot disable HTTP/2; Veeam ships the fix through Veeam Updater (Veeam, 2026-11-25). GitLab's Linux package and Docker images carry nginx 1.31.9 from 19.6.2, 19.5.9 and 19.4.11 (GitLab, 2026-11-25).
Detection
Process-creation or audit telemetry for any program started by the worker's user, since a normal nginx worker runs no external programs and that is the clearest sign of success; worker exits and core dumps in the error log mark attempts, not successes (Xint, 2026-11-18; CERT-EU, 2026-11-18).

Triage: a large upload is a legitimate cause of an inbound-heavy connection and workers crash for unrelated reasons, so a program started by the worker is the discriminator, not the traffic shape alone (Xint, 2026-11-18).

Defender takeaway
Update and restart nginx, because a configuration reload does not replace the running executable; disabling HTTP/2 on exposed listeners blocks only the two HTTP/2 flaws (Xint, 2026-11-18) and, if it stays on elsewhere, leaves connection pressure (Unit 42, 2026-11-24), and Xint gives interim measures for the others: a fixed upstream group in place of request-time DNS lookups for CVE-2026-123634, no QUIC listeners for CVE-2026-121810 and bound or firewalled mail listeners for CVE-2026-113425 (Xint, 2026-11-18). An empty execution-audit result after the update cannot rule out an earlier compromise, and Xint chained CVE-2026-123007 with a separate Linux kernel SCTP flaw, unpatched when it published, to reach root on the host and escape a Docker container; hosts that do not use SCTP can block the module from loading (Xint, 2026-11-18).
Update21 Nov 2026 04:37 UTCrun 2026-11-21T0355Z-intelsummaryaffected_productsentitiessourcesevidenceactionsbody

Palo Alto Networks lists PAN-OS and Panorama (virtual and M-Series) as affected by CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 only where the HTTP/2 option is enabled, and says it knows of no malicious exploitation; disabling HTTP/2 is its workaround (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-11-20). The fixed builds are PAN-OS 12.2.4-h3, 12.1.10-h6 and 11.2.16-h3; 12.1.7-h15, 11.2.10-h19 and 11.2.13-h6 carry an ETA of 2026-11-23, and 12.1.2 to 12.1.4 and 11.2.0 to 11.2.7 need no action (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-11-20).

CVE-2026-19707, Airlock Gateway 8.5.0 to 8.5.2 and 8.6.0: attacker-controlled HTML in a backend response overflows a buffer in the Smart Form Protection feature and can cause denial of service or code execution on the gateway; fixed in 8.5.3 and 8.6.1, no exploitation reported (CVSS 4.0 9.5)

Airlock (Ergon) published CVE-2026-19707 on 2026-11-18 as the CNA. It says attacker-controlled HTML in a backend response can exploit the Smart Form Protection feature of Airlock Gateway 8.5.2 and earlier and 8.6.0, possibly leading to a denial of service or remote code execution against the gateway, and that the issue is fixed in 8.5.3 and 8.6.1 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18). The attack needs Smart Form Protection, or the corresponding expert settings, enabled on a mapping whose backend returns a response containing certain multi-byte HTML character references, and the overflow happens while the gateway parses that response; the response can come from a malicious or compromised backend or from a trusted backend that returns attacker-supplied HTML, for example an application that stores and serves user-provided HTML files (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18). The record scores CVSS 4.0 9.5 with high attack complexity and says that compromising the gateway could also affect the availability and protection of other backends deployed behind it (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18). Airlock's release notes for 8.6.1 and 8.5.3 list a fix for a buffer overflow when decoding HTML entities in the same releases, without a CVE id (Airlock documentation, 2026-11-19; Airlock documentation, 2026-11-19). Airlock's support table shows 8.5 supported until 06/2027, 8.4 past its end of support in 08/2026 and 8.3 no longer supported (Airlock documentation, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
Airlock Gateway 8.5.0 to 8.5.2 or 8.6.0 with Smart Form Protection enabled, which Airlock's documentation says requires URL encryption to be activated first, on a mapping whose backend can return attacker-supplied HTML (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18; Airlock documentation, 2026-11-19). Gateways on 8.4 and older are outside support and have no listed fix.
Detection
The record names no indicator; gateway process crashes or restarts and unexpected child processes on the gateway, and backend responses with unusual multi-byte HTML character references, follow from the mechanism (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
Update to 8.5.3 or 8.6.1, backends that serve user-supplied HTML behind a gateway with Smart Form Protection first; no source reports exploitation, so the order follows exposure rather than a known campaign (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-18).

CVE-2026-131914, Idunno.AntiCsrf 0.9.1 and earlier, a defunct anti-CSRF module for ASP.NET WebForms: one unauthenticated POST with a crafted CSRF form field is deserialized without validation and runs code in the IIS worker process; Mandiant observed exploitation in the wild and no patch exists, so the module has to be removed (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

Mandiant published advisory MNDT-2026-0048 and CVE-2026-131914 on 2026-11-18 for Idunno.AntiCsrf, a defunct open-source anti-CSRF HTTP module for ASP.NET WebForms, last released as 0.9.1 Beta in December 2008 on the since-retired CodePlex platform and with no active maintainer or official patch (Mandiant, 2026-11-18). In the module's PreRequestHandlerExecute step, once the CSRF cookie and the CSRF form field are both non-empty, it deserializes the form field with a parameterless ObjectStateFormatter, which performs no MAC, signature, encryption or machineKey validation and enforces no SerializationBinder restrictions, so a crafted serialized .NET object in that field runs code in the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe; one POST with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token suffices (Mandiant, 2026-11-18).

The module runs before the page lifecycle, so any anonymously reachable .aspx page, or any page that relies on application-level session checks inside Page_Load, is reachable unless it opts out through ISuppressCsrfCheck or the SuppressCsrfCheck attribute; pipeline-level authentication rules run earlier and keep anonymous requests away from pages they protect (Mandiant, 2026-11-18). After the sink the module raises its own error, so the response is HTTP 302 when customErrors is active and HTTP 500 when its mode is Off, and recompiled or customised copies keep the sink under different file hashes (Mandiant, 2026-11-18). Mandiant states that active exploitation in the wild has been observed, names no actor, and says Google's FLARE team completed the root-cause analysis during an incident-response investigation on 2026-11-04 (Mandiant, 2026-11-18); the ENISA record scores the flaw CVSS 4.0 9.3 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
An ASP.NET WebForms application whose Web.config registers Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule under httpModules or modules, or whose bin directory holds Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll; Mandiant says to search by name, not by hash (Mandiant, 2026-11-18).
Detection
IIS logs for anomalous POST requests to .aspx endpoints that return 302 or 500 with elevated request size (cs-bytes, where logged), carrying the module's default cookie __CSRFCOOKIE and form field __CSRFTOKEN, and process-creation telemetry for children of w3wp.exe, which follows from code execution in the worker; if the csrfSettings section is omitted from Web.config, a setter bug overwrites the fallback form field name with RaiseException, so the default field name is not a reliable hunting key on every deployment (Mandiant, 2026-11-18).

Triage: the module's own tokens are a GUID cookie and a short serialized GUID in the form field, so a cookie that is not a GUID, or a large Base64 value in the CSRF form field, is not legitimate token traffic (Mandiant, 2026-11-18).

Defender takeaway
Remove the module and its DLL and replace it with a supported anti-forgery mechanism, since no patch exists; on environments with evidence of exploitation, Mandiant says to rotate all secrets stored in Web.config and applicationHost.config, machineKey and encryption keys and database credentials included, and to inspect the web roots for unauthorized files (Mandiant, 2026-11-18).

CISA added CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18, naming neither Confluence nor N-able N-central, and Apache's announcement says authentication handlers configured on a service do not protect against the fault and recommends migrating off the end-of-life Axis 1.

CISA added CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18 on evidence of active exploitation, naming neither Confluence nor N-able N-central and no actor; the exploitation reported so far is against N-able N-central, not Confluence (CISA, 2026-11-18). Apache's announcement adds that the fault is parsed while the engine resolves the target service, before any per-service handler chain runs, so authentication handlers configured on a service do not protect against it, and recommends migrating from the end-of-life Axis 1 to a different SOAP engine such as Apache Axis 2/Java (Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06). Atlassian's advisory is unchanged and still says it cannot confirm whether instances were affected (Atlassian, 2026-11-09).

Sources: Atlassian (security advisory CVE-2026-90436) · BSI CERT-Bund (WID-SEC-2026-4427) · Apache Axis project (via oss-security) · Huntback · Previdian · BleepingComputer · CISA · Apache Axis project (announcement thread)

Obsidian Security: a three-CVE chain turns any LiteLLM user into root on the AI gateway; CISA lists the guardrail sandbox escape CVE-2026-40217 as exploited

First published 2026-06-16 · open finding →

Update19 Nov 2026 05:04 UTCrun 2026-11-19T0355Z-intelactionsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquesaffected_productstitleverificationconfidenceevent_date

CISA added the LiteLLM guardrail sandbox escape CVE-2026-40217, the last step of Obsidian Security's chain, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18; LiteLLM's own advisory now supplies the description, the proxy-admin prerequisite, the CVSS 4.0 5.9 score and the endpoint block.

CISA added CVE-2026-40217 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-18). LiteLLM's own advisory describes the flaw as a sandbox escape using bytecode-level techniques at POST /guardrails/test_custom_code that gives code execution in the proxy process, root in the default Docker image, requires a proxy-admin credential in default configurations, rates it Moderate at CVSS 4.0 5.9 and offers blocking the endpoint at the reverse proxy as the workaround; it names 1.83.11 as the fix in its text and 1.83.10 in its patched-versions field (LiteLLM advisory, 2026-05-07). v1.83.14-stable remains the fix for the whole chain.

Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938, OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and Oracle Java SE on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI: a heap overflow in the Base64 decoder that Calif chains into pre-authentication code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate; fixed in 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, GreyNoise reports exploitation attempts, none confirmed successful against its sensors (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

GreyNoise reports exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-114938 as of 2026-11-18, none confirmed successful against its sensors, and VulnCheck says a working RCE exploit is available to its customers; Cisco lists 13 products as affected with fixed releases still to be determined, Fortinet is still investigating, BACS's warning adds internal systems and supplier clarification, and Tenable says Red Hat and Ubuntu had released no fix and Debian only an unstable-branch fix as of 2026-11-18, with Keycloak recommending a JVM option as the interim mitigation.

Cisco's product impact: Secure Network Analytics, Secure Workload and further products are affected, Cisco offers no workaround, and its PSIRT is aware of proof-of-concept code but not of malicious use (Cisco, 2026-11-23). Fortinet says it is investigating the impact on its products and lists none as confirmed affected, with dozens under investigation (Fortinet, 2026-11-18). Tenable relays GreyNoise's report of exploitation attempts as of 2026-11-18, none confirmed successful against its sensors, and VulnCheck's statement that a working RCE exploit is available to its customers (Tenable, 2026-11-17). BACS's warning of 2026-11-18 asks operators to prioritise internet-reachable applications and central sign-in services, to include internal systems, to clarify other Java software such as banking software with their suppliers and to have externally operated services confirm the fix, and says an update removes no compromise that has already happened (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-18). Tenable adds that as of 2026-11-18 Red Hat and Ubuntu had released no fix and Debian had fixed only its unstable branch, so hosts on those distributions had no stable vendor build yet, and that the Keycloak project recommended starting its server with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as an interim mitigation, its x86-64 container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 carrying an affected Java build (Tenable, 2026-11-17).

First published 2026-11-18 · open finding →

Update19 Nov 2026 05:02 UTCrun 2026-11-19T0355Z-intelactionsbodycvesevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitleupdated_at

Drupal published the announced core security release on 2026-11-18: SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165, Critical, installer reinstall leading to site takeover or remote code execution) and SA-CORE-2026-018 (CVE-2026-132166, not directly exploitable), fixed in 11.4.13, 11.3.22 and 10.6.22. No exploitation is reported.

The release the pre-announcement described is out. Drupal published SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165, Critical 18 of 25) and SA-CORE-2026-018 (CVE-2026-132166, Moderately critical 14 of 25, not directly exploitable) on 2026-11-18, fixed in Drupal 11.4.13, 11.3.22 and 10.6.22 (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18, Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18). SA-CORE-2026-017 says an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, which can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the only workaround is to secure the installer (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18). The 18 of 25 rating in the pre-announcement is SA-CORE-2026-017's; neither advisory reports exploitation.

Sources: Drupal Security Team (PSA-2026-11-16) · NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub · Drupal Security Team (SA-CORE-2026-017) · Drupal Security Team (SA-CORE-2026-018) · NCSC-NL · Drupal Security Team (SA-CORE-2026-019) · CISA · Searchlight Cyber · StepSecurity

04Action items18 items

  • List every page of your organisation's sites, and of the agencies that build them, that has loaded Optimizely project JavaScript since 2026-11-16, or Kissmetrics i.js, a StorifyMe widget or the minute-ly loader since 2026-11-13, capture the bytes the browser receives and compare them with the provider's own project content (a search for the loader's host name misses the variant that hides it in base64), and where a file carries the injected loader remove it, keep the response bytes as evidence and treat the payment, login and form pages that loaded an affected Optimizely file as exposed to card and session theft.
    FindingCVE-2026-132224→
  • If your organisation or an agency building its sites has an Optimizely Web Experimentation account, audit every Project JavaScript field for code nobody wrote and rotate the API tokens, session tokens and integration keys tied to it, because the attacker impersonated users on targeted accounts to edit that field.
    FindingCVE-2026-132224→
  • For every page that loaded an Optimizely snippet on 2026-11-16, review the card and cryptocurrency transactions made on it during Optimizely's exposure window (07:51 to 22:24 UTC; Report URI saw the first injection at 04:21 UTC) and keep the web server, CDN, WAF and payment logs that cover the day, because Optimizely says the script was meant to take card details typed into a site's own forms and cryptocurrency transfers.
    FindingCVE-2026-132224→
  • Upgrade every REDCap server to 16.0.49 LTS, 17.3.10 LTS or 17.4.4 Standard and, on any server that was internet-reachable on an older build, check for transient Blade-template files under the web temp cache, crontabs, the authorized_keys of every account, ~/.profile and Monero miner processes, treating a hit as a server compromise, because Unit 42 saw the chain used for mining with persistence that an upgrade does not remove.
    FindingCVE-2026-90817→
  • Update every internet-facing nginx to 1.31.10 or 1.30.8 (NGINX Plus to 37.3.1.1 or 37.0.9.1) and restart the process, because a reload does not replace the running executable, 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 leave the ssl_early_data CPU-exhaustion flaw open and five unauthenticated flaws reach code execution as the worker with Rapid7's proof of concept for one of them public.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • On every Veeam Software Appliance and Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 install the Veeam Updater package now instead of waiting for the automatic Sunday 14:00 install, and limit TCP 443 to trusted networks until then, because Veeam lists both as affected by the two HTTP/2 flaws and HTTP/2 cannot be disabled on them.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • Update Synology DSM 7.4 to 7.4.1-90080-2 or above, DSM 7.3 to 7.3.2-86009-6, DSM 7.2.2 to 7.2.2-72806-11, DSM 7.2.1 to 7.2.1-69057-14, DSM 7.1 to 7.1.1-42962-10, BeeStation OS 1.5 to 1.5.6-68000 and APM 2.0, 1.2, 1.1 and 1.0 to 2.0.2-88107 (Synology recommends 7.3.2-86009-6 or above on DSM 7.2.x), and on DSM Enterprise 1.0, where the fix is still listed as ongoing, turn HTTP/2 off under Control Panel, Network, Connectivity, because CVE-2026-123007 affects DSM with HTTP/2 enabled.
    FindingCVE-2026-123007 +10→
  • Update every Drupal site to 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 (a site on 11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22 is still open to the second installer flaw) and run update.php, then on any site that ran an affected build with the installer reachable check the user 1 account, the administrators and settings.php for changes nobody made, because Drupal reports both installer flaws exploited on live sites.
    FindingCVE-2026-132165 +2→
  • Update every Synology DSM to the fixed build of its branch now (7.4-90075, 7.3.2-86009-4, 7.2.2-72806-9 or 7.2.1-69057-12, and 7.2-64570-4, 7.1.1-42962-7 or 6.2.4-25556-8 on the branches for which SA-26:13 names no fix; on DSM 7.1, 7.2 and 6.2 those builds close only the SA-24:20 flaws, so also move to a branch with an SA-26:13 fix), taking the management interface of any NAS that is reachable from the internet offline first, because Synology confirms ransomware is exploiting outdated DSM, CISA lists CVE-2024-10441 as exploited and Synology lists no mitigation for the September flaws.
    FindingCVE-2026-13684 +4→
  • On every NAS that was reachable from the internet on an older build, look in its shares for files renamed to .L0CK3D and for read-me3.txt notes, and isolate any hit.
    FindingCVE-2026-13684 +4→
  • Audit every FortiGate and SonicWall VPN gateway for VPN accounts with default or guessed passwords (guest, admin, test) or passwords that appear in credential dumps, reset or remove them, and search VPN logs since May 2026 for logins by such accounts that are followed by a broad LDAP enumeration from the VPN address pool, because Cyderes found a broker's toolkit and logs showing root-level tunnels into multiple victims.
    FindingCyderes: 'tcherber' VPN toolkit for FortiGate and…→
  • On every host that runs CyberPower PowerPanel Business, domain controllers first, compare the extcmd and temp\\profile\\extcmd folders with the product defaults and compare the extcmd folders and the console's event-to-command assignments with what administrators configured and treat unknown scripts as hostile; where the techniques Symantec lists are found (ntdsutil or esentutl on a domain controller, scripts staged under extcmd that no administrator configured, a side-loaded implant), assume Active Directory credentials are exposed and plan a krbtgt reset and wider credential rotation, because Symantec saw this channel used to export ntds.dit from a domain controller.

2026-11-19T0355Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 6 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Window 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-18T0356Z-intel). Six new entries and eight changelog records, no deep dive, no critical. The will-publish set was 14 items, over the ~8 a main-agent deep read should carry, so two scoped cti-research follow-ups read the primaries and returned claim tables whose passages were grep -F checked against saved bodies: DR1 (the six new entries, 2026-11-19T04:39:20Z to 05:05:15Z) and DR2 (the eight records, 04:39:21Z to 04:58:45Z); the main agent composed every entry and record from those tables and the findings files. Stop-hook commit nudges arrived mid-run and were not acted on; the commit follows the gate and the verifier loop.

Coverage and dispositions

  • KEV sweep (work/2026-11-19T0355Z-intel/kev-window.txt): CVE-2026-90817 REDCap → new entry 2026-11-19/redcap-cve-2026-90817-unauth-survey-rce-exploited-kev (Unit 42 had reported exploitation as of 2026-10-07, so the CISA listing was not the only evidence S1 reported); CVE-2024-10441 → update on the Synology DSM entry; CVE-2026-40217 → update on the LiteLLM entry (a v2-shaped legacy record, brought to the current schema in the same record: classification, techniques, affected_products, per-CVE fixed versions; the CVE's CVSS now follows the vendor advisory, 5.9, not an unsourced 8.8); CVE-2026-90436 → update on the Confluence entry (CISA's listing and Apache's no-fix and handler statements are the reader-facing delta; an earlier draft typed it improvement and the verifier asked for update, so it moves updated_at). No RANSOMWARE rows.
  • Backlog: no open rows at the start. Two rows opened and held with named conditions: the PHP critical release pre-announced for 2026-11-19 14:00 to 14:30 UTC (expiry 2026-11-26) and the Basel-Landschaft cantonal-administration incident (no vector, actor or behaviour, so no evidence-bound technique; expiry 2026-12-03).
  • Scheduled releases: Drupal core released 2026-11-18 (update on the pre-announcement entry; priority stays notable); NGINX and F5 2026-11-18 (new entry; BIG-IP rows dropped below); Oracle CSPU and TYPO3 carried by yesterday's entries with no revision; Microsoft revisions informational; Trend Micro KA-0024802 status of 2026-11-18 (update; DR2 corrected S1: the Mobile Security for Enterprise patch is on the Download Center dated 2026-11-17 although the advisory row still shows it pending).
  • Revised advisories: HPE HPESBNW05162 revision 2 (update; the entry carried CVE-2026-79845, which revision 2 replaced with CVE-2026-95787, and the FIPS build is now in the fixed strings); Java4Shell vendor impact from Cisco and Fortinet plus the BACS warning page (update; the entry cited BACS's 2026-11-17 announcement page for a compromise-check quote that only the 2026-11-18 warning page carries, so the citation was moved); OptimJack (update; Optimizely's status entry now names the flaw).
  • Source-slice rotation: 102 sources were excluded as attempted by the previous two fires; the breach pool (S4) is small, so nine of its ten records had to be drawn from recently attempted ones, oldest cursor first.
  • Corrections to the sub-agents' findings applied at composition: S2's claim that NGINX Plus 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1 also fix CVE-2026-113425 was wrong (F5's record: only CVE-2026-123633); tcherber's orchestrator automates only the VPN connect, route parsing and LDAP enumeration, SMB reconnaissance and port scanning are manual tools; S1's list of Fortinet products as affected by Java4Shell was dropped (all are under investigation); CERT-EU states no exploitation for the nginx2root flaws, NCSC-NL only predicts it.
  • Single-source entries: Airlock Gateway (vendor CNA text via ENISA EUVD, corroborated by the vendor's release notes only), Idunno.AntiCsrf (Mandiant as CNA, sole observer of the exploitation; the CISA assessment entry in the CVE record lists exploitation as none), CyberPower PowerPanel (Symantec), tcherber (Cyderes; VMRay corroborates only the developer identity).
  • Candidate sources: nginx-security-advisories, unit42-timely-threat-intel, polizeiticker-ch (added); mitel-security-advisories promoted. Two source_health UNSOLVED items (typo3-security-advisories, cnil-fr) got health_cmd fixes that were not re-probed because the tool has no single-source mode; the next audit's run confirms them.
  • Operator signals: lab52 has failed on every transport for six fires (newest post 2026-10-05); the jina reader pool is dead (HTTP 402); cisa csaf-recent returned only a legacy bulk re-publish.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-18
item.description:
• Mitel MiCollab AWV flaws exploited pre-advisory per Accenture APEX, CISA lists them; patching alone does not evict. Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0012 of 2026-11-16, revised on 2026-11-24 to list the CVE ids, covers five flaws in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier, led by an unauthenticated blind command injection scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 (CVE-2026-133323) and an unauthenticated XML injection scored 9.0 that could run commands (CVE-2026-133303). CISA added all five to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 without naming an actor, victim or technique, while Mitel's own page says nothing on attacks; Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before Mitel's 2026-11-16 advisory, with web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15 and root within about 30 minutes, so a server patched now cannot be assumed clean. Mitel offers a patch through its portal (KB000129195) and says restricting external access to the AWV component reduces the risk; the 10.3.0.18 release that Mitel named as the fix for its July advisory is itself in the affected range. →
  • TYPO3: backend user to installer to admin and RCE (SA-027 Critical); Form Framework flaw SA-029 exploited; update now. TYPO3 published ten core advisories on 2026-11-17 for 10.0.0 to 14.3.11, fixed in 14.3.12 LTS, 13.4.40 LTS, 12.4.52 ELTS, 11.5.57 ELTS and 10.4.63 ELTS. The one rated Critical (SA-027) lets a file named FIRST_INSTALL placed in the web root re-enable the installer without authentication, which creates an administrator and leads to remote code execution, and SA-026 lets any low-privileged backend user create such a file. TYPO3 states that SA-029, a Medium information disclosure in the Form Framework that can become cross-site scripting through uploaded HTML, is known to be actively exploited, naming no actor or victim. →
  • Drupal installer flaws SA-CORE-2026-017 and -019 exploited; update to 11.4.14, 11.3.23, 10.6.23 and run update.php. Drupal published SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165) and SA-CORE-2026-018 (CVE-2026-132166, Moderately critical, not directly exploitable) on 2026-11-18 and SA-CORE-2026-019 (CVE-2026-136716, Highly critical 21 of 25) on 2026-11-25: under specific conditions an attacker can use the installer to reinstall Drupal, which can lead to site takeover or remote code execution, and sites in unusual or incomplete install states stay open after the first fix. Drupal says both installer flaws are exploited on live sites (SA-CORE-2026-017 from 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC) and CISA listed CVE-2026-132165 as exploited on 2026-11-24; the fixed releases are 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23, update.php must be run, and securing the installer is strongly recommended. →
  • Java4Shell: OpenJDK Base64 heap overflow chained to pre-auth RCE in Jira and Keycloak; update Java, attempts seen. Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update and the OpenJDK advisory of 2026-11-17 fix CVE-2026-114938, an out-of-bounds write in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder that Calif, one of its two credited reporters, scores CVSS 4.0 9.2 and says it turned into pre-authentication code execution in the default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate; Oracle scores it CVSS 3.1 8.1 with high attack complexity. Only x86-64 hosts with AVX-512 VBMI are affected, a trigger proof of concept is public, Calif withholds its product chains, a second researcher claims a working exploit with no release stated, GreyNoise reports exploitation attempts without a confirmed success against its sensors, and VulnCheck says a working exploit is available to its customers. NCSC.ch and BACS warn operators to update internet-reachable Java applications and identity services first, and Cisco's advisory, at version 1.4, lists Catalyst Center, IOS XE and ISE as not affected while Siemens lists Siveillance Control, Siveillance Control Pro and Industrial Edge Management Pro and Virtual with no fix yet. →

Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Trending vulnerabilities 6Updates to prior coverage 3Action items 15

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

NOTABLENATOB2

COLD RELIC: Mandiant shows the FSB-linked group reusing data stolen from one US organisation as the impersonation pretext for the next, then holding cloud tenants through MFA push fatigue and enrolled passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices that survive password and session resets

Mandiant reports a series of linked intrusions in which COLD RELIC, the name Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) now uses for the group formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057 (also Star Blizzard, Callisto and Gossamer Bear), turned data stolen in one US organisation into the pretext for the next (GTIG, 2026-11-17). GTIG cites a US Department of Justice assessment that the group operates within Russia's FSB and names government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America among its targets (GTIG, 2026-11-17). In 2026 the operators approached a second US organisation over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee of the first, shared phishing links that stole Entra ID credentials and tokens and sent the victim on to document lures matching the conversation, and registered a new MFA device on the account (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

In the late-2025 case the operators used the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account from a US residential proxy network close to the victim, pressed the user with MFA push notifications until one was accepted, registered a device model new to the tenant and kept access with passkeys, MFA backup codes and rogue MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They took the whole cloud drive by mass sharing to an operator-run mailbox and by direct download, queried the admin investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, viewed, modified and deleted Alert Center notifications, exported the employee list and ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout export (GTIG, 2026-11-17). Access lasted several months through OAuth mail sync to an external client and re-authentication with enrolled passkeys that survived password and session resets, and in one case a password reset without revoking sessions did not evict the operators (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They searched for credentials, personnel data and .pst archives (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Google Workspace tenants, and Entra ID tenants that federate sign-in to Workspace as in the second case, whose privileged or staff accounts accept push, SMS or voice MFA or let users enrol passkeys, backup codes and devices without a second approval (GTIG, 2026-11-17).
Detection
In authentication logs, repeated failed logins or MFA challenges followed by a success from the same address, privileged sign-ins from residential-proxy networks that geolocate near the user, logins with a backup code, and new passkey or device registrations. In administrator audit logs, Customer Takeout creation, user-list downloads, audit-log investigation queries and Alert Center batch deletions. In Drive and OAuth logs, download spikes, external sharing to free mail providers, and authorisations of broad mail scopes to unapproved clients such as Thunderbird or Proton (GTIG, 2026-11-17). After a compromise, password changes alone are insufficient: revoke all sessions, refresh tokens and third-party OAuth permissions and remove unauthorised passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Triage: a directory export, a Customer Takeout or a passkey or device enrolment by an administrator can be routine; the cues in GTIG's account are an unfamiliar device, a non-corporate or residential-proxy network, or an enrolment right after an MFA-fatigue pattern (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Defender takeaway
Move administrators and exposed staff to FIDO2 or WebAuthn hardware keys, which GTIG says cannot be approved through fatigue or intercepted by reverse proxies, require existing-administrator or out-of-band approval for new MFA devices and passkeys, and write session and OAuth revocation into compromise playbooks (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Builds on: 2026-09-30/star-blizzard-redflick-cosmicpulse-single-click-chain

threat18 Nov 05:05Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 published on 2026-11-17, carried a credential stealer that a .pth startup hook runs every time Python starts, collecting environment secrets and requesting Azure managed-identity, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions OIDC tokens; both versions were removed and 1.26.0 is the last clean release

Socket reports that the Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package was compromised on 2026-11-17, in versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, both of which install Python startup hooks that collect credentials, environment data and cloud identity tokens and send them to a web endpoint (Socket, 2026-11-17). SafeDep, which flagged both releases independently, says the project is Microsoft's official metapackage, that 1.26.1 appeared at 20:35 UTC and 1.26.2 at 21:08 UTC, that each is a single wheel where earlier releases shipped a wheel and a source archive, and that both were removed from PyPI and 1.26.0 is the last clean release (SafeDep, 2026-11-18). The attacker published 1.26.2 after 1.26.1 was gone, so removing one version did not stop it (SafeDep, 2026-11-18). PyPI lists two maintainers, microsoft and vibiret, an account that joined on 17 November and can also publish five sibling projects; SafeDep reads the join date as pointing to vibiret as the uploader, which neither PyPI nor Microsoft has confirmed, and how the account got maintainer access is not known (SafeDep, 2026-11-18).

Nothing has to import the package: a .pth file runs on Python startup, imports a module and launches collection in a background process or thread, so a pip install in a CI job is enough (Socket, 2026-11-17; SafeDep, 2026-11-18). 1.26.1 routes through the package's own initializer, while 1.26.2 moves the payload to a new top-level module and restores the legitimate initializer byte for byte, so checking only the initializer misses it (Socket, 2026-11-17). The code matches environment variables by substring, such as TOKEN, SECRET, KEY and AZURE, reads other processes' environments and credential files for pip, npm, netrc, git, Docker, Hugging Face and Foundry, and actively requests fresh Azure managed-identity and Azure DevOps tokens, with GitHub Actions OIDC tokens added in 1.26.2; it compresses the result and posts it to a web endpoint and downloads no further code (Socket, 2026-11-17). There is no persistent on-disk marker, so fresh process trees can trigger collection again (Socket, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Any developer machine, CI job or container that installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 and then ran Python; lockfiles and requirements files show the installed version, and the last clean release is 1.26.0 (SafeDep, 2026-11-18). While vibiret keeps its access, a fresh install of 1.26.0 also pulls in any new release of agent-framework-openai, -purview, -redis or -tools, which 1.26.0 accepts below 2.0 (SafeDep, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Lockfiles and requirements files naming the two versions, and a .pth file added to site-packages by the package, looked for on disk without starting the environment's Python, because starting it runs the stealer again (SafeDep, 2026-11-18); outbound POSTs to a web-hook service from build and developer hosts; because the stealer requests identity tokens, review sign-in and activity logs for the managed identities and federated credentials the environment could use, from the install time onward (SafeDep, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
Remove both versions, rotate every secret and federated identity a host or job could read, and lock the whole dependency tree with hashes rather than pinning agent-framework alone, which leaves its four sibling dependencies free to update (SafeDep, 2026-11-18); Socket advises rotating potentially exposed credentials where either version was installed (Socket, 2026-11-17).
Update22 Nov 2026 14:47 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesummary

SafeDep updated its analysis on 2026-11-18: PyPI shows that vibiret, an account created on 17 November, the day both malicious versions went up, is a maintainer of agent-framework and can publish five related projects (agent-framework-openai, -purview, -redis, -tools and -postgres), and on 18 November it still had access to all six (SafeDep, 2026-11-18). Version 1.26.0 requires agent-framework-core with an extra that accepts any release of four of those siblings below 2.0, so SafeDep advises locking the whole dependency tree with hashes, since a pin on agent-framework alone leaves the siblings free to update, and holding off on new releases until Microsoft removes vibiret and confirms the releases are clean (SafeDep, 2026-11-18).

incident18 Nov 05:11Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Socket Research Team · SafeDep
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

RIKEN Fugaku and Rikyu supercomputers: an intruder entered the internal operational network through the internet-facing operating-status dashboard, planted malicious programs on internal servers and took users' stored SSH private keys and access keys, then tried them on other systems

RIKEN's Center for Computational Science says that between 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-13 an external third party entered Fugaku's internal operational network through the publicly accessible web page that displays the supercomputer's operating status, and that the exact method is still under investigation (RIKEN, 2026-11-17). The intruder tampered with multiple internal servers, some of them with malicious programs; up to 4,222 Fugaku users and 375 Rikyu users are affected (RIKEN, 2026-11-17). From users' home directories it collected and exfiltrated credentials for connecting to external systems such as other organisations' supercomputers and cloud services: 430 SSH private keys, 233 of them without a passphrase and 197 with one (RIKEN, 2026-11-20). RIKEN has confirmed that the intruder tried some of the obtained credentials against other systems and is checking whether damage or secondary misuse followed (RIKEN, 2026-11-17).

RIKEN and the external provider that maintains the system began investigating suspicious network traffic on 2026-11-12, confirmed the access on 2026-11-13 and suspended Fugaku on 2026-11-14 (RIKEN, 2026-11-17). It replaced the administrative keys, invalidated the public keys all users use to log in and halted all running and queued jobs, and it names no actor; it says there is no evidence yet that research data was exfiltrated (RIKEN, 2026-11-17; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
A shared compute or research system whose operating-status page is reachable from the internet and sits on a network path to its internal operations servers, and whose users keep SSH private keys or cloud access keys in their home directories (RIKEN, 2026-11-17). Relevant to Swiss research and high-performance-computing operators as a transferable pattern of exposure.
Detection
Authentications to other systems with keys that belong to users of the affected host, arriving from unfamiliar addresses, and changes or unknown programs on the servers that run the system's operation; RIKEN's own reviews cover the network configuration and the rebuilding of compromised servers (RIKEN, 2026-11-17).
Defender takeaway
Treat every private key and access key stored on a compromised host as stolen, and a key without a passphrase as usable at once: RIKEN asks users to revoke the matching public key at each external service where it is authorised and to generate a new pair, and to replace any other stored credential through the service concerned (RIKEN, 2026-11-17). A status page that is public should not give a route into the operations network.
Update22 Nov 2026 14:47 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessummary

RIKEN's second notice confirms what the first said only might have happened: the intruder collected and exfiltrated SSH private keys and similar credentials for external systems from users' home directories, 430 keys in all, 233 without a passphrase and 197 with one (RIKEN, 2026-11-20). It has also identified access traces to the registration data of the 4,222 Fugaku users (address, affiliation, phone numbers and the type of identity document used), reports no misuse beyond the connection attempts already disclosed, and says Fugaku resumes only after public services are separated from the administrative network and the servers are rebuilt (RIKEN, 2026-11-20).

incident18 Nov 05:08Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: RIKEN (notice of 2026-11-16, English page dated 2026-11-17) · RIKEN (second notice) · BleepingComputer
NOTABLENATOA2

Barracuda's own account of a 44-hour intrusion into its cloud: a key given to an AI vendor and never retired, found in that vendor's compromised development environment, led an intruder across about ten cloud accounts to Kubernetes; notified Managed XDR customers must recreate their integration credentials

Barracuda says the attacker did not break in but used a valid cloud access key that Barracuda had issued to a third-party vendor, a company working in AI, for an earlier project and had not retired when the work ended (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11). The key had been stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository, which was exposed when the vendor's development environment was compromised (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13). The first call with the key came on 2026-11-01 at 04:33 UTC; within minutes the attacker was mapping what the key reached and reading stored secrets such as AWS access keys and Azure service principal secrets, and each secret opened the next system, from cloud accounts to a data analytics system, to a source-code access token and on to Kubernetes clusters (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11). In just under four hours on 2026-11-02 it pushed short-lived branches to a handful of repositories to trigger a build workflow written to print the build system's secrets into the job log, encoded so that log masking would not hide them, and its last recorded activity was at 23:31 UTC, about 10 cloud accounts and 44 hours after the start (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11).

In a Kubernetes cluster the attacker deployed a container that mounted the underlying server's file system read-only, enough to harvest that server's credentials, and tried to create a new administrative cloud identity, which was blocked (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11). On servers where it had a shell, its commands searched for environment variables named WALLET, MNEMONIC, SEED and PRIV, Ethereum keystore files, extended private keys, seed phrase files and Kubernetes secrets with wallet-related names, and Barracuda calls the activity consistent with a financially motivated actor seeking cryptocurrency and reusable credentials (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13). Barracuda says the resource names, the sequence of activity and the credential and wallet hunting routines match ARTEX, which many groups use, so the match shows how the attacker operated, not who it was (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
A system the attacker reached stores the credentials Barracuda Managed XDR uses to collect data from customers' connected systems such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and endpoint security platforms; only organisations using the API integration for Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint are affected, and Barracuda notified those with potentially affected credentials (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13). Logging in that environment was not detailed enough to rule out access to the credentials (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11). Relevant as a supplier incident for any organisation whose monitoring runs on Managed XDR, and as a worked example of ARTEX-style cloud tradecraft.
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, a long-lived key used by a non-vendor address, secret-store reads followed by use of those secrets in other accounts, resources named with the letter i followed by digits and no hyphen, short-lived branches in a handful of repositories that trigger a workflow, and container deployments that mount the node's file system (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13; Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11).
Defender takeaway
A notified customer revokes and recreates its integration credentials and reviews connected-system activity since 2026-11-01 (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13). Barracuda's own lesson is to remove standing credentials, especially long-lived keys held by third parties (Barracuda Blog, 2026-11-11), and to expire vendor credentials when an engagement ends (Barracuda Trust Center, 2026-11-13).

incident18 Nov 05:06Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Barracuda Trust Center (published 2026-11-10, updated 2026-11-13) · Barracuda Blog

02Trending vulnerabilities6 items

HIGHCVE-2026-114938updatedNATOA2

Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938, OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and Oracle Java SE on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI: a heap overflow in the Base64 decoder that Calif chains into pre-authentication code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate; fixed in 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, GreyNoise reports exploitation attempts, none confirmed successful against its sensors (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update and the OpenJDK advisory of 2026-11-17 list CVE-2026-114938 in the hotspot compiler component, which Oracle rates CVSS 3.1 8.1 with high attack complexity (Oracle, 2026-11-17; OpenJDK, 2026-11-17). Calif, one of the two reporters Oracle credits (Oracle, 2026-11-17), says HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic, which uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions, calculates a negative output length for a short padded input and that length becomes a full 64-byte write that sends 62 bytes past the end of the array; only the landing position of the write is controllable, a misplaced write can crash the JVM (Calif, 2026-11-17). It scores the flaw CVSS 4.0 9.2 and reports pre-authentication code execution in the default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, authenticated execution in several further server products, and a client-side path in which a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is compromised (Calif, 2026-11-17). Tenable relays Immersive's claim of a working exploit with no release stated (Tenable, 2026-11-17).

The flaw needs an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI and affects OpenJDK from 17.0.6 on, ARM64 hosts are not affected (Calif, 2026-11-17). CISA published an alert to patch immediately (CISA, 2026-11-17), and the NCSC.ch Cyber Security Hub says the published research demonstrates exploitation without establishing malicious exploitation (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-17); Talos has seen no exploitation in the wild yet and expects probing (Talos, 2026-11-18), while Tenable relays GreyNoise's report of exploitation attempts as of 2026-11-18, none confirmed successful against its sensors, and VulnCheck's statement that a working RCE exploit is available to its customers (Tenable, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
A Java 17, 21, 25 or 27 runtime, or the Java 8 performance build, at or below the affected builds (Oracle, 2026-11-17), fixed in Oracle's 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513-perf (Tenable, 2026-11-17); BACS says to check that the running applications actually use the corrected Java version (BACS, 2026-11-18). The CPU must report the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 flags, which means Intel Ice Lake to Granite Rapids and AMD Zen 4 or newer (Upwind, 2026-11-17). Pre-authentication reach depends on the application decoding attacker-controlled Base64 with the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64 before it authenticates the caller (Upwind, 2026-11-17). Cisco's advisory (version 1.4) lists Secure Network Analytics and Secure Workload as affected and Catalyst Center, IOS XE and ISE as not (Cisco, 2026-11-23); Fortinet lists none as confirmed affected and dozens as under investigation (Fortinet, 2026-11-18); BACS adds internal systems and supplier-run Java software (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs on internet-facing Java applications, where the log may not name Base64 because the crash comes later (Equixly, 2026-11-17); child processes of the server and administrative activity on identity, build and artifact platforms follow from Calif's chains. In request and application logs, Upwind suggests Base64-alphabet tokens of 32 or more characters that end in = with a length not a multiple of 4, starting with Authorization headers, and bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64$Decoder or of restarts (Upwind, 2026-11-17). An update does not remove a compromise that has already happened (BACS, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
Update and restart, internet-reachable and identity services first. Where an update waits, Calif gives two JVM options, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 hosts only, because OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and fails to start (Calif, 2026-11-17).
Update19 Nov 2026 05:03 UTCrun 2026-11-19T0355Z-intelaffected_productsbodycvesevidencesourcessummaryheadlinesourcing_notetitleentities

Cisco's product impact: Secure Network Analytics, Secure Workload and further products are affected, Cisco offers no workaround, and its PSIRT is aware of proof-of-concept code but not of malicious use (Cisco, 2026-11-23). Fortinet says it is investigating the impact on its products and lists none as confirmed affected, with dozens under investigation (Fortinet, 2026-11-18). Tenable relays GreyNoise's report of exploitation attempts as of 2026-11-18, none confirmed successful against its sensors, and VulnCheck's statement that a working RCE exploit is available to its customers (Tenable, 2026-11-17). BACS's warning of 2026-11-18 asks operators to prioritise internet-reachable applications and central sign-in services, to include internal systems, to clarify other Java software such as banking software with their suppliers and to have externally operated services confirm the fix, and says an update removes no compromise that has already happened (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-18). Tenable adds that as of 2026-11-18 Red Hat and Ubuntu had released no fix and Debian had fixed only its unstable branch, so hosts on those distributions had no stable vendor build yet, and that the Keycloak project recommended starting its server with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as an interim mitigation, its x86-64 container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 carrying an affected Java build (Tenable, 2026-11-17).

Update20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelentitiesaffected_productssourcesbodysummarycves

Three more vendors published product status. Elastic says Elasticsearch 7.17.3 and later is affected with mitigating factors: remote code execution needs an authenticated user with at least read access on an affected CPU architecture, while unauthenticated actors can cause denial of service; Logstash 8.6.2 and later is affected only through the elastic_integration filter when an ingest pipeline decodes Base64 from an untrusted source, with a crash as the result, and Kibana, Beats, Elastic Agent, APM Server, the ECK operator and Elastic Maps Server are not affected, while Elasticsearch clusters that ECK manages follow the Elasticsearch rule (Elastic, 2026-11-19). Elastic plans fixes in 8.19.26, 9.4.10, 9.5.7 and 9.6.0 with a bundled JDK 27.0.1.1+4 and gives no dates, hot-fixed Elastic Cloud Serverless on 2026-11-18, and says fewer than about 5% of Elastic Cloud Hosted deployments, on Azure only, run an affected CPU architecture; a self-managed node is affected only on an x86-64 CPU with AVX512_VBMI (Elastic, 2026-11-19).

Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier, MISA-2026-0012: an unauthenticated blind command injection in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component (CVSS 3.1 10.0) and four more flaws there, one an XML injection that can run commands (9.0); CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133303 lead the five assigned CVE ids, patch KB000129195, Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory and CISA lists all five as exploited since 2026-11-25

Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0012, first issued on 2026-11-16, covers five flaws in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier; Mitel tracks them by internal ids and, since its revision 2.0 of 2026-11-24, lists the CVE identifiers against them (Mitel, 2026-11-16); MITRE published the record for CVE-2026-133323 on 2026-11-19 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19). MTLVULN-1864 lets an unauthenticated attacker conduct a blind command injection through insufficient parameter sanitization and is scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 with changed scope; MTLVULN-1862 lets an unauthenticated attacker leverage pre-staged malicious content for an XML injection that could run arbitrary commands, scored 9.0 with high attack complexity (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Three further flaws are rated Medium: an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload through weak file-type validation (MTLVULN-1861, 5.3), unauthorized access that needs a system-generated random identifier or pre-staged content (MTLVULN-1863, 5.9) and an authentication bypass (MTLVULN-1877, 5.3) (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Mitel says exploiting them together can significantly amplify their impact (Mitel, 2026-11-16).

Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory: web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, root within about 30 minutes, and the credentials stored for MiCollab's LDAP connector used against a domain controller 32 minutes after the first request (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). The internet-facing reverse proxy at that victim did not stop it, and APEX does not say which of the five flaws were used (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).

The fix is a patch for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18), delivered through knowledge-base article KB000129195 on Mitel's customer portal, or an upgrade to a later release that Mitel does not name; Mitel's partners can supply it to customers without portal access (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Mitel's July advisory named 10.3 (10.3.0.18) as the release that fixed its earlier AWV command injection, so a system moved there in July is inside the new affected range (Mitel, 2026-07-22). CERT-FR lists the advisory on 2026-11-17 (CERT-FR, 2026-11-17); BSI's revision of 2026-11-25 rates it critical, says active exploitation was reported and describes a remote anonymous attacker who can manipulate files, run code with the service's rights and bypass security measures (BSI, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier whose AWV component external users can reach, including through a reverse proxy or MiVoice Border Gateway web proxy, which APEX says cannot be assumed to protect it (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24); Mitel assesses only supported versions and states no branch before 10.3 (Mitel, 2026-11-16).
Detection
Child processes of the AWV service, new files in the component's upload paths and unauthenticated requests to conferencing endpoints that carry shell metacharacters or XML payloads, which follow from the command-injection, upload and XML-injection mechanisms the advisory names (Mitel, 2026-11-16). APEX adds POSTs to AWV CGI scripts from unfamiliar sources followed by requests for new files in the web pictures directory, the LDAP connector account authenticating to many domain controllers, and system logs that suddenly shrink (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).
Defender takeaway
Apply the patch now; where that waits, restrict external access to the AWV component, the mitigation Mitel names (Mitel, 2026-11-16). APEX says patching alone will not close an intrusion that started earlier, and the actor filtered local logs: image the server first, compare its logs with proxy and WAF logs, and treat a suspected compromise as a directory compromise by resetting the LDAP connector account and Kerberoastable service accounts (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).

Accenture APEX Labs reports that the MISA-2026-0012 flaws were exploited before Mitel published its advisory and patch. At one victim organisation it places web-shell activity before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, with high confidence, when it was still 15 November in every time zone from UTC−12 to UTC+1 and Mitel dated its advisory 16 November (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Counted from the first observed request, the actor checked the version, bypassed authentication within a minute, had two uploads accepted at 9 minutes, ran its first web-shell command as the web service account at 12 minutes, reached root between 15 and 30 minutes with system logs reset as a side effect, and at 32 minutes used the credentials recovered from MiCollab's LDAP configuration to authenticate to a domain controller over LDAPS; it then filtered web-shell requests out of the local web, error and admin logs and, 20 to 23 hours in, dumped databases on a backup server and a database server and uploaded the archives over many short HTTPS sessions (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). APEX withholds how root was obtained and does not say which of the five flaws were used.

A second organisation's MiCollab server, on a 10.0-series release exposed to this advisory and to the July one, has held a persistent HTTPS channel to the same actor server since 2026-11-09, and APEX has not determined how it was compromised. APEX assesses that AI-assisted tooling operating on the actor's server drove parts of the intrusion, an inference from sampled traffic to two commercial AI API services that it says cannot show exactly how they were used, and it names no group (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). Mitel's advisory is unchanged at revision 2.0 and makes no exploitation statement; BSI's revision of 2026-11-25 rates it critical and says active exploitation was reported (BSI, 2026-11-25).

TYPO3 core security releases of 2026-11-17 (ten advisories): a low-privileged backend user can write a file into the web root and re-enable the unauthenticated installer, which creates an administrator and leads to code execution (SA-026, SA-027 Critical), and TYPO3 states that a Form Framework flaw (SA-029) is actively exploited; fixed in 14.3.12, 13.4.40, 12.4.52 ELTS, 11.5.57 ELTS and 10.4.63 ELTS

TYPO3 released ten core advisories on 2026-11-17, fixed in 14.3.12 LTS, 13.4.40 LTS, 12.4.52 ELTS, 11.5.57 ELTS and 10.4.63 ELTS (TYPO3, 2026-11-17); versions 10.0.0 to 10.4.62, 11.0.0 to 11.5.56, 12.0.0 to 12.4.51, 13.0.0 to 13.4.39 and 14.0.0 to 14.3.11 are affected (TYPO3 SA-027, 2026-11-17). SA-027 is rated Critical: placing a file whose name starts with FIRST_INSTALL in the public web root or the project root re-enables the installer on a configured instance without authentication, which allows changing the database connection and creating a new administrator and system maintainer account, and that leads to remote code execution; leftover or restored marker files also work (TYPO3 SA-027, 2026-11-17). SA-026, rated High, supplies the file: the backend endpoint for adding online media accepts a target folder in the fallback storage, which points to the public web root, so any authenticated low-privileged backend user can create media files with a partially controllable name there (TYPO3 SA-026, 2026-11-17).

TYPO3 states that SA-029, a Medium information disclosure in the Form Framework, is known to be actively exploited, and names no actor, victim or behaviour (TYPO3 SA-029, 2026-11-17). A failed upload shows the raw storage error with the upload sub-folder, so an attacker can derive the public URL of an uploaded file, and where the form accepts HTML this becomes cross-site scripting unless the web server applies TYPO3's recommended Content-Security-Policy to the upload folder (TYPO3 SA-029, 2026-11-17). SA-032 closes the matching gap, an empty allowedMimeTypes list that was treated as no restriction and let unauthenticated visitors upload HTML or SVG to a public folder (TYPO3 SA-032, 2026-11-17). SA-028 lets ImageMagick's MVG coder disclose any web-server-readable file through a processed image; it needs ImageMagick with its default configuration allowing the MVG coder, and unauthenticated visitors reach it where such an upload form exists (TYPO3 SA-028, 2026-11-17). SA-025 is an Import/Export path traversal that writes arbitrary files and needs an administrator or a user enabled for import (TYPO3 SA-025, 2026-11-17). Four lesser flaws are an incomplete open-redirect fix (SA-030), page-cache flooding where cHash validation is not enforced (SA-031), file-dump token reuse (SA-033) and an SSRF in the 14.x Dashboard RSS widget (SA-034) (TYPO3 SA-030, 2026-11-17; SA-031; SA-033; SA-034).

Exposure
Any TYPO3 instance on an affected version; the installer chain needs only a low-privileged backend account, and the Form Framework flaws need a public form with an upload element (TYPO3 SA-026, 2026-11-17; TYPO3 SA-032, 2026-11-17).
Detection
Files whose name starts with FIRST_INSTALL in the web root or project root, and administrator or system maintainer accounts nobody created (TYPO3 SA-027, 2026-11-17); HTML or SVG files in the form upload folder and web-server logs for direct requests to them (TYPO3 SA-032, 2026-11-17).
Defender takeaway
Update to the fixed release of each branch now. After updating, configure at least one allowed MIME type for every upload element, because an empty list now refuses uploads (TYPO3 SA-032, 2026-11-17); on 14.x configure the dashboard_rss allowed hosts, because the update alone does not mitigate SA-034 (TYPO3 SA-034, 2026-11-17); and deliver the form upload folder with a restrictive Content-Security-Policy, which nginx needs configured by hand (TYPO3 SA-029, 2026-11-17); and, after updating, configure image formats outside the default raster set, such as psd or ppm, explicitly in fileExtensionToMimeType so ImageMagick still processes them (TYPO3 SA-028, 2026-11-17).
