Drupal core: SA-CORE-2026-017 and SA-CORE-2026-019 (CVE-2026-132165, CVE-2026-136716, both Highly critical) let an attacker use the installer to reinstall a site and take it over or run code, Drupal reports both exploited on live sites, and 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23 are the fixed releases that close both

Drupal shipped its core security release on 2026-11-18 and added a second installer advisory on 2026-11-25. SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165, Highly critical 20 of 25) says that under specific conditions an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, which can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18); SA-CORE-2026-018 (CVE-2026-132166, Moderately critical 14 of 25) is a gadget chain that Drupal says is not directly exploitable (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18). SA-CORE-2026-019 (CVE-2026-136716, Highly critical 21 of 25) says certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain open to takeover after the first fix, that the user interface does not show whether a site is in that state, and that it is being exploited in the wild (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25). Drupal reports SA-CORE-2026-017 exploited on live sites from 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-18), and CISA listed CVE-2026-132165 as exploited on 2026-11-24 (CISA, 2026-11-24).

Affected are core before 10.6.23, from 11.0.0 before 11.3.23 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.14, with 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23 as the fixed releases, so a site on 11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22, the fixed releases of the first advisory, is still open to the second; update.php must be run because an update hook repairs sites already in that state (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25). Drupal says a site that has secured the installer is not vulnerable and strongly recommends securing it everywhere, that Drupal 8 and 9, 10.5.x and below and 11.2.x and below are end of life with no fix, and that Drupal Steward covers both advisories (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25). Searchlight Cyber's write-up turns database or source-port exhaustion into installer re-entry and code execution on Drupal's official images (Searchlight Cyber, 2026-11-24), while Drupal rates the target distribution Uncommon (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25). StepSecurity reproduced the re-entry on 11.4.12 and not on 11.4.13 and says the stock .htaccess rule blocking direct PHP requests is unchanged, so code execution survives for an attacker who can write a PHP file into a code directory; no source tests the newest builds (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26).

Exposure
Any Drupal site on core before 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 whose /core/install.php can be requested from outside, and every site on an end-of-life line, which has no fix; patched Drupal publishes only its major version, so check the installer path and the drupal/core version the site was built from (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26). NCSC-NL says the condition arises when the installer is not correctly secured or removed after the initial installation (translated from Dutch) (NCSC-NL, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Web access logs for requests to the installer on a site that is already installed and, as StepSecurity describes, a burst of database connection-refusal errors together with a burst of HTTP 500 responses and requests to install.php; on a site that ran an affected build, changes to settings.php, a later install time or a changed user 1 (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26). Drupal advises checking logs for unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25).
Defender takeaway
Update each site to 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 out of cycle, run update.php, secure the installer and move end-of-life sites to a supported branch; on any site that ran an affected build with the installer reachable, check user 1, the administrators and settings.php, since patching does not undo a takeover (Drupal Security Team, 2026-11-25).

Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update of 2026-11-17 carries 655 new patches (Oracle, 2026-11-17). Its risk matrices score 62 rows at CVSS 3.1 9.0 or above, 56 of them marked remotely exploitable without authentication and without privileges (Oracle, 2026-11-17); Tenable counts 62 critical patches across 57 CVEs (Tenable, 2026-11-17). Six of them score 10.0 with changed scope: Oracle Access Manager 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0 in the Admin Console (CVE-2026-114835) and twice in the Authentication Engine (CVE-2026-91500, CVE-2026-91510), WebLogic Server TopLink Integration (CVE-2026-91569), Platform Security for Java (CVE-2026-114824) and Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition Platform Security (CVE-2026-114784), all over HTTP (Oracle, 2026-11-17).

WebLogic Server 12.2.1.4.0 to 15.1.1.0.0 carries further unauthenticated rows at 9.8: Core over T3 and IIOP (CVE-2026-91470) and over SOAP (CVE-2026-91456), and TopLink Integration over HTTP (CVE-2026-91570, CVE-2026-91583) and TCP (CVE-2026-91585); Oracle words the T3 and IIOP row as an easily exploitable flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access compromise WebLogic Server (Oracle, 2026-11-17). E-Business Suite 12.2.3 to 12.2.15 has four unauthenticated HTTP rows at 9.8 in Attachments (CVE-2026-114880), Application Object Library (CVE-2026-114924), Applications Framework REST Services (CVE-2026-114925) and Universal Work Queue (CVE-2026-114863), and APEX and REST Data Services have two at 9.8 over HTTPS (CVE-2026-114849, CVE-2026-114850) (Oracle, 2026-11-17). Oracle's footnote says the patch for the E-Business Suite row CVE-2026-114918 also addresses CVE-2025-61882 (Oracle, 2026-11-17), which CISA lists as exploited with known ransomware use (CISA, 2026-11-17). The release also carries three unauthenticated 9.8 rows for the Brotli flaw CVE-2026-111497 in Communications Diameter Signaling Router, Communications Unified Assurance and PeopleSoft PeopleTools (Oracle, 2026-11-17), a flaw CISA has listed as exploited since 2026-10-27 (CISA, 2026-11-17).

Oracle's matrices carry no exploitation flag of their own, and its interim relief is blocking the network protocols an attack requires or, for attacks that need certain privileges or package access, removing those; patches exist only for versions under Premier or Extended Support, and Oracle says earlier versions are likely affected too (Oracle, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Communications Diameter Signaling Router, Communications Unified Assurance and PeopleSoft PeopleTools instances reachable over HTTP, whose Brotli rows are the KEV-listed CVE-2026-111497 (Oracle, 2026-11-17), and Access Manager, WebLogic Server, E-Business Suite, APEX or REST Data Services, Platform Security for Java and Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition instances on the listed versions that untrusted networks can reach over HTTP, HTTPS, SOAP, TCP, T3 or IIOP (Oracle, 2026-11-17).
Defender takeaway
Patch Communications Diameter Signaling Router, Communications Unified Assurance and PeopleSoft PeopleTools first, since their Brotli rows are the KEV-listed CVE-2026-111497, then internet-reachable identity, middleware, ERP and APEX instances, and until then block the protocols a row needs, T3 and IIOP for the WebLogic Core row (Oracle, 2026-11-17). Oracle names no per-flaw workaround, so unsupported versions have no vendor fix.

CVE-2026-115731, Puppet Enterprise before 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1: deserialization of a crafted agent report gives code execution as the Puppet service user to any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate, and unauthenticated where the CA autosigns; CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.4)

CISA added CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-17 on evidence of active exploitation, naming no actor or victim (CISA, 2026-11-17). The flaw sits in Puppet's report-processing code as used by Puppet Server: a client that holds any CA-signed agent certificate can run arbitrary code on the server as its service user by sending a report with a crafted rich-data type in a PUT request, and where the certificate authority autosigns requests without strong verification an unauthenticated network attacker can first obtain such a certificate (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03). The CNA scores it CVSS 4.0 9.4 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03) and Red Hat CVSS 3.1 9.9 (Red Hat, 2026-11-03).

The discoverers at Neodyme call the bug authenticated in the strict sense, because it needs a valid agent certificate, and say it allows code execution on the management server in a default configuration (Neodyme, 2026-11-03). The OpenVox advisory of the same day includes a full trigger event and says autosign is common in enterprise deployments and that code execution as the puppet user gives access to the CA signing key (OpenVox, 2026-11-03). Puppet's 2026.0.1 release notes list the flaw among the fixes in Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet, 2026-11-12), and the EUVD record names 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13 as the fixed releases of the other two lines (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03); OpenVox fixes it in server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (oss-security, 2026-11-03), and Vox Pupuli says open-source Puppet will not receive any more updates (Vox Pupuli, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
A Puppet Enterprise or OpenVox server below the fixed releases that accepts agent connections; the reachable condition is a CA-signed agent certificate, which an outsider obtains where the CA autosigns without strong verification, a setup the OpenVox advisory calls common in enterprise deployments (OpenVox, 2026-11-03).
Detection
On the Puppet server, PUT requests to the agent report endpoint from hosts that enrolled recently, newly signed certificate requests that nobody approved, and child processes of the server's service account. Huntback's access-log sequence is a PUT to the certificate-request path from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within a second or two, then a PUT to the report path (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A server that untrusted clients could reach before the upgrade should be treated as having exposed its CA signing key, since code execution as the puppet user reaches it (OpenVox, 2026-11-03), and the upgrade does not undo a key that was copied.

Huntback, which runs decoy servers, reports that on 2026-11-19 one decoy received the whole chain from one address in 1.47 seconds: a certificate request for a generated node name, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later that tests whether the CA autosigns, and a report upload carrying a type definition with a Ruby method annotation. Huntback calls it a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy returned no marker and Huntback does not tie it to the exploitation CISA holds evidence for (Huntback, 2026-11-20).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade now and, until then, avoid autosigning certificate requests without strong verification (Red Hat, 2026-11-03). The 2026.0.1 upgrade changes auth.conf wildcard matching, so a rule for *.example.com no longer matches example.com itself and rules that relied on that need review (Puppet, 2026-11-12).

The same Perforce advisory fixed a second flaw, CVE-2026-115732, an authorization bypass in the certificate-name matching of Puppet's authorization library, scored CVSS 4.0 9.0: a CA-signed certificate whose name extends or shortens an authorised host name is authorised as that host (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03). Neodyme's example is that an attacker who got a certificate for evil.target.lab.local can authenticate as target.lab.local, then fetch that host's catalog, which can carry configuration files with database credentials and API tokens, push spoofed facts and add exported resources (Neodyme, 2026-11-03). Where the CA autosigns, such a certificate can be requested for a name that does not exist yet, and OpenVox says autosign is not the default but is common in real deployments (OpenVox, 2026-11-03); NCSC.ch adds that in Puppet Enterprise the bypass also enables CA administration and remote command execution on managed nodes (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

The fix is in the same Puppet Enterprise builds and in Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2 (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-18); OpenVox ships it in OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (OpenVox, 2026-11-03) and in OpenVoxDB 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (oss-security, 2026-11-03). CISA's catalog entry covers only CVE-2026-115731 (CISA, 2026-11-17); NCSC.ch labels the pair actively exploited with a proof of concept available and lists a community report as an additional source (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19), while the report The Hacker News quotes describes a CVE-2026-115731 intrusion, so exploitation of CVE-2026-115732 itself is not established (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). NCSC.ch's temporary measures are to disable certificate autosigning, enforce strong request validation, audit the issued certificates for colliding names and review the CA configuration for signs of compromise (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

Update27 Nov 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsourcing_notesourcesevidenceactionsbodyupdated_at

Huntback, a research firm that runs decoy servers, captured the whole exploit chain on one Puppet Server decoy on the morning of 2026-11-19, in 1.47 seconds from one address (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The chain is a bare certificate request for a generated node name, which a CA that asks for a shared secret or other proof would refuse, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later without polling, which answers 200 only where the CA signs automatically, and a report upload whose wrapper is ordinary and whose event carries a type definition with a Ruby method annotation (Huntback, 2026-11-20). Huntback reads it as a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy signed the certificate, accepted the report with a 200 and returned no marker, and the same address had tried exploits for four other products in the previous ten days (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A scout from a different address had probed the status service and the CA paths about two and a half hours earlier without asking for a certificate. Huntback's advice is to list the signed certificates (puppetserver ca list --all) and account for every name, to refuse at a reverse proxy any report containing RubyMethod, since no agent sends a type definition in a report, and to keep TCP 8140 closed to networks that are not agents'; none of this is vendor guidance (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The capture is a single source and Huntback names no actor or victim.

Update18 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

N-able released Hotfix 3 (build 2026.4.1.39, 2026-11-16): 17 more CVE ids fixed, Agent and Probe authentication hardened, the Legacy API permanently blocked, and every Agent and Probe must be upgraded even from Hotfix 2. N-able does not say Hotfix 3 fixes 4EverAble2Shell or Agent2Shell, and Huntress reports public proof-of-concept code for all 17 ids.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3, build 2026.4.1.39, on 2026-11-16 as a critical security update that builds on and supersedes Hotfix 2; it fixes 17 further CVE ids, adds missing authentication and permission checks to server operations, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate with the server, adds validation to file publishing, path and XML import handling, and permanently blocks the legacy APIs (N-able, 2026-11-16). Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation, and all customers, hosted and on-premises, must upgrade every Agent and Probe to 2026.4.1 HF3 whether or not they already run Hotfix 2 (N-able, 2026-11-16).

The release notes name neither 4EverAble2Shell nor Agent2Shell nor the Apache Axis flaw and do not say they are fixed; what changes is the Legacy API, which N-able itself said both chains need and which is now blocked permanently (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17). Among the 17 ids, the release notes title CVE-2026-129272 "MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode", CVE-2026-129280 "ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks" and CVE-2026-129286 "SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE", and Huntress counts three critical, eight high and six medium scores, all assigned by N-able as CVE numbering authority (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Huntress reports that public proof-of-concept code for all 17 CVE ids appeared on the evening of 2026-11-16, shortly after the hotfix, says any unpatched server should be treated as exposed, and has not observed exploitation of them in its partners' environments (Huntress, 2026-11-17). Field Effect reports that technical details on 24 further N-central vulnerabilities were published and are reported to be addressed by Hotfix 3, a count that the 17 CVE ids in N-able's notes do not reconcile (Field Effect, 2026-11-09). Huntress advises confirming the Patch Management Engine is at 2.14.4.5829 or later, rotating secrets embedded in Automation Manager policies on a server that was exposed before patching, not relying on Take Control audit records from an unpatched server, and enforcing MFA on all N-central accounts (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

OptimJack: poisoned scripts served by Optimizely, Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly route iPhones to exploit-kit stages, the Optimizely files also carry a crypto clipper and card skimmer, and the University of Basel site loaded a poisoned StorifyMe widget on 2026-11-14

First published 2026-11-17 · open finding →

Update18 Nov 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummary

Optimizely's own status entry says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add the JavaScript to some customer projects, Report URI counts 178 organisations that served the code on 2026-11-16, and the Optimizely files carried the code from 2026-11-16 rather than 2026-11-13. The loader also hides in base64 where a host-name search misses it.

Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, that it has fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code, and that it secured affected user accounts; that post named no flaw class, CVE or count, and the status entry's later post of 2026-11-18 is described below (Optimizely, 2026-11-18). The status entry covers the Optimizely files only; how the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly scripts were reached is still unknown.

Report URI's timeline adds that the card skimmer was added to the clipper at 13:43 UTC on 2026-11-16, that a mass clean-up ran between about 20:40 and 21:10 UTC, and that a snippet cleaned and then re-infected shows the writer still had access at that point (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Contradiction on dates: Ohey puts the change to the Optimizely project files at 2026-11-13 together with the Kissmetrics and StorifyMe scripts (Ohey, 2026-11-17), while Report URI's first Optimizely injection is at 04:21 UTC on 2026-11-16; Report URI's logged first-hand record is the better dated one, and the earlier wave through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media is not in the 178 (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

The injected loader came in three forms: a plain script tag, the same address hidden in base64 and decoded with atob(), which a search for the host name misses, and a full inline copy that runs through eval (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of the skimmer's reach, while cards typed into a site's own form fields were not (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

  • Apply the November 2026 CSPU first to Communications Diameter Signaling Router, Communications Unified Assurance and PeopleSoft PeopleTools, whose Brotli rows are the KEV-listed CVE-2026-111497, then block T3 and IIOP to every WebLogic Server from networks that untrusted hosts can reach and patch internet-reachable Access Manager, WebLogic Server, E-Business Suite and APEX or REST Data Services instances, because Oracle marks 56 rows at CVSS 9.0 or above as exploitable without authentication and names blocking the required network protocols as its interim measure for attacks that need no privileges.
    FindingCVE-2026-114835 +17→
  • If Barracuda notified you that your Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint integration credentials may be affected, revoke and recreate each integration credential and review activity in the connected systems (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, endpoint security platforms and others) since 2026-11-01; Barracuda says an organisation it did not notify needs no action.
    FindingBarracuda: an unretired vendor cloud key led an…→
  • Upgrade every Puppet Enterprise server to 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 or 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core to 9.1.3 or 8.22.2, OpenVox Agent to 9.3.0 or 8.32.0 and OpenVox Server to 9.2.0 or 8.18.0; open-source Puppet gets no fix) and, until the upgrade is in, stop the CA from autosigning certificate requests without strong verification and audit the certificates it issued for names nobody enrolled or that collide with an existing node name, because CISA lists the deserialization flaw as exploited, any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate reaches code execution on the server and a colliding name authenticates as another host.
    FindingCVE-2026-115731 +1→
  • On every internet-facing Apache HTTP Server that loads mod_http2, update to 2.4.71 or to your distribution's fixed package (Debian bookworm 2.4.71-1~deb12u1, trixie 2.4.71-1~deb13u1 or forky and sid 2.4.71-1, Ubuntu per USN-9090-1, Alpine 2.4.71-r0, RHEL 9 mod_http2 2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, RHEL 10 mod_http2 2.0.29-5.el10_3.1) and restart it; update SUSE Linux Enterprise 15 SP7 to apache2 2.4.71-150700.4.30.1; where no fixed package exists yet, as on the SUSE products still in progress, remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive until one does, because Red Hat reports an unauthenticated code-execution path and a public exploit, though it rates its RHEL 9 and 10 packages Important rather than Critical for their harder exploitation.

  • On every Axis network device on AXIS OS version 6.50.5.10 or higher, set System.HTTP2.AllowH2 and System.HTTP2.AllowH2c to no through param.cgi now (Axis Device Manager mass-deploys it) and install the service release when Axis ships it, then revert the settings, because Axis says an unauthenticated attacker could gain administrator access and has released no fixed AXIS OS.

Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-18T0356Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 10 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Window 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-17T0355Z-intel). Ten new entries and three changelog records. The will-publish set was too large for a main-agent deep read, so four scoped cti-research follow-ups (FU1 to FU4, Sonnet 5.5, 04:36:43Z to 05:05:26Z) read the primaries and wrote claim sheets under work/2026-11-18T0356Z-intel/deepread.FU*.md; the entries were composed from those sheets and the saved bodies, and each evidence quote was checked as a literal substring of its saved body.

  • Backlog: TYPO3 (published, 2026-11-18/typo3-core-security-releases-2026-11-17-installer-chain) and Oracle CSPU (published, 2026-11-18/oracle-november-2026-cspu-56-unauthenticated-critical-rows) were struck as published; the Open table is empty.
  • KEV: the only in-window addition, CVE-2026-115731 (Perforce Puppet Enterprise), is the entry 2026-11-18/cve-2026-115731-puppet-enterprise-report-deserialization-rce; no covered CVE newly flags ransomware use.
  • Updates: OptimJack (update: Optimizely confirmed an exploited vulnerability; the entry's 2026-11-13 start for the Optimizely files was wrong and is corrected in place), N-able N-central (update: Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVE ids, blocks the Legacy API permanently; the "no fix, follow-up hotfix planned" statements are replaced), Apache httpd CVE-2026-119618 (update: Axis OS 6.50.5.10 and higher affected, no fixed release).
  • Single-source: COLD RELIC (Mandiant/GTIG first-hand, no independent coverage), Barracuda and RIKEN (victim's own disclosure; their press relays add nothing independent), Drupal PSA, TYPO3, Mitel and Oracle (disclosing vendor), Puppet (CISA carries exploitation alone, no actor or telemetry; the flaw itself is multi-source).
  • Contradictions surfaced in entries: Java4Shell impact (early source-reading analyses expected a JVM crash, Calif demonstrates code execution, vendors rate CVSS 3.1 8.1 against Calif's 4.0 9.2); TYPO3's "actively exploited" sits on SA-029 (Medium), not on the Critical SA-027 chain, and an automated CISA record says exploitation none; Mitel's range ("10.3.0.18 and earlier") against CERT-FR and BSI ("before 10.3.0.18"); OptimJack's start date for the Optimizely files; Barracuda's ARTEX statement grows in strength across its three pages.
  • First-pass statements the deep reads corrected: a public trigger proof of concept and a CVE record exist for Java4Shell (S3 said neither); the Drupal PSA never says "proof of concept" (the risk vector carries E:Proof); the Axis PDF never says "HTTP/2 flaw on the web interface"; Oracle's "21 families" and "640 CVEs" are Tenable's counts and only the TopLink row is 10.0 (the T3 and IIOP row is 9.8).
  • Lookback item: Barracuda (primary 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-13, first coverage from BleepingComputer's 2026-11-16 sighting within its 49 h lookback; event_date 2026-11-10).
  • Calibration: high on Java4Shell and TYPO3 (OptimJack and the N-able N-central entry stay high); everything else notable. Held at notable after the verifier's iteration-1 challenge: Puppet (exploited per CISA KEV, but constituency use of Puppet Enterprise is not established), Drupal (pre-announcement without CVE, component or fixed version, PSA rates target distribution uncommon and exploit status proof of concept; the update on the release is the point to re-grade) and Apache httpd (Axis finding adds an unauthenticated 9.8 with no fix, but no exploitation is reported and the flaw needs HTTP/2 enabled). No critical: no source shows exploitation of an exposure the constituency demonstrably runs with a time-critical action.
  • Next fire: the Drupal core security release is due 2026-11-18 17:00 to 21:00 UTC, after this run publishes; the heads-up entry needs the SA-CORE advisory (CVE ids, fixed versions, exploitation status) as an update record. Also re-check ZDI advisories for the Oracle APEX and ORDS rows and Huntress's N-central Hotfix 3 exploitation reports.
  • borderline-drop: Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 (S1.2), CNA-stated exploited but a niche blog server with no constituency exposure established.
  • borderline-drop: Broadcom AutoSys CA20261117-01 (S1.8), internal workload-automation tier, no exploitation, regular patch cycle.
  • borderline-drop: ASUS Control Center hard-coded keys (S1.9), niche, single EUVD record, no exploitation.
  • borderline-drop: Eclipse Mosquitto CVE-2026-110486 (S1.10), websockets listener only, no exploitation, fixed version stated inconsistently (2.1.3 against 2.1.4).
  • borderline-drop: Brotli vendor-impact long tail (S1.14: Siemens ICSA, Oracle rows, Xerox and Lexmark, Cisco revision 1.14); the covered entry already carries the Siemens and Cisco lists and is over its analysis bound; the Oracle rows are in the CSPU entry.
  • borderline-drop: Juniper Junos OS Evolved CVE-2026-98432 (S1.15), single CERT-FR relay, vendor page unreadable, fix pending.
  • borderline-drop: Danfoss AK-SM 800A (S2.3); the covered entry's 2026-11-14 record already carries Midnight Blue, CCB and the BSI position; BSI version 1.1 changes no decision.
  • borderline-drop: BACS weekly review 46 (S2.4), phishing awareness, no new technique.
  • borderline-drop: Operation Endgame Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC (S2.5), takedown with no defender-side decision change.
  • borderline-drop: FBI and DOJ FaceStealer (S2.6), DPRK crypto-theft social engineering, a class already covered (Binance, Sophos, PolinRider).
  • borderline-drop: Quantum Systems QBase update server (S2.7), press-reported, no Swiss customer, no vector beyond the update server.
  • borderline-drop: Reka (S2.8), Swiss private cooperative, no vector or actor, below the incident floor.
  • borderline-drop: Zurich cloud strategy RRB 1155/2026 (S2.9), cantonal procurement policy with no SOC decision.
  • borderline-drop: Microsoft 365 outage 12 to 13 November (S2.10), availability, not security.
  • borderline-drop: Project Zero "Full X" disclosure policy (S2.11), no near-term defender decision.
  • borderline-drop: Operation ShadowCloud (S3.2), Kaspersky and Sophos corroborate each other, but victims are in Asia and Africa, no source ties it to Europe, and neither post carries the cloud-service detection points the first pass proposed.
  • borderline-drop: ARTEX delta from Amazon MadPot, Cloudflare and Talos (S3.5), financially motivated campaigns against LLM gateways with no government target, mostly roll-up of covered reporting, and the covered entry already exceeds its analysis bound; the Dosu post-mortem that names ARTEX is a lead for the audit.
  • borderline-drop: Turla Cereal delta, Romania's SRI statement (S3.6), names Turla only in an opening clause, says only that unspecified Microsoft system vulnerabilities were exploited, and does not say it is the ESET case.
  • borderline-drop: Fireworks AI two-incident bulletin and Uber (S4.3), no source ties the second incident to the Cursor marketplace compromise; the delta concerns other victims and no Swiss or European public-sector party.
  • borderline-drop: Microsoft device-code phishing against Copilot CLI (S3.8), laboratory proof of concept, not observed, device-code class already covered.
  • borderline-drop: Enea SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA (S3.9), single vendor, Asian operators.
  • borderline-drop: Infoblox third-party migration breach (S4.4), thin statement, detail rests on anonymous sources relayed by two outlets, no Swiss link.
  • borderline-drop: Kreiskrankenhaus Greiz-Ronneburg (S4.5), no actor, vector or confirmed attack type, below the incident floor.
  • borderline-drop: California v. OpenAI (S4.6), legal milestone, no technical delta.
  • Leads not pursued (below the bar today): N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts server incident (N-able status page, 2026-11-18 03:05Z, vendor channel, no vector), CNIL's ten fines on French local authorities (2026-11-09, outside the lookback), Maileva (freshest source 2026-11-16, no Swiss client).
  • Included with reduced confidence: none.
  • Coverage gaps: belden-psirt (403), connectwise-trust-center (403), sygnia (403) and lab52 (no route) were not in any slice; perforce-portal (script-rendered page), juniper-psirt (script-rendered page), europol-newsroom (React shell, head metadata only), drupal.org page URLs (client challenge to extract, read through the PSA feed and WebFetch), justice.gov (Akamai interstitial), the Maine and Oregon breach filings behind the Uber count (not read, count not carried), mainichi.jp (paywall).
  • Operational: S3 reported two scratch files written at the filesystem root through a mis-scoped shell variable and moved to its scratchpad; nothing in the repository was touched outside work/. discovered_at stamps were set to the real composition clock. Mid-run stop-hook nudges to commit were not acted on before Phase 6.
  • Verification: five iterations (NEEDS_FIXES at 1 to 5: 32, 10, 7, 4 and 2 findings). Iteration 5 returned two low-confidence F3 findings and no F1 or F4, so the loop ended by the early exit (truth + editorial = 2); both findings were fixed after the pass and not re-verified by a further iteration, hence verification_residual_count: 2. The three F16 priority challenges from iteration 1 were declined and not re-raised. No CLEAN verdict was reached, so there is no double-CLEAN; the entries ship on the early exit.
  • Source health: the sweep left one UNSOLVED row, typo3-security-advisories (candidate added this run), verdict irrelevant: the feed works and is current (newest item 2026-11-17), but its titles carry only two of the health check's relevance terms (RELEVANCE_MIN is 3) because the vocabulary lacks words such as advisory and forgery. Left for the quality audit to widen the vocabulary or accept the verdict; no tool was changed in this fire.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-17
item.description:
• OptimJack: Optimizely names the exploited signup-flow flaw; Report URI counts 178 organisations, Zscaler 450+ domains. Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation account signup flow to impersonate users and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, fewer than 5% of its customers, and Report URI counts 178 organisations that served the code on 2026-11-16 while Zscaler ThreatLabz counts more than 450 domains; the Optimizely files carry a crypto clipper and card skimmer and were all clean again by 23:11 UTC that day. Ohey reports that scripts served by Kissmetrics and StorifyMe gained a loader from 2026-11-13 that routes iPhones to the Coruna and DarkSword exploit-kit stages and that minute-ly's loader was replaced outright; Hudson Rock names 21 web properties, among them the University of Basel's StorifyMe widget, and calls the iPhone stages delivery observations, not confirmed compromises. How the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly files were altered is unknown. →
  • Craft CMS unauthenticated SQL injection gives admin takeover; CCCS reports exploitation; update to 4.18.9 or 5.11.2. CVE-2026-123488 is an unauthenticated SQL injection in the front-end search of Craft CMS 4.0.0 to 4.18.8 and 5.0.0 to 5.11.1 on MySQL and MariaDB that gives read and write access to the database, including setting the admin flag or overwriting password hashes. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says open source reporting indicates exploitation in the wild and VulnCheck lists it in its own KEV database; no first-hand telemetry or CISA listing was found. Craft fixed it in 4.18.9 and 5.11.2 and offers a query-string block as a workaround. →
  • GTIG quarterly: exploit_agent automates n-day exploitation, suspected DPRK cluster abuses .claude/settings.json. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant's quarterly AI threat update of 2026-11-16 reports an exposed multi-agent framework, exploit_agent, that compares code before and after patch announcements, drafts exploits and runs them with no human in the loop, the first such full automation GTIG has identified. It also reports a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE (North Korea) cluster that modified .claude/settings.json in victims' internal repositories so that Claude Code downloads the SOMBERMEME backdoor at startup, and PRC-nexus actors using an LLM platform's file-hosting backend for staging and exfiltration. →

TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01OptimJack: Optimizely names the exploited signup-flow flaw; Report URI counts 178 organisations, Zscaler 450+ domains. Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation account signup flow to impersonate users and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, fewer than 5% of its customers, and Report URI counts 178 organisations that served the code on 2026-11-16 while Zscaler ThreatLabz counts more than 450 domains; the Optimizely files carry a crypto clipper and card skimmer and were all clean again by 23:11 UTC that day. Ohey reports that scripts served by Kissmetrics and StorifyMe gained a loader from 2026-11-13 that routes iPhones to the Coruna and DarkSword exploit-kit stages and that minute-ly's loader was replaced outright; Hudson Rock names 21 web properties, among them the University of Basel's StorifyMe widget, and calls the iPhone stages delivery observations, not confirmed compromises. How the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly files were altered is unknown. →
  2. 02Craft CMS unauthenticated SQL injection gives admin takeover; CCCS reports exploitation; update to 4.18.9 or 5.11.2. CVE-2026-123488 is an unauthenticated SQL injection in the front-end search of Craft CMS 4.0.0 to 4.18.8 and 5.0.0 to 5.11.1 on MySQL and MariaDB that gives read and write access to the database, including setting the admin flag or overwriting password hashes. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says open source reporting indicates exploitation in the wild and VulnCheck lists it in its own KEV database; no first-hand telemetry or CISA listing was found. Craft fixed it in 4.18.9 and 5.11.2 and offers a query-string block as a workaround. →
  3. 03GTIG quarterly: exploit_agent automates n-day exploitation, suspected DPRK cluster abuses .claude/settings.json. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant's quarterly AI threat update of 2026-11-16 reports an exposed multi-agent framework, exploit_agent, that compares code before and after patch announcements, drafts exploits and runs them with no human in the loop, the first such full automation GTIG has identified. It also reports a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE (North Korea) cluster that modified .claude/settings.json in victims' internal repositories so that Claude Code downloads the SOMBERMEME backdoor at startup, and PRC-nexus actors using an LLM platform's file-hosting backend for staging and exfiltration. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Trending vulnerabilities 1Research, reports & policy 1Updates to prior coverage 2Action items 7

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

HIGHCVE-2026-132224exploitedupdatedNATOB2

OptimJack: poisoned scripts served by Optimizely, Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly route iPhones to exploit-kit stages, the Optimizely files also carry a crypto clipper and card skimmer, and the University of Basel site loaded a poisoned StorifyMe widget on 2026-11-14

Per Ohey, from 2026-11-13 the scripts served by Kissmetrics and StorifyMe gained a few lines that load a small router script for iPhones, and minute-ly's loader was replaced outright (Ohey, 2026-11-17). Optimizely's customer project files followed on 2026-11-16, when Report URI saw its first injection at 04:21 UTC and counted 188 infected snippets of 178 organisations, a floor (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation account signup flow on 2026-11-16 to impersonate users on targeted customer accounts and insert malicious JavaScript into their projects, that it closed the vulnerability within three hours of detection, that this was not a credentials breach and that fewer than 5% of its customers were affected (Optimizely, 2026-11-18); Zscaler ThreatLabz counts more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the script (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18). Hudson Rock names 21 web properties, among them BBC, Zoom, HSBC UAE and the University of Basel (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). The Basel capture of 2026-11-14 recorded a poisoned StorifyMe web component (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). How the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly files were altered, who operates the campaign and how many visitors loaded them are unknown (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).

The financial theft sits in the Optimizely files: Ohey says that on 2026-11-16 they switched to a script that swaps copied wallet addresses and skims card numbers in every browser and adds the router only on iPhones and iPads (Ohey, 2026-11-17). Hudson Rock describes the stealer as skimming card number, expiry and CVV from form and fetch POST bodies, and a conditional path that sends readable cookies with a page image only after a recorded wallet address matches (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). In Hudson Rock's reading the router sends iOS 13 to 17 to a Coruna-associated entry and iOS 18 to 25 to a DarkSword-labelled one (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16), and Ohey states that DarkSword attacks iPhones running iOS 18.4 to 18.7.2 through Safari (Ohey, 2026-11-17); Hudson Rock calls them delivery observations, not demonstrated compromises (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
Any page that loads an Optimizely project snippet, whether from cdn.optimizely.com or from the customer's own host name (Report URI, 2026-11-16), Kissmetrics i.js, a StorifyMe widget or web component, or the minute-ly loader; Hudson Rock's advice is to verify what visitors actually receive (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).
Detection
Web proxy and DNS telemetry for a vendor script that causes a further script load from a host unrelated to the vendor, payment-form POST bodies sent to an unfamiliar host, and response-body diffs of served third-party bundles; Content-Security-Policy script-src violation reports naming unknown hosts, which Amirul Cyber says stopped the payload on two affected sites (Amirul Cyber, 2026-11-16). After removal, review the provider-side project change history, API credentials and integrations, because the poisoned output does not show how the attacker got in (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16); Zscaler advises customers to review recent changes, user activity, account creation events and administrative access in the Optimizely account (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party scripts on public, payment and e-government pages now and verify what each serves; a DNS or network block alone does not remove the poisoned trusted script (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16), so keep the evidence, remove the file and set an allow-listed script-src policy.
Update18 Nov 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummary

Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, that it has fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code, and that it secured affected user accounts; that post named no flaw class, CVE or count, and the status entry's later post of 2026-11-18 is described below (Optimizely, 2026-11-18). The status entry covers the Optimizely files only; how the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly scripts were reached is still unknown.

Report URI's timeline adds that the card skimmer was added to the clipper at 13:43 UTC on 2026-11-16, that a mass clean-up ran between about 20:40 and 21:10 UTC, and that a snippet cleaned and then re-infected shows the writer still had access at that point (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Contradiction on dates: Ohey puts the change to the Optimizely project files at 2026-11-13 together with the Kissmetrics and StorifyMe scripts (Ohey, 2026-11-17), while Report URI's first Optimizely injection is at 04:21 UTC on 2026-11-16; Report URI's logged first-hand record is the better dated one, and the earlier wave through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media is not in the 178 (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

The injected loader came in three forms: a plain script tag, the same address hidden in base64 and decoded with atob(), which a search for the host name misses, and a full inline copy that runs through eval (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of the skimmer's reach, while cards typed into a site's own form fields were not (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

Update19 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-19T0355Z-intelactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

Optimizely's status entry now says that on 2026-11-16 an unauthorized third party exploited a flaw in the Optimizely Web Experimentation account signup flow to impersonate users on targeted customer accounts and insert malicious JavaScript into their projects, that it detected the activity the same day, blocked delivery and closed the vulnerability within three hours of detection, that this was not a credentials breach, that the incident was limited to Web Experimentation and that fewer than 5% of its customers were affected; it gives no CVE and no absolute count (Optimizely, 2026-11-18). Zscaler ThreatLabz says the flaw let the attacker edit the project JavaScript field and counts more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script, without stating its vantage point or time window, so the figure is not reconciled with Report URI's 178 organisations (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18). It advises customers to review recent changes, user activity, account creation events and administrative access, to audit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code and to rotate the API tokens, session tokens and integration keys associated with Optimizely (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18).

Update22 Nov 2026 14:54 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbodysourcessourcing_notesummary

Report URI's update of 2026-11-17 says all infected Optimizely files were clean from 23:11 UTC on 2026-11-16 and stayed clean, and that the main payload and data-collection server was put on a registrar hold (clientHold) at 00:37 UTC on 2026-11-17 and no longer resolves (Report URI, 2026-11-16), which bounds the browser exposure from Optimizely-served pages to 2026-11-16. Ohey reports that the iPhone exploit router is a rental service: its operator rents it by channel code, renters get a console that lists each phone's wallets, keystores, Keychain, messages and photos, Ohey holds 31 renter codes in use since 2026-08-31, and the vendor attack ran on the operator's own channel (Ohey, 2026-11-19). The vendor scripts loaded the router from an address of a seller of hidden backlinks on hacked sites; registrars took that loader down on 17 and 18 November, while nine router hosts still answered on the evening of 18 November (Ohey, 2026-11-19).

Improvement24 Nov 2026 04:29 UTCrun 2026-11-24T0355Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Optimizely's customer incident report, shortened on 2026-11-20 with a link to the full version in its customer portal, says the first malicious code was written at 07:51 UTC on 2026-11-16, detected at 13:34 UTC, the vulnerability closed at 16:10 UTC and the injected code removed from all affected projects by 22:24 UTC, and tells customers the exposure window is 07:51 to 22:24 UTC (Optimizely, 2026-11-20); Report URI logged its first injection earlier, at 04:21 UTC (Report URI, 2026-11-16), and the two accounts are not reconciled. Optimizely says the attacker acted as administrator users without their credentials, so no customer password was stolen, that only Web Experimentation was involved, that the script was meant to take card details typed into the site's own forms and cryptocurrency transfers, and that cards entered in hosted payment iframes such as Stripe or Adyen were not reachable (Optimizely, 2026-11-20).

The vendor's early advice of 2026-11-16 to switch the snippet off has been withdrawn, and re-enabling it is stated to be safe (Optimizely, 2026-11-20). Its customer actions are to confirm which pages ran the snippet in the window, review Content-Security-Policy violation reports and outbound requests to unfamiliar domains, review card and cryptocurrency transactions, keep web server, CDN, WAF, CSP-report and payment logs that cover 2026-11-16, assess legal notification duties, check that a strong Content-Security-Policy is in place, and remove the snippet from payment or crypto pages that run no experiments (Optimizely, 2026-11-20). Report URI counted 68 of the affected sites with no policy, 50 with a policy that still allowed the payload and the data theft, and 24 (15 percent) with one that fully blocked the payload (Krebs on Security, 2026-11-17).

Improvement25 Nov 2026 04:47 UTCrun 2026-11-25T0356Z-intelcvessourcessourcing_notetags

CISA added CVE-2026-132224, an external control of critical state data vulnerability in Optimizely Web Experimentation, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-24, on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-11-24); the catalogue record points to Optimizely's incident page (CISA, 2026-11-24). Optimizely says it closed the vulnerability exploited on 2026-11-16 in its hosted service (Optimizely, 2026-11-18); the customer actions above are unchanged.

Sources: Hudson Rock (InfoStealers) · Ohey (Kirk), living page · Amirul Cyber · Optimizely status page · Report URI Blog (Scott Helme) · Zscaler ThreatLabz · Ohey · Optimizely (customer incident report) · Krebs on Security · CISA · CISA (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue)
NOTABLENATOB2

TGR-STA-0049: Unit 42 describes the PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT implants, which use HTTP/3 over QUIC for command and control against government networks entered through unpatched Exchange servers, then spread through domain logon scripts and grant FullAccess on every mailbox

Unit 42 describes a campaign by TGR-STA-0049, also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux and Ink Dragon, against Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025, and says the group's targeting also includes government organizations in South America and Europe (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Server exploitation is the primary entry: unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers receive web shells, among them variants of ASPXSpy, Godzilla, Bysunue.aspx and Suo5, while phishing with decoy PDFs from lookalike government domains is secondary (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The implants are two previously undocumented families: the Go-based PerfectPioneer RAT, active since July 2025 and run through DLL side-loading of a modified legitimate executable, decoy installers or phishing, and its modular C++ successor KUKURAT, deployed since March 2026, which loads at least 12 DLL modules from the command server into memory (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Unit 42 says both families use HTTP/3 over QUIC as the primary command channel, with an automatic HTTP/2 fallback in the PerfectPioneer variant it analyzes, separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 builds of KUKURAT, and two PerfectPioneer variants, RatAAkk-tt and PerfectRat, that rely on HTTP/2 alone, and that some firewalls and inspection engines handle QUIC less well than TCP traffic (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Two of the six PerfectPioneer variants, Pioneer and rat_http3_cc, carry a built-in blocklist that stops operators running noisy or destructive commands, and KUKURAT generates synthetic network, registry and file activity as camouflage (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

After taking a domain controller, the operators installed malicious domain logon scripts, so each user's logon pulled KUKURAT; they also used PsExec, WMI and WinRM (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Credentials came from LSASS dumps taken with rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll by ordinal rather than by the MiniDump name, from DCSync, and from Mimikatz, ProcDump, SharpDPAPI and SAM and SYSTEM hive dumps (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). On Exchange, the operators first listed accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and, when none was found, ran a hidden PowerShell loop that granted a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The exfiltration targeted pdf, docx, xlsx and png files whose names suggest international relations and internal political affairs (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
On-premises Exchange and other web servers that are unpatched and internet-facing, and Active Directory domains in which an attacker with domain controller access can edit logon scripts in SYSVOL or Group Policy.
Detection
Egress telemetry for outbound UDP 443 (QUIC) from servers that do not browse, since Unit 42 advises logging or blocking it so traffic falls back to TCP, paired with proxy and TLS egress telemetry because the HTTP/2-only variants and the KUKURAT HTTP/2 build never use UDP 443; SYSVOL and Group Policy change audit plus endpoint alerts on an uncommon startup process running under a domain user SID at logon, which raised an alert in Unit 42's telemetry; process events for rundll32 loading comsvcs.dll with an ordinal argument; and Exchange audit of ApplicationImpersonation role holders and of Add-MailboxPermission loops that grant FullAccess across all mailboxes (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).
Defender takeaway
Patch or isolate internet-facing Exchange and web servers first, then check domain logon scripts, ApplicationImpersonation holders and mailbox permissions, and decide whether servers need outbound UDP 443 at all.

BundID: automated mass login attempts against Germany's federal citizen accounts lock accounts; the BSI confirms the attack, password sign-in was switched off on 16 November and returned that afternoon behind an e-mail security code, and no compromise is evidenced

Germany's BSI confirmed to heise security and Handelsblatt on 2026-11-16 an IT security incident involving BundID accounts: automated, mass login attempts whose failures locked accounts, triggered automated mails and prompted account holders to reset their passwords (heise, 2026-11-16). The federal government switched off username-and-password sign-in on Monday morning for security reasons (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16), while sign-in with the online ID card (eID) and the Elster certificate stayed possible (WEB.DE, 2026-11-16). The BSI says countermeasures it does not name repelled the attack and that it has no indication of a compromise of any account, and heise reports that locked accounts are apparently not being unlocked in bulk, so account holders must pass the password-reset flow or use another sign-in method (heise, 2026-11-16). Handelsblatt, citing government circles, describes the attack as credential stuffing, the automated replay of credentials from earlier leaks at other services (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16). That afternoon the BundID site notice said two-factor authentication had been switched on for all accounts, with a security code by e-mail at every sign-in by username and password (Spiegel, 2026-11-16). An aggregator attributes the credential-stuffing label to the BSI, which neither heise nor Handelsblatt does (ad-hoc-news.de, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
Citizen-facing or employee-facing login portals that accept a password and lock an account after repeated failures.
Detection
Authentication logs showing a surge of failed password sign-ins spread over many usernames and sources, followed by lockout notices, password-reset mail volume and helpdesk contacts; a lockout storm is itself the alert.
Defender takeaway
The operator's containment was to switch off the password-only path while eID and other sign-in means stayed open, as heise and Handelsblatt report it, and to bring it back the same day only with an e-mail security code (Spiegel, 2026-11-16); a lockout-after-failures control turns credential stuffing into mass lockouts and reset mail even when no account is taken over, so settle that containment lever for your own portals before a run starts.

Symantec: a September 2026 intrusion at a US retailer shows attackers switching to AI-generated PowerShell and, about ten minutes after first querying SolarWinds Orion, using the RabbitMQ Erlang cookie bundled with it to run a command on a second server

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team describes a September 2026 intrusion at a US retail organization in which the attackers first worked by hand on a compromised web server, with typing errors and every staged payload terminated by security software, and then, the next day, submitted about 50 long, error-free PowerShell scripts over roughly two hours, with labelled output sections and comments that read as a model's reasoning (Symantec, 2026-11-12). Symantec assesses AI assistance with high confidence and an operator relaying output to an AI tool, not an autonomous agent, with moderate confidence; it could not identify the model (Symantec, 2026-11-12). The initial infection vector is unknown (Symantec, 2026-11-12).

The earliest activity, on 2026-09-18, ran cmd.exe directly under sqlservr.exe on three SQL Servers, which Symantec reads as commands issued through the database service, most likely xp_cmdshell; on one host the attackers compiled the public EfsPotato exploit with csc.exe from base64 text decoded by certutil and saved the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives (Symantec, 2026-11-12). On a web server compromised through w3wp.exe they side-loaded malicious DLLs with a legitimate Bitdefender executable and a G DATA executable placed in ProgramData, used a utility called BreakChain to relaunch them so they no longer appeared as children of w3wp.exe, copied one to a file named w3wp.exe, and planted ASP web shells in the application's images folder (Symantec, 2026-11-12). The AI-style scripts then harvested credentials from connection strings, FileZilla, WinSCP and PuTTY settings, saved RDP files and IIS configuration, read the Erlang cookie file of the RabbitMQ broker that ships with Orion; running Orion's bundled erl.exe with that cookie, they called the broker on a second web server to run an encoded operating system command (Symantec, 2026-11-12). Later activity searched a probable domain controller for NTDS.dit, SYSVOL cpassword values and LAPS passwords and ran a Chisel tunnelling tool and a password sprayer (Symantec, 2026-11-12).

Symantec says no second-phase technique was new and suggests a possible link, through a shared address and the retail focus, to the operation Gambit Security described on 2026-09-22 (Symantec, 2026-11-12). No Swiss or public-sector victim is named; the case matters for the transferable chain and its AI-assisted tempo.

Exposure
Windows estates running SolarWinds Orion with its bundled RabbitMQ broker alongside SQL Server hosts and IIS web applications; the Erlang cookie file on the Orion host is the pivot.
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage for cmd.exe or PowerShell started under sqlservr.exe or w3wp.exe, csc.exe started by PowerShell on a server, certutil decoding a text file in ProgramData, a vendor-signed security executable running from ProgramData and loading a DLL beside it, an executable named w3wp.exe outside the IIS directory, and erl.exe started from the Orion directory with a cookie argument and a remote broker call; registry hive save events for SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY.

Triage: long, labelled PowerShell is not the signal on its own, because administrators write such scripts too; a parent of sqlservr.exe or w3wp.exe rather than an administrator session, credential-store targets and a blocked loader returning rebuilt are.

Defender takeaway
Hunt SQL Server and IIS hosts for this lineage, treat an Orion server as a lateral-movement bridge to every host that runs its RabbitMQ node, and alert on behavior rather than file names, since the tools were renamed and rebuilt after each block.

CVE-2026-123488, Craft CMS 4.0.0 to 4.18.8 and 5.0.0 to 5.11.1: an unauthenticated SQL injection in front-end search lets a visitor become an administrator on MySQL and MariaDB; the Canadian Cyber Centre reports exploitation in the wild and 4.18.9 and 5.11.2 fix it (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

Craft CMS 4.0.0 before 4.18.9 and 5.0.0 before 5.11.2 contain an unauthenticated SQL injection in front-end search: the attribute parameter is concatenated into the query unsanitized and emulated PDO prepares allow stacked statements, so a remote attacker can read and write the database, setting the admin flag or overwriting password hashes in the users table to gain administrator access (CVSS 4.0 9.3) (VulnCheck, 2026-11-06). Craft's own advisory, published on 2026-10-22 as critical, places the flaw on the front end of any site that uses craft.search, says it affects only MySQL and MariaDB, and says the write primitive was used to set the admin flag on user ID 1 (Craft CMS, 2026-10-22). The fixed releases are 4.18.9 and 5.11.2, and Craft's temporary workaround is to block front-end requests that carry the bracketed attribute token, plain or encoded, in the query string (Craft CMS, 2026-10-22). ENISA's record for CVE-2026-123488 lists Craft's advisory among its references (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-06).

On exploitation, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's update of 2026-11-12 says open source reporting indicates the flaw is exploited in the wild (CCCS, 2026-11-12), and VulnCheck's advisory page states that it is in the VulnCheck KEV database (VulnCheck, 2026-11-06). No first-hand telemetry, victim statement or CISA listing was found.

Exposure
Craft CMS 4.0.0 to 4.18.8 and 5.0.0 to 5.11.1 on MySQL or MariaDB whose public pages use craft.search.
Detection
Web access logs for front-end search requests whose query string carries the bracketed attribute token that Craft's workaround blocks; database audit for changes to the admin column or password hashes in the users table, and new administrator accounts or sessions afterwards. Updating closes the injection but not an administrator flag or hash that was already written.
Defender takeaway
Update every Craft CMS site to the fixed release now, since the attack needs no account and ends in administrator access, and check the users table on any internet-facing site that ran an older build.

03Research, reports & policy1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

GTIG AI Threat Tracker, November 2026: an exposed exploit_agent framework automates patch diffing, exploit drafting and execution without a human, a suspected North Korean cluster plants a Claude Code startup download in internal repositories, and PRC-nexus actors stage and exfiltrate through an LLM platform's file hosting

Three findings from GTIG's quarterly update on adversary use of AI, published 2026-11-16, change what defenders can look for (GTIG, 2026-11-16). First, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates frontier and local LLMs and runs continuous differential analysis of popular web application software: it compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes the findings, drafts exploits and executes them automatically, which GTIG says is the first time it has seen LLM frameworks fully automate discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop (GTIG, 2026-11-16). The server also held scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing web shells and removing other attackers' web shells, and its victim telemetry suggested interest in French media, entertainment and education websites (GTIG, 2026-11-16).

Second, in intrusions against cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe, a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE cluster used fraudulent recruiter profiles, sent targets to fake meeting platforms with ClickFix lures that ran likely LLM-authored staging scripts, and then pivoted into internal code repositories and modified .claude/settings.json so that Claude Code startup triggered the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor; it masked lateral movement with GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot (GTIG, 2026-11-16). Third, in what GTIG calls a new trend, PRC-nexus actors abused LLM platforms and file-hosting backends for staging, dead-drop command channels and exfiltration, in one case staging lure archives and exfiltrating stolen data through a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure (GTIG, 2026-11-16). GTIG separately assesses that the open-source agentic pentest frameworks it tracks, among them ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, currently trade stealth for velocity: they generate forensic traffic, rely on recognizable identifiers and leave distinct code-level traces (GTIG, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
Organizations whose developers run Claude Code against shared repositories, where a committed project settings file executes at startup, and internet-facing web applications and plugins whose patches are public, since exploit_agent works from patch diffs.
Detection
Repository change monitoring for edits to .claude/settings.json and its hook or startup commands, and GitHub audit events that create personal access tokens named after a vendor assistant; for agentic scanning, the forensic traffic, recognizable identifiers and code-level traces that GTIG says pentest frameworks leave behind (GTIG, 2026-11-16).
Defender takeaway
Review a change to a project-level Claude Code settings file like a code-execution change, and move internet-facing web components to the fastest patch lane, because GTIG describes patch diffs being turned into executed exploits without a human.

Update17 Nov 2026 04:35 UTCrun 2026-11-17T0355Z-intelentitiessourcesevidenceactionsbodytitletechniques

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians: on 2026-11-12 a guest-pushed batch file ran on a technician's client with no prompt and installed a rogue ScreenConnect client within about nine seconds, while attacker guests were making 688,000 run-file requests on 42 MSP servers between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16. Updating the server does not fix it; every technician host client must be on 26.6.5 or later.

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians in a campaign it separates from the crypto-exchange-named decoy sessions it reported on 2026-11-13, and it describes the SCKit malware as appearing to leverage a vulnerable server-side extension, not to exploit this flaw directly (Huntress, 2026-11-16). On 2026-11-12 a technician at one MSP joined a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server and the host client ran a batch file the guest had pushed, with no prompt; within about nine seconds a hidden PowerShell relaunch, a curl download and an administrative-image unpack of an MSI ended with a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to an attacker relay on port 8041 (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Huntress read the delivery side from server databases: between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16 attacker guests made 688,000 run-file requests for update.bat-style files from 29 source addresses on 42 MSP servers, repeating them in case a technician joined, and Huntress assesses with high confidence that the spray operator and the relay operator are the same (Huntress, 2026-11-16). In October an attacker also joined three real customer support sessions as an extra guest and asked the technician's client to run a path-traversal file into the Startup folder; two of the three technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients and the Mac client failed (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

The vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine, so updating the server alone does not close it, and Huntress saw many technicians on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after 26.6.5 shipped (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Server-side, Huntress points to guest-originated file-run events (RanFiles, EventType 85, or SentFiles, 86) in App_Data\Session.db, read from a copy, that overlap an open host connection; on workstations it points to the ScreenConnect client running batch or script files from its Temp folder, and to any client whose command line names a relay the organisation does not own (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

  • Verification: four iterations, low-residual early exit on iteration 4 (truth 0, editorial 1, advisory 1, residual 1). Iteration 1 found 11 truth defects, mostly attribution drift in the new entries (OptimJack's capability and dates spread across all four providers, the Ohey citation date, PerfectPioneer's HTTP/2 fallback and blocklist scope, GTIG's stealth-for-velocity sentence) and three in the ScreenConnect update (a count spliced onto another date, a nine-seconds start, an HVCI inference in a pre-existing sentence); all were fixed. Iterations 2 and 3 narrowed to small residuals (Ohey dating, HTTP/2-only variants, the aggregator's BSI attribution of the credential-stuffing label, router scope, an SCKit clause). Iteration 4's editorial finding (the ScreenConnect entry had no Exposure or Detection line and an unrevisited ATT&CK mapping) was fixed after the pass and not re-verified. Left as advisory by design: Craft's actively-exploited tag and exploited status (attributed to CCCS and VulnCheck in the body, CISA KEV absent), the file names of legitimate signed executables in the Symantec and Unit 42 bodies, and the ScreenConnect action that overlaps one step of the SCKit entry's action. The next quality audit should give the ScreenConnect and Fortinet entries an independent pass.
  • Candidate sources not added: Dassault Systèmes advisories listing and Craft CMS GitHub advisories (single-item yield), enea-insights (telecom-only relevance).
  • Source health: 321 records probed; one flagged (anssi-cyber-gouv-actualites, challenge shell), repaired with a sitemap recipe and clean on the re-probe.
  • Process notes: the reader pool is dead (402 on every key, 401 on the anonymous tier) and extract on a 403-walled host ends in a chain of reader errors before it fails; WebFetch's summariser refused an exploit-kit research page, so such pages read through extract.
  • Coverage gaps: sygnia (403 on every transport), belden-psirt (403 on every transport), lab52 (feed reset, WebFetch 503), connectwise-trust-center (bulletin page 403, GitHub Atom feed reads), handelsblatt.com (extract returned a script shell; a syndicated copy was read), inside-it-ch Plus articles (paywall), the Splunk and Oracle releases (not yet published).
  • Watchlist: products checked=0, hits=0; suppliers checked=0, hits=0
  • Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records attempted.

• ARTEX in AWS: CloudWatch log searches for secrets, Cognito self-sign-up for credentials; hunt CloudTrail for both. Datadog Security Labs reports that in October 2026 operators of the ARTEX agentic penetration-testing framework worked against several AWS environments with a focus on financial data: sessions opened with anonymous S3 reads, a stolen long-term IAM key drove CloudWatch Logs FilterLogEvents searches for company names, passwords and access keys, and where no key was held the agent self-registered in a public Cognito user pool and traded the tokens for AWS credentials. Datadog says the distributions it studied do not appear to carry a cloud playbook of their own, so the steps follow the model behind them. →
  • Ransom-ISAC: Gentlemen affiliate, VPN without MFA to Domain Admin in an hour; GPO locker likely lost a replication race. Ransom-ISAC's incident-response report describes an early-August 2026 intrusion by a Gentlemen ransomware affiliate that began with an SSL-VPN account without MFA and reached Domain Admin in under an hour, most likely with credentials taken from an end-of-life Windows Server 2003 host that a dormant local administrator account opened, then used a Rust credential harvester and the EtherRAT implant. The locker's GPO disabled antivirus across the estate but the task that runs it most likely never reached clients because of a replication race, so the locker ran on one host; the report names the telemetry at each step. Single source, no victim named. →
  • Huntress: 2,223 crypto-named fake sessions sit on 118 ScreenConnect servers, likely bait for unpatched technicians. Huntress counted 2,223 unauthorized guest sessions on 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers at 109 MSP and organisation accounts, enrolled between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-13 and named after crypto exchanges; on the 29 servers with complete history an operator revisited every 151 seconds to keep them online. Huntress's leading hypothesis, which it has not observed, is that they are bait for a technician with a client older than 26.6.5 to connect, so that CVE-2026-84869 runs a file on the technician's workstation; it saw no malicious activity from the sessions and found no overlap with the SCKit indicators. →
