Datadog says the distributions it studied do not appear to carry a cloud playbook of their own, so the steps follow the model behind them. →
  2. 02Ransom-ISAC: Gentlemen affiliate, VPN without MFA to Domain Admin in an hour; GPO locker likely lost a replication race. Ransom-ISAC's incident-response report describes an early-August 2026 intrusion by a Gentlemen ransomware affiliate that began with an SSL-VPN account without MFA and reached Domain Admin in under an hour, most likely with credentials taken from an end-of-life Windows Server 2003 host that a dormant local administrator account opened, then used a Rust credential harvester and the EtherRAT implant. The locker's GPO disabled antivirus across the estate but the task that runs it most likely never reached clients because of a replication race, so the locker ran on one host; the report names the telemetry at each step. Single source, no victim named. →
  3. 03Huntress: 2,223 crypto-named fake sessions sit on 118 ScreenConnect servers, likely bait for unpatched technicians. Huntress counted 2,223 unauthorized guest sessions on 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers at 109 MSP and organisation accounts, enrolled between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-13 and named after crypto exchanges; on the 29 servers with complete history an operator revisited every 151 seconds to keep them online. Huntress's leading hypothesis, which it has not observed, is that they are bait for a technician with a client older than 26.6.5 to connect, so that CVE-2026-84869 runs a file on the technician's workstation; it saw no malicious activity from the sessions and found no overlap with the SCKit indicators. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Updates to prior coverage 16Action items 18

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

NOTABLENATOB2

ARTEX against AWS: Datadog sees agent sessions open with anonymous S3 reads, search CloudWatch Logs for secrets with stolen long-term IAM keys, and self-register in public Cognito user pools to obtain AWS credentials

Datadog Security Labs reports that in October 2026 operators of ARTEX, the agentic penetration-testing framework Microsoft ties to Storm-0940, worked against several AWS environments with a focus on financial data, and that every session it reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 reads, which CloudTrail records with a userIdentity type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09). Where S3 hosted a web front end, the agent read build manifests and runtime configuration, and it requested objects named like placeholders just before bursts of key guesses (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09), the habit Wiz saw as a request for a path that should not exist before each fuzzing run (Wiz Research, 2026-10-22).

With a valid long-term IAM access key, the agent's most frequent call was CloudWatch Logs FilterLogEvents, always with a limit of 1,000 events: it first searched log text for the names of cryptocurrency firms, hedge funds and invoicing terms and, in a later session on 2026-10-20, for storage links, internal addresses, database references, passwords and AKIA-style access keys (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Without a key, the agent self-registered in a public Cognito user pool, iterating against a PreSignUp Lambda that checked a tenant domain, then ran InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken and traded the tokens for short-term AWS credentials, which CloudTrail shows under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name; some SignUp calls named the tool in the user agent (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09). It then tried read-only discovery calls such as ListBuckets, ListSecrets, DescribeParameters, ListTopics, DescribeLogGroups, GetRestApis, DescribeRepositories and ListFunctions, all of which failed because the identity pool's authenticated role was narrow (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Datadog found hundreds of internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin, and says the distributions it analysed do not appear to carry a cloud methodology of their own, so the post-exploitation playbook depends on the model in use; some versions block .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn targets by default (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
AWS accounts with long-term IAM access keys that may have leaked, applications whose public Cognito user pools allow self-registration with identity pools that vend AWS credentials to authenticated users, and S3 buckets that serve web front ends without authentication.
Detection
In CloudTrail and S3 access logs, anonymous read bursts that include requests for placeholder-named objects; FilterLogEvents calls with a fixed limit of 1,000 from a long-term user key; Cognito SignUp spikes with PreSignUp failures, followed by CognitoIdentityCredentials sessions issuing broad read-only discovery calls that end in access-denied errors; and instance-role credentials used from an address outside AWS, which Datadog lists among the unusual patterns to hunt (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Triage: FilterLogEvents is a routine call for log tooling and engineers; the discriminator is a long-term user key searching log text for credentials, internal addresses or company names at a constant page limit, from an address that key does not normally use.

Defender takeaway
Check which Cognito user pools allow open self-registration and what their identity pools' authenticated roles can read, rotate long-term IAM keys found in code or logs, and hunt CloudTrail for the sequences above; a narrow authenticated role is what stopped the Cognito path in the case Datadog describes.

Builds on: 2026-10-22/artex-storm-0940-agentic-llm-pentest-spraying-oauth-abuse · 2026-11-14/cyberstrikeai-aws-cloudtrail-intrusion-one-source-ip · 2026-11-06/exposed-app-credentials-entra-signins-msp-clients-artex · 2026-11-08/workos-artex-agent-escaped-sandbox-internal-tool-breach

threat15 Nov 15:09Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Datadog Security Labs · Wiz Research
NOTABLENATOC2

The Gentlemen affiliate: an SSL-VPN account without MFA, a Windows Server 2003 host and a dormant local administrator gave Domain Admin in under an hour; the GPO locker most likely lost a replication race, so antivirus was disabled estate-wide but only one host was encrypted (Ransom-ISAC)

Ransom-ISAC reconstructs an early-August 2026 intrusion into a small company by a Gentlemen ransomware affiliate from forensic images of two domain controllers, event logs of 41 hosts and firewall logs (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13). Entry was an SSL-VPN account without MFA that succeeded on the first attempt from an unusual country; neither egress address appears in any earlier failed login, so the credential was most likely held beforehand. Within the hour the actor ran an anonymous SMB sweep, three Kerberoast-style service-ticket requests (the KDC logged an RC4 and DES downgrade against an AES-only account) and hundreds of failed SMB logons against a domain controller, then used a dormant, weak-password local administrator on an end-of-life Windows Server 2003 SQL host that allowed null sessions. A Domain Admin session opened on the domain controller less than an hour after the first login; Ransom-ISAC could not prove how and says the credentials were most likely taken from that host. The actor then pushed a Rust credential harvester, which takes the DPAPI domain backup key, and EtherRAT, a Node.js implant that reads its command address from an Ethereum smart contract and never reached it; data left through the VPN tunnel over about two days of a weekend (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

The locker, run on a domain controller in domain-wide mode, built a GPO linked enforced at the domain root and the Domain Controllers container, with eight registry values that disable antivirus and a Preferences scheduled task in SYSVOL. The call that declares the Preferences extension reached a domain controller the GPO had not replicated to, the script suppressed the error and no client read the task: antivirus was off estate-wide but the locker ran on one host, which wiped its logs (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
An SSL-VPN gateway with accounts that lack MFA, and any end-of-life host reachable from the VPN address pool that allows null sessions or keeps dormant local administrators.
Detection
In KDC and authentication logs, RC4 or DES advertised against an AES-only account, bursts of SMB logon failures from one client (expired-password answers show valid credentials) and null-session logons with random sixteen-character workstation names followed by a dormant local account's logon on a legacy host; in directory change records, a new GPO linked enforced at the domain root or a Preferences task file written into SYSVOL outside the management console; on servers, a Run value named like a browser updater, node.exe fed its script on standard input by a node.exe parent, resolution of three or more public Ethereum RPC providers and antivirus preference changes that disable real-time monitoring (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Triage: scanners and inventory tools also sweep SMB anonymously and legacy applications use null sessions (the finding is a dormant account logging on right after); developers resolve Ethereum RPC providers, so scope that rule to servers; administrators edit GPOs, so correlate with the change calendar (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Ransom-ISAC concludes that the actor needed one credential without MFA and one end-of-life server to reach Domain Admin (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13), so MFA on every SSL-VPN account and retiring or isolating the legacy host with its dormant local administrator each remove a link; Ransom-ISAC advises that a GPO of this shape found in a domain be unlinked and deleted, with its Preferences task file, before hosts are cleaned or credentials rotated (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).
threat15 Nov 04:28Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Ransom-ISAC
NOTABLENATOB2

ScreenConnect: Huntress finds 2,223 fake guest sessions named after crypto exchanges on 118 self-hosted servers, enrolled from 2026-11-03 and, in its leading hypothesis, bait for technicians whose clients predate 26.6.5; it saw no malicious use and no overlap with SCKit

Huntress counted 2,223 fake guest sessions on 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers across 109 MSP and organisation accounts, enrolled between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-13: always-online "computers" named after crypto exchanges (an exchange word joined to a role word) with a trading-desktop thumbnail (Huntress, 2026-11-14). An MSP asked about them on 2026-11-12; its own server showed no web shells, suspicious child processes or new accounts, and the first Access installer Huntress examined was publicly downloadable, which ScreenConnect allows without authentication by design, and a guest client needs the server's relay address, which is embedded in that server's guest installer, to register. Huntress saw no malicious activity from the sessions: technicians who opened them mostly stayed under 30 seconds, and in one case a technician used the send-text feature, which ScreenConnect does not log, so Huntress treated it as a possible credential exposure. On 29 servers with complete history the operator revisited every 151 seconds to keep the sessions online (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Huntress's leading hypothesis, which it has not observed, is bait: a technician who connects with a client older than 26.6.5 would let a malicious guest use the file-transfer flaw CVE-2026-84869 to run a file on the technician's workstation, often the MSP's most privileged machine; it cannot rule out capturing what a technician types, and it found no overlap with the published SCKit indicators (Huntress, 2026-11-14). It considers the public suggestion that the sessions are a malware sandbox detonating installers unlikely.

Exposure
A self-hosted ScreenConnect server whose Access guest installer is public or leaked, and every technician host client older than 26.6.5; server session history shows client versions (Huntress, 2026-11-14).
Detection
In the server session database, new guest sessions with ClientType 1 (Windows), an empty guest public key, empty company or site fields and crypto-site thumbnails (guest version 25.3.4.9288 is context, not unique on its own); in web or relay logs, many new Access guests from one external address in a short window; on technician workstations, ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or msiexec.exe on a file under a Documents Temp folder, which Huntress calls the host-side shape of CVE-2026-84869 exploitation. A fake alone shows reachability, not exposure: compare technician-side with guest-side events (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Triage: a malware-analysis sandbox detonating a ScreenConnect installer also creates guest sessions; per Huntress, a sandbox session sends a key and JPEG screenshots of the analysis VM, while these send no key, reuse seven screenshot families and randomise hardware and OS details (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade technician host clients to 26.6.5 or later, keep Access installer links private and rebuild leaked ones, restrict installer and web access where supported, bar technicians from joining sessions they cannot tie to a customer, and move unfamiliar sessions into a group technicians do not browse; in Huntress's hypothesis the target is a technician client below 26.6.5 (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Builds on: 2026-09-12/cve-2026-84869-connectwise-screenconnect-worm-file-transfer · 2026-11-12/screenconnect-sckit-toolkit-pushed-to-hundreds-of-endpoints

threat15 Nov 04:27Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Huntress
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

PolinRider: a North Korea-linked loader reaches developers through force-pushed forged commits in at least 7,609 GitHub repositories, hijacked npm releases and a fake employer's take-home test, and reads its server address from an Ethereum wallet

Apiiro calls PolinRider a North Korea-linked worm and found it in at least 7,609 GitHub repositories owned by 2,330 accounts, mostly developers' own (Apiiro, 2026-11-09). Three routes, none relying on an npm install script. Forged commits: with stolen GitHub access the worm force-pushes a copy of a commit the owner already made, with the same author, message and date, plus a loader hidden after hundreds of spaces in a build configuration file; in 94% of 9,990 injection pushes the copy claims to be more than an hour older than the push, so git log shows an old commit under the owner's name. Cloning runs nothing; building the project or running its dev, build or lint scripts loads the file, and in the newest wave opening the folder in VS Code is enough (Apiiro, 2026-11-09). Hijacked npm releases: Sonatype found concealed loaders in 12 releases across 10 hijacked packages with no install or postinstall hook, so disabling install scripts does not help (Sonatype, 2026-11-04). A fake employer: JFrog traced AccuraSoftHire, a decoy recruiter with ID-verified LinkedIn recruiters and job ads, whose take-home loads a look-alike npm package and whose scripted camera check fails and hands the candidate a command that installs the same loader (JFrog, 2026-11-09); StepSecurity says taking its site down, as had happened by 2026-11-13, does not end the operation (StepSecurity, 2026-11-13).

The loader reads the latest outbound transaction of a hard-coded Ethereum wallet and decodes two IPv4 addresses from its recipient field (Apiiro, 2026-11-09), then fetches XOR-encoded JavaScript over plain HTTP on port 443, so blocking one server changes nothing; the wallet in the hijacked npm releases also appears in GitGuardian's GhostAction report, which Sonatype says does not establish a shared operator (Sonatype, 2026-11-04). Cleanup does not hold: 1,949 repositories were infected again after being publicly listed, and where owners cleaned up the stolen access often still worked; Apiiro counts roughly 2,300 developers reached (Apiiro, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
Any developer machine, CI runner or coding agent that builds or opens a checkout the worm reached, installs one of the hijacked npm packages, or runs a take-home from an unverified recruiter. Apiiro's checks are a semicolon followed by 200 or more spaces on any branch, a .vscode/tasks.json task with runOn set to folderOpen that runs node, and force-pushes in the GitHub Activity view whose commit is dated days before the push (Apiiro, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In process telemetry, a detached node child with no console started from a build script, editor or package entrypoint; in egress telemetry, build hosts and CI runners resolving public blockchain RPC endpoints and then making plain HTTP requests on port 443 to a bare IP address; in GitHub audit telemetry, force-pushes whose replacement commit repeats the replaced commit's author and message (Apiiro, 2026-11-09; Sonatype, 2026-11-04).

Triage: blockchain developers legitimately call public RPC endpoints; the discriminator is a build or lint process in a project with no Web3 purpose doing so and then spawning a detached node child (Apiiro, 2026-11-09).

Defender takeaway
Treat a machine or runner that built an infected checkout as compromised and rotate what it could reach, because the stolen access, not the file, reinfects; run take-home tests from unknown recruiters only in a throwaway virtual machine with no tokens or keys, and block public blockchain RPC from CI runners (Apiiro, 2026-11-09; JFrog, 2026-11-09).
Update26 Nov 2026 05:07 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelsummarytechniquessourcessourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

SafeDep reports that PolinRider now plants a Python loader in GitHub repositories, hidden in a small utils package or in conftest.py with five import lines added to a start file, and found it in 375 public repositories under 260 accounts on 2026-11-24; no PyPI or npm package carries it, and because it uses only the standard library a scan of requirements files or a lockfile does not show it (SafeDep, 2026-11-24). When Python imports the file, the loader reads the input data of the newest transaction an Ethereum wallet sent to itself, writes it as JavaScript to a temporary file and runs node on it; the next stage is written to the standard input of a detached interactive node process, so it is absent from the process command line, and the node child starts from python or pytest. pytest runs the loader through conftest.py every time, and fixing an import error for the missing utils package also starts it. SafeDep did not contact the command server, so later stages are unobserved, and the stealer behavior it describes comes from the September chain. Its remedy is to delete the planted package, import lines and conftest.py loader, then clean the machines that push to the repository and replace their GitHub tokens and SSH keys (SafeDep, 2026-11-24).

StepSecurity reports that the loader reached open-source projects through commits force-pushed on 2026-10-19 into pull requests that were still open, from one GitHub account, at AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse and Open Food Facts; the malicious commits reuse a clean commit's message and date but are unsigned and carry a different committer name, and none of the merged pull requests contains the loader (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26). In the files it read, the added line is about 315 tab characters followed by the loader, so GitHub's diff looks empty, and the loader runs from a prefix on the build and dev scripts, from a Jest or PostCSS config file or from a hidden VS Code folder-open task. CircuitVerse's pull_request workflows ran on the poisoned fork commits with no approval step, and its maintainers confirmed the loader ran in the desktop build and deleted 40 installers that had stayed downloadable for more than a month; AsyncAPI's CI did not run it, and Open Food Facts' builds failed and its maintainers rotated a secret. StepSecurity counts 576 infected repositories of 622 it fetched, across 311 accounts, and assesses from a shared funding wallet that the fake interviews and these infections share an operator (StepSecurity, 2026-11-26).

Builds on: 2026-10-10/ghostaction-fake-audit-workflow-git-history-credential-theft

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-123039, Check Point Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls: PHP2Shell on the Mobile Access and VPN web interfaces, chained with a local root escalation, is exploited against unpatched gateways (implant, ESXi wiper); the fix is in Jumbo takes R81.20 take 174, R82 take 132, R82.10 take 52 and R82.20 take 14

Check Point's hotfix article says R82.20 gateways are protected by the built-in "PHP Remote Code Execution" IPS signatures even with IPS disabled and HTTPS Inspection inactive, and Check Point Research saw hundreds of segmentation faults in the portal's Apache and PHP workers during the exploitation window, a crash pattern defenders can look for.

Check Point's hotfix article states that R82.20 firewalls protect themselves through the "PHP Remote Code Execution" IPS signatures even when IPS is not enabled and HTTPS Inspection is not active, while the fix itself ships in the R82.20 Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator from take 14 (Check Point, 2026-11-12). Check Point Research reports that during the exploitation window the Mobile Access portal's Apache and PHP workers recorded hundreds of segmentation faults, which it reads as evidence of repeated exploitation attempts; a burst of portal worker crashes on a gateway with Mobile Access enabled is therefore a signal to investigate (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12).

Sources: Google (Chrome Releases) · CISA · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog · NCSC Switzerland (Cyber Security Hub) · SecurityWeek · Google (Chrome Releases, Extended Stable) · Microsoft Security Update Guide (CVE-2026-125350) · Microsoft Edge security release notes
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

Cursor marketplace: a tampered Claude Code extension (versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313) planted an SSH key, a reverse tunnel and persistence for about eleven hours on 2026-10-29; uninstalling it does not remove the persistence

First published 2026-10-31 · open finding →

Update15 Nov 2026 04:24 UTCrun 2026-11-15T0356Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencetechniquesactionssourcing_notebody

Cursor's own report of 2026-11-13 gives the origin the entry lacked: an access key Cursor issued to its vendor Fireworks AI was exposed, the attacker copied a bucket of coding-agent traces holding some unredacted credentials, and a stolen credential let it write the extension onto the marketplace cache; Open VSX never carried it and the last attacker activity, on 2026-11-01, was blocked.

Cursor's incident report of 2026-11-13 says an attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to its vendor Fireworks, which Fireworks exposed, and used it to copy a read-only storage bucket of historical coding-agent traces from sessions not in Privacy Mode; a small number of the traces held credentials that had not been redacted, and less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed (Cursor, 2026-11-13). From those credentials the attacker reached select SaaS tools and, through them, archived non-production source code repositories, limited customer support data and credentials users had sent to Cursor support (Cursor, 2026-11-13). On 2026-10-29, "using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system", the attacker placed the malicious copies directly on the cache that serves the marketplace; Cursor says Anthropic did not publish them, that this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product, that Open VSX never had the malware, that at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions that day potentially received the build, and that the last attacker activity, on 2026-11-01, was blocked (Cursor, 2026-11-13). Where credentials were exposed Cursor emailed team admins a list of the keys to rotate (Cursor, 2026-11-13).

Fireworks' bulletin of 2026-11-09 describes its own intrusion, which it links to a financially motivated group that sells tokens from unauthorized access to language models to illicit routing gateways ("LLMjacking"), and further activity on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-24 after a security incident at a cloud provider that hosted its development machines; it does not mention Cursor (Fireworks AI, 2026-11-09). Neither company names an actor for the extension.

Sources: Cursor (security notice) · Phorion · Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Sophos X-Ops · heise online · NCSC Switzerland (Cyber Security Hub, post 13121) · Cursor (incident report) · Fireworks AI (security bulletin update)

03Action items18 items

  • Find every Dixell or Copeland XWEB EVO supervisor reachable from the internet and put it behind a VPN now; on each unit that was exposed, review its users, alarm settings and setpoints and read cabinet temperatures directly, because VulnCheck sees two of its unauthenticated flaws exploited and the password flaws will never be fixed.
    FindingCVE-2026-124007 +7→
  • Update Chrome to the current Stable build, 157.0.8103.78 or later (157.0.8103.50 is the first fixed build), and Extended Stable to 156.0.8078.100 or later on every managed endpoint, force the browser relaunch now, update Edge to 157.0.4341.46 or later and Edge for Android to 157.0.4341.53, and install the other Chromium-browser updates as soon as each vendor lists CVE-2026-125350 as fixed.
    FindingCVE-2026-125350→
  • Upgrade every FortiMail to 8.0.2, 7.6.7 or 7.4.9 (a 7.2 unit moves to a fixed release; 7.2.10 for CVE-2026-126150 is not released), every FortiAuthenticator to 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, every FortiOS to 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 or 7.2.14 (a 7.0 unit migrates), and every FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer on 8.0.0 or 8.0.1, 7.6, 7.4 or 7.2 to 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 or 7.2.13 (7.0 migrates), internet-facing units and FortiMail first, because the advisories describe unauthenticated code execution and account takeover and Fortinet warns that patch differences show attackers where the weakness sits; keep the FGFM and oftp ports and every administrative interface off untrusted networks.
    FindingCVE-2026-126147 +18→
  • On every FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager (Cloud variants included) on 8.0.0 through 8.0.2, set rpc-permit none on every administrator profile that has the JSON API enabled until Fortinet releases 8.0.3, because no 8.0 build fixes the unauthenticated 9.8 flaw CVE-2026-126170 and 8.0.2 is affected.
    FindingCVE-2026-126147 +18→
  • Find every AhsayCBS server your organisation or your managed-service suppliers run, including those on v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, and install v9.17.0 on v9 or v10.3.6 (current build v10.3.6.14) on v10, or the latest partner hotfix (v9.15.2.78 for v7 to v9, v10.3.4.55 for v10) and reboot after it, now; until then keep the management web interface behind a VPN or an allowlist of trusted addresses.
    FindingCVE-2026-105133 +1→
  • Compromise-check every AhsayCBS server that was internet-reachable since 2026-10-04, re-image any host with a finding from a trusted backup and rotate the credentials stored on or reachable from it, other backup software on the same network included, because the fix does not remove a webshell or persistence that is already there.
    FindingCVE-2026-105133 +1→
  • On every self-hosted ScreenConnect server your organisation or its IT providers run, list guest sessions with an exchange-and-role name or empty company or site fields, copy App_Data\\Session.db and its WAL file before deleting any, and where a technician connected to one from a client older than 26.6.5, inspect that workstation's ScreenConnect Temp and Startup folders and process history and treat text sent through the session as exposed credentials, because Huntress suspects the sessions are bait for the file-transfer flaw CVE-2026-84869.
    FindingHuntress: 2,223 crypto-named fake sessions sit on…→
  • Search every branch of your organisation's and suppliers' GitHub repositories for a semicolon followed by 200 or more spaces or tabs in JavaScript, TypeScript and build configuration files, for a utils package or conftest.py that runs node, and for .vscode/tasks.json tasks that run node when a folder opens; on any hit, rotate every GitHub and npm token reachable from the developer machines and CI runners that built the repository and review force-pushes, deploy keys, Actions secrets and releases since the infection, because deleting the loader does not revoke the access that pushed it.
    FindingPolinRider: forged backdated commits, npm hijacks…→
  • On every internet-facing Apache HTTP Server that loads mod_http2, update to 2.4.71 or to your distribution's fixed package (Debian bookworm 2.4.71-1~deb12u1, trixie 2.4.71-1~deb13u1 or forky and sid 2.4.71-1, Ubuntu per USN-9090-1, Alpine 2.4.71-r0, RHEL 9 mod_http2 2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, RHEL 10 mod_http2 2.0.29-5.el10_3.1) and restart it; update SUSE Linux Enterprise 15 SP7 to apache2 2.4.71-150700.4.30.1; where no fixed package exists yet, as on the SUSE products still in progress, remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive until one does, because Red Hat reports an unauthenticated code-execution path and a public exploit, though it rates its RHEL 9 and 10 packages Important rather than Critical for their harder exploitation.
    FindingCVE-2026-119618→
  • On every Axis network device on AXIS OS version 6.50.5.10 or higher, set System.HTTP2.AllowH2 and System.HTTP2.AllowH2c to no through param.cgi now (Axis Device Manager mass-deploys it) and install the service release when Axis ships it, then revert the settings, because Axis says an unauthenticated attacker could gain administrator access and has released no fixed AXIS OS.
    FindingCVE-2026-119618→
  • On every developer endpoint that runs Cursor, check extension-install telemetry for Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 installed between 09:27 and 20:35 UTC on 2026-10-29; where it is found, isolate the host, remove the unauthorized SSH key, the persistence and any running tunnel process, because uninstalling the extension removes none of them, and rotate every credential reachable from the host from a trusted system.
    FindingCursor marketplace served a trojanised Claude Code…→
  • Ask the admin of every Cursor team your organisation uses whether Cursor's email listing exposed keys arrived, and rotate every key it lists, because Cursor says coding-agent traces from sessions outside Privacy Mode held unredacted credentials.
    FindingCursor marketplace served a trojanised Claude Code…→
  • On every internet-facing Linux server and every XenServer or XCP-ng host with its Workload Balancing and Conversion Manager appliances, install the vendor's fixed kernel or firmware and reboot, then confirm the running version.
    FindingCVE-2026-98432→
  • On Veeam estates, run Veeam Updater on the appliances, install the private fix for the Linux helper appliances of Windows-based Backup & Replication and of Recovery Orchestrator 13.1, redeploy virtual labs and helper appliances that stay deployed and replace recovery media made before the update.
    FindingCVE-2026-98432→
  • On hosts that cannot reboot yet, drop IPv4 TCP packets that carry IP options ahead of the TCP stack as CIQ, AWS and Vates describe, after testing on one non-production host because it also drops legitimate option-bearing traffic; disabling MPTCP alone does not close the path.
    FindingCVE-2026-98432→
  • Update every non-browser TLS client that keeps its own CA bundle or does not check revocation to a fixed version: standalone Java runtimes, including those already updated on 2026-10-21, to the update of Oracle's Security Alert CVE-2026-114820 or OpenJDK (Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch installations too), Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 or 3.11.18 together with pip 26.2.2 or later, Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, self-managed GitLab to a fixed patch release together with GitLab Runner 19.5.1, and SonicWall Gen7 firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled to SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 or later and Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015 or later; then confirm with curl against the incident tracker's test host that the client rejects the certificate; on managed Macs update to macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3, or where that is not possible remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from /etc/ssl/cert.pem as Apple describes (AAA Certificate Services is optional and can stop tools that read only that file from verifying some unaffected sites).
    FindingCVE-2026-91403 +3→
  • Replace, by hand where the ACME client does not support ACME Renewal Information, every TLS certificate your organisation holds that chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or to another of the seven certificates Microsoft removed from the Windows and Edge trust lists, or that was issued by one of the eight RSA G2B and G2C issuing CAs eMudhra revoked on 2026-11-07, because Chrome's removal of the G3 root was due on 2026-10-27 and the Windows change takes effect when the trust-list update reaches a device; deliver the updated Disallowed Certificate Trust List and the trust-list changes Microsoft describes, including its out-of-band update of 2026-10-26, to Windows devices that do not receive automatic certificate-trust updates; do not renew or reissue under emSign Root CA - G1 after 2026-11-16, because Chrome 153 and higher will not trust by default a certificate under it whose earliest SCT is later, and Windows, Edge and WebView2 stop trusting the remaining eMudhra roots on 2026-11-16 as Microsoft's update of 2026-11-10 describes.
    FindingCVE-2026-91403 +3→
  • Apply Cisco's remediation now for the products its eMudhra advisory (version 1.11) lists with a fix or a procedure available: the CA-trust distrust guide for IOS XE and the guidance for Secure Firewall ASA, FTD and FMC, Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager (run the updatenow command where updates are manual), Duo Access Gateway 3.2.0, Duo Network Gateway 3.4.1, Duo Agentic Authorization Connector 1.0.1 and ThousandEyes Enterprise Agent (Application-hosting Agent 5.2.2).

Verification & coverage notes2 runs

2026-11-15T1407Z-audit · audit · Opus 5.5 · window 170 h · 1 entry published

Scope and outcome

Scheduled weekly audit of 2026-11-08T13:09Z to 2026-11-15T14:07Z (anchor: the 2026-11-08 audit, the last with re-sweeps). Fifty-six entries with activity from the week's seven intel fires were truth-checked whole in six passes: 27 clean, 24 with imprecisions, 5 with factual errors (Fortinet 7.2 fix, SSHole NCSC.ch rating, Chrome/Edge fix, Apache httpd SUSE fix, Dixell XWEB EVO exploitation and fixes). Twenty-seven entries carry one record each from this fire (6 updates, 10 corrections, 11 improvements; 12 internal), and one entry was recovered (Datadog's ARTEX activity in AWS). The report is docs/audits/2026-11-15-quality-audit.md.

Verification & coverage notes

  • Claims: the open partial claim of cleanup wave 05 (2026-10-21T1147Z-audit, partial 2026-10-21T11:47:42Z wave=05) still stands on main; the scheduled audit ignores a partial claim (Phase 0 step 2), and it is more than 48 h old.
  • Scope: 38 entries filed in the window and 18 older entries the week's fires updated; 23 entries set aside as checked by the 2026-11-08 audit's own loop (20 with only its records in the window, 3 it recovered).
  • Truth passes: six batches, 1,646 ledger claims, every claim answered. Pre-pass leads: the Danfoss French original carried a stray word (fixed); the out-of-scope LiteLLM quote sits in a collapsed GitHub comment and is now bound to Wiz, which carries it.
  • Declined truth-pass findings, with reasons in the report: Danfoss "France alone" (Unit 42's figure caption says France), seven advisory technique-description gaps at the word bound, the Qubole self-claim, three append-only or metadata advisories, Node2Shell release-page sources.
  • KEV: twelve additions since 2026-11-08 (work/2026-11-15T1407Z-audit/kev-window.txt), eight covered; GPUStack, Openwave, BroadWorks and UnrealIRCd carry the week's fires' borderline-drop lines. No COVERED-STALE or RANSOMWARE row.
  • Stale-truth sweep: exploitation-consistency passes over the 56 window entries; supersession defects found by the passes (Chrome headline, Apache action, Dixell title and summary, AhsayCBS headline and action) are fixed through their records.
  • Calibration alarm: high 14 of 56 (25.0%); all 14 re-graded; Certighost moved to notable, Dixell XWEB EVO moved to high.
  • Backlog: empty at Phase 0. Duplicates: no CVE-sharing pair touching the window lacks a references[] link.
  • Recovered entry: Datadog's 2026-11-09 post on ARTEX in AWS clears PD-11(d) (cloud control-plane detection for an agentic framework the store tracks), at notable; it references the ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, exposed-app-credentials and WorkOS entries as distinct findings.
  • borderline-drop: OpenAM 16.1.4 (CVE-2026-123549/-123550/-123551), Azul Payara (CVE-2026-110003, CVE-2026-90908), Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320, GPUStack CVE-2026-102895, UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713, Node.js 2026-11-11 releases, React Server Components CVE-2026-126187, Adobe AEM APSB26-189, Roundcube 1.7.6, Drupal GraphQL Core Schema, Plex2Shell: the week's fires' drop grounds hold (no constituency footprint shown, authenticated, or regular patch cycle).
  • borderline-drop: Oracle's pre-announcement of the 2026-11-17 Critical Patch Update (the release falls to the 2026-11-17 and 11-18 fires); VulnCheck's Langflow overlap with the agentic secret-hunting address (one vendor canary, no CVE).
  • borderline-drop: Danfoss: Belgium's "indications" of Iranian links (one wire relay) and CERT-FR's naming of Shahid Shoostari for earlier attacks; Erowa, Gleis D/Medi Porta, Liechtenstein register investigation, Vaud CYBER26, Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing, Operation Endgame 2026-11-12, Saxony pagers, Berlin forensic interview, France NIS2 bill, BACS ESTV warning: no vector, nexus or obligation change.
  • borderline-drop: Huntress ClickFix roundup, Malbear Operation Snowball, Proofpoint Europe's Threat Landscape 2026, Kaspersky Q3 statistics, Sophos retail ransomware, Krebs on the Qilin administrator, Morphisec, TrendAI MCP and Hermes, Enea SilentAir, Greeter/Flowise, Citizen Lab Webloc, lab-only AI-agent research: no constituency decision.
  • Reverted update: the SonicWall CVE-2026-19868 entry received an update record citing CERT-FR AVI-1507 on SNWLID-2026-0021 as a second SonicOS fix (7.3.4-7015); verifier iteration 1 read the bulletin through SonicWall's PSIRT API and found it is the informational eMudhra DPI-SSL advisory, already carried by the eMudhra entry, so the entry file was reverted to its base and removed from updated_entry_ids[].
  • Systemic: a short out-of-slice check moved datadog-security-labs' rotation cursor on 2026-11-12 (fixed in v4.25); entry-shape did not check sources an update adds (fixed in tools/check_run.py, with a test).
  • Registry: ambiguous_labels added for SRG on actor:silent-ransom-group and Cereal on malware:cereal; six product records from sync_products.py.
  • Source health: connectwise-trust-center and bfv-verfassungsschutz-de repaired and now relevant; safeonweb-be answers HTTP 500 site-wide and stays the one UNSOLVED record. The five essential sources with no contribution all week read cleanly in the re-sweeps.
  • Reader pool (context): every jina key exhausted.
  • ATT&CK pin: up to date (local v20.1 == upstream v20.1).
  • Verifier loop: seven iterations; truth and editorial findings fell 18, 9, 3, 4, 5, 0, 0; iteration 6 CLEAN on a 101-claim post-fix pass, confirmed by iteration 7's full cold pass over all 183 claims. Iteration 5 found a defect in this fire's Check Point section outside its sampled scope, so a post-fix pass's quarter sample can miss what the confirmation pass then has to catch. Three low-confidence advisories from iteration 7 are left for the next audit (Chrome Exposure citation scope, Dixell takeaway citation, the declined file-name point).
  • Budget: 16 spawns (6 truth passes, 3 re-sweeps, 7 verifier iterations), 8,667,965 sub-agent tokens (work/2026-11-15T1407Z-audit/budget.tsv).
  • Coverage gaps: sygnia (blocked on every transport), nict-cynex-lettice (JS shell, no reader credit), belden-psirt (no content on any transport), lab52 and anssi-cyber-gouv-actualites (no working transport this audit), the EFS press page and the SentinelLABS post (unreadable to TA).

2026-11-15T0356Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 28 h · 3 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Window: gap 25.0 h (daily cadence, previous intel fire 2026-11-14T0255Z), window 28 h; a Saturday-to-Sunday window with the home-region feeds quiet (CERT.at newest 2026-10-21, BACS press 2026-11-05, NCSC Security Hub post 13178 of 2026-11-13). No outage backfill was triggered (the gap is the normal daily cadence); S3 swept the majors' listing pages for posts since 2026-11-13 anyway. KEV sweep: 0 additions in the window, no ransomware-flag flip on a covered CVE. Source slices were ranked on the rotation cursor alone; the previous-two-fires exclusion was not applied because it left the breaches slice empty.

Published: three new entries (PolinRider, ScreenConnect crypto-exchange bait sessions, The Gentlemen affiliate report) and one update record on the Cursor marketplace entry (Cursor's own report of 2026-11-13 gives the origin the entry said nobody had published). Deep dive: none, nothing cleared the bar.

  • Single-source: 2026-11-15/screenconnect-crypto-bait-guest-sessions-118-servers (Huntress alone, hypothesis stated as unobserved, ConnectWise bulletin unreadable); 2026-11-15/gentlemen-affiliate-vpn-no-mfa-da-gpo-locker-failed (Ransom-ISAC, reliability C, no victim named).
  • borderline-drop: jDownloads CVE-2026-117551 (Joomla), needs upload permission, no exploitation, Swiss footprint unknown.
  • borderline-drop: Fortinet FG-IR-26-187 revision of 2026-11-13 (Brotli decoder flaw), product-status list only, no fix or workaround, advisory not cited by the covered entry, so no patch decision changes.
  • borderline-drop: Qubole Wiz update of 2026-11-11; the "n0n" claim is relayed from a newsletter and unverified, the separate key-testing is already in the entry's sourcing note, no deployment of the bootable image is known.
  • borderline-drop: GeoVision camera software abuse (Huntress, 13 organisations), initial access unnamed, no CVE, no region; dropped on 2026-11-14 for the same reason.
  • borderline-drop: Unit 42 CL-STA-1238 (Cairn) and Elastic, Talos and Arctic Wolf agentic-framework internals (ARTEX, AntiFox), US-centred targets, class already covered by the ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI entries; dropped on 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14.
  • borderline-drop: FBI FLASH and DOJ action on FaceStealer, Swiss nexus indirect; dropped on 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14, no new fact.
  • borderline-drop: Project Zero "Full X" policy, effective 2027, no near-term decision.
  • borderline-drop: Elastic SANSAR (Ray job agent), CloudSEK Silent Lynx (Central Asia), Recorded Future survey (vendor survey), AMD SEV-SNP Mior and Skyfall (hypervisor-level attacker, CVSS 5.9).
  • borderline-drop: React Server Components CVE-2026-126187, application-code preconditions, no exploitation or proof of concept; dropped on 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13.
  • out-of-window: Saxony emergency pager exposure (heise 2026-11-12, Spiegel 2026-11-11) and the Operation Endgame round (Europol 2026-11-12), window_hours=28; both were also dropped by the 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14 fires, the pager item for lack of an access vector or actor.
  • borderline-drop: Quantum Systems QBase update-server compromise (sources 2026-11-13, no Swiss customer), Mittwald MCP-server intrusion (German host, post-mortem pending), Fireworks AI incident (folded into the Cursor update), Microsoft 365 outage of 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13 (capacity upgrade, not an attack).
  • Backlog: the one open row (ChimeraZ claim against the Belgian rescue zone Hainaut-Est) struck on 2026-11-15: six French-language searches found no confirmation and the cited page does not mention the zone.
  • Coverage gaps: belden-psirt (403 on every transport); sygnia (403 on every transport); lab52 (connection resets, reader pool dead); anssi-cyber-gouv-actualites (Incapsula challenge); databreaches-net article pages (403, feed works); fbi-gov, quantum-systems.com, beobachter.ch and connectwise-trust-center HTML pages (403, other routes used); jina reader pool exhausted.
  • Watchlist: none configured, sweeps were no-ops.
  • Candidate sources considered and not added: norforge (no feed), fireworks-ai-security-bulletins (low volume, the Cursor update carries the bulletin), lemagit-cyberhebdo (weekly issue URLs change each week).
  • Mid-run stop-hook nudges to commit were declined; the run commits once, after the gate and the verifier loop.
  • Verification: three iterations, all NEEDS_FIXES (iteration 1: 11 truth, 1 editorial; iteration 2: 3 truth, 2 editorial; iteration 3: 1 truth, 0 editorial, a low-confidence wallet-attribution wording). The final residual of 1 was fixed after the pass and not re-verified; the loop stopped on the low-residual early exit. Iteration 1 caught two timestamps written ahead of the clock and a dropped hedge, both fixed.
  • The gate's dedup advisory on actor:thegentlemen is deliberate: the 2026-11-07 Kaspersky entry covers a different incident (a monitoring server's root password on ESXi and Proxmox), this one an SSL-VPN intrusion with a GPO locker failure.
  • Note for the next audit: the Cursor update was trimmed twice to stay within the 550-word analysis bound; the entry carries its original wording otherwise.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-14
item.description:
• Kaspersky: BlackNevas used vCenter Host Profiles to enable SSH on ESXi, destroyed backups first, then wiped datastores. Kaspersky GERT describes a ten-day engagement in which an adversary, identified as BlackNevas from its ransom notes, used credentials taken from systems outside the virtualisation layer to reach both vCenter appliances, persisted on one with a remote-access agent and a tunnel installed as a VMware-lookalike systemd service, then used vCenter Host Profile remediation to switch SSH on across four ESXi hosts, destroyed the backup environment first and detonated a wiper-capable locker that took every virtual machine. Kaspersky states no initial access vector, victim sector or country, and no virtualisation-layer vulnerability was exploited. →
  • GitLab critical patch: a merge request can reach a Git heap overflow on Gitaly; update to 19.5.4, 19.4.6 or 19.3.8. GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch release on 2026-11-10 for CVE-2026-105437, a heap overflow in Git that, per GitLab, any user who can create a project and open a merge request reaches, and that can run commands as the git user with access to every repository on that Gitaly node. Git 2.56.1 and its backports fix the same flaw and five others, among them CVE-2026-111760, code execution when a malicious repository is cloned with --recurse-submodules; no source reports exploitation. →
  • Red Hat Quay: anonymous signing-key takeover and cross-tenant token theft; update to your branch's fixed release. Red Hat's CNA records say an unauthenticated client of Red Hat Quay can obtain an anonymous registry token, present it to the service-key rotation endpoint and install its own signing key (CVE-2026-123710, CVSS 3.1 9.8), and that an account that can create a namespace containing an underscore can retrieve other tenants' robot tokens (CVE-2026-110697, 9.9). Red Hat fixed both in Quay 3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 and 3.18.3, lists Quay 5 and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift 2 as affected with no fix, and NCSC Switzerland lists exploitation as unknown. →

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures3 items

NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT BlackNevas case: credentials from systems outside the virtualisation layer reach both vCenter appliances, a remote-access agent and a VMware-lookalike tunnel service persist, vCenter Host Profile remediation switches SSH on across the ESXi hosts, backups are destroyed first and a wipe of the datastores detonates over ten days, with no vulnerability exploited

Kaspersky GERT describes an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organisation's virtualisation estate over ten days: four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine on them, both vCenter Server Appliances and all connected backup infrastructure (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). No virtualisation-layer vulnerability was exploited: credentials obtained from non-virtualisation systems inside the perimeter reached the appliances, and every action against ESXi ran through legitimate VMware management interfaces (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The activity is attributed to BlackNevas through the ransom notes (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

The attackers logged in as root over SSH to the vCenter appliance that manages virtualisation disaster recovery, fetched and deployed MeshAgent with a shell script 43 seconds later, and about four hours later returned through MeshAgent to install the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit whose name, description and Restart=always imitate appliance housekeeping (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). They then used vCenter Host Profiles to change the TSM-SSH service state: eleven minutes after the first configuration read SSH was enabled on the target ESXi hosts, and direct SSH to the hosts then came from the vCenter appliance address (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). Payloads went to ESXi over SFTP, a self-test of the executable ran about three hours before the final detonation, and about the first 2 KB of the virtual disk files were overwritten (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The backup environment fell first: the attacker extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on the backup infrastructure, disabled antivirus there days earlier, then stopped backup services and encrypted the recovery infrastructure, all before ESXi detonation (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A vCenter and ESXi estate where accounts from systems outside the virtualisation layer can reach the vCenter appliances and where Host Profile remediation can change the SSH service state; the article names no version (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In vCenter events and tasks and in vpxa.log and vobd.log, Host Profile remediation that changes TSM or TSM-SSH from policy-disabled to running outside an approved change window, which Kaspersky rates critical when an SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance to the same host follows within 15 minutes; on the vCenter appliance, a new VMware-looking systemd unit absent from the organisation's list of trusted services; in ESXi shell logs, execution of a newly staged executable under /tmp followed by access to /vmfs; and preserved hostprofiletrace.log (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). ESXi logs sit in a ramdisk that is cleared at reboot, so Kaspersky says not to begin by rebooting a host (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Triage: each Host Profile step is legitimate alone, so the distinguishing context is authorisation, timing, source account, change window and whether the desired state weakens security; a VMware-looking service is not malicious by default, since custom integrations exist, but one absent from the trusted list is a high-confidence anomaly, and chmod +x is ambiguous alone while execution of a newly staged executable from /tmp is itself a strong indicator (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Treat the vCenter appliances as the control plane to protect: alert on Host Profile changes to TSM-SSH outside change windows and on SSH from vCenter to ESXi that follows them, review VMware-looking services on the appliances against a trusted list, and keep backup-platform credentials and administration separate from the systems that can reach vCenter, because the backup environment was destroyed before the hosts (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Luna Moth returns to law firms that likely did not pay, with a token handoff: a video-call 'IT support' agent has the employee copy a Microsoft Graph access token out of Microsoft 365 Copilot through browser developer tools, then bulk-downloads files from the attacker's own server (ReliaQuest)

ReliaQuest says Luna Moth, also called Silent Ransom Group, has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023 and in October and early November went back to firms it had extorted in May and August; those firms appear on the group's leak site, which ReliaQuest says suggests they likely did not pay, and the group exfiltrated a second round of data (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). The approach reverses the group's earlier flow: a blank-subject email from a free address carries a deliberately invalid PDF that crashes the viewer, and the attacker then calls the target, often on a personal number outside corporate call controls, posing as IT support responding to a "malicious email" (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). By late August the group paired video calls with a built-in remote-assistance tool, and by October the video call alone carried both the conversation and the screen control (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

On the call the attacker has the employee open Microsoft 365 Copilot in the browser on a managed, compliant laptop, open the browser's developer tools to find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph and copy the access token it carries, and paste the token into a public text-sharing site where the attacker retrieves it (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Within a minute the attacker replays the token from its own server and downloads files en masse through the Graph API, thousands in about an hour (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). The stolen token passes Conditional Access because the device check runs only at sign-in, not when the token is later used, and, unlike device-code phishing, the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and then handed over (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Nothing is installed, and the video-call applications are signed legitimate software (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant whose staff can open browser developer tools and take calls from outside IT, with Microsoft 365 Copilot reachable in the browser; ReliaQuest says law firms are the current focus and other sectors holding similarly sensitive data could be next (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).
Detection
With no malware or endpoint alert, the evidence is ordinary-looking events, a blank email, an external video-call session and Graph access from an unfamiliar address, which ReliaQuest says to correlate across email, video-call and Microsoft 365 logs; a video-call screen share, a Copilot session, a visit to a text-sharing site and Graph file access from an unfamiliar address are each ordinary alone and together can indicate a token handoff (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). Video-call platform logs, web proxy or DNS logs and Microsoft 365 audit logs each record part of the handoff but rarely reach a detection pipeline (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).
Defender takeaway
Disable developer tools through Group Policy on managed browsers and block Graph Explorer and the browser net-export pages, because the handoff depends on users reading tokens out of browsers; pilot Continuous Access Evaluation with strict location enforcement, defining every egress address including secure web gateway ranges as a named location; and tell staff that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12). ReliaQuest notes that default Microsoft access tokens last 60 to 90 minutes and that Continuous Access Evaluation can extend supported tokens to as long as 28 hours (ReliaQuest, 2026-11-12).

CyberStrikeAI turned on AWS: Elastic reads one server's 16 days across eight identities in four accounts, 56 user-data reads in 141 milliseconds, and why six detections each rated medium or low and only the source address tied them together

Between 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-16 one server serving a CyberStrikeAI web interface used the credentials of eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts, the first case Elastic has seen of this tooling turned on AWS (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). It started by validating identities: GetCallerIdentity on four IAM users in three accounts within 51 minutes, three of the calls in the same second (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). An instance role then read a secret, made one user-data request and fired 56 more in 141 milliseconds, spacing Elastic says fits tooling working through a prepared list of instance IDs (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). On 2026-10-02 another instance role read an encrypted Systems Manager parameter and issued a SendCommand 29 seconds later, which Elastic calls the highest-risk activity; the audit log does not show the command or its outcome (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). After 14 quiet days the server returned and revalidated credentials, including a user in a fourth account (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Elastic does not know how the credentials were obtained and infers that the instance-role sessions, used from an outside address, were taken from the instances, for example through SSRF or host compromise (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Team Cymru counted 21 unique addresses running CyberStrikeAI between 2026-01-20 and 2026-02-26 (Team Cymru, 2026-03-02).

Exposure
AWS accounts where IAM user keys or instance-role credentials can leave the account and the principals may read EC2 user data or Secrets Manager values or send Systems Manager commands; secrets in user data are readable by any such principal and Elastic says to treat them as exposed (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, a burst of user-data requests from one role session; a first-time GetCallerIdentity from one external address across several users or accounts within a minute; GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance-role session whose source address is neither the instance nor your NAT; and a decrypting GetParameter followed within a minute by an SSM SendCommand from the same role (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). Six rules fired at medium or low severity, and Elastic recommends correlating such alerts by source address over a flexible window, since the gaps between steps ran from 141 milliseconds to 14 days (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

Triage: each call is one a legitimate role makes every day, so the discriminators are the source address, the number of distinct identities, accounts or instances one address touches in minutes, and the decrypt-then-SendCommand pairing (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Correlate low and medium cloud alerts by source address, restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for user data to the roles that need it, move secrets out of user data, and on a hit rotate instance-role credentials by replacing the instance profile or the instance, because stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13). As of November none of the three servers served the CyberStrikeAI interface, so the indicator addresses are for retrospective hunting (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-13).

NOTABLECVE-2026-105437 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-105437, GitLab self-managed 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 critical patch release: a heap overflow in Git's merge code that a user who can open a merge request can trigger for command execution as the git user on the Gitaly node; Git 2.56.1 also fixes CVE-2026-111760, code execution when a malicious repository is cloned with submodules; no exploitation reported

GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch release on 2026-11-10, 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 for CE and EE, for CVE-2026-105437, a vulnerability in Git that under certain conditions gives out-of-bounds heap writes that could run arbitrary commands in Gitaly's environment; it affects all versions from 16.2 before 19.3.8, 19.4 before 19.4.6 and 19.5 before 19.5.4, while GitLab.com and Dedicated already run a patched version (GitLab, 2026-11-10). GitLab's detection page says any user who can create a project and open a merge request reaches the flaw, which gives command execution as the git operating-system user and read and write access to every repository on that Gitaly node (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Git 2.56.1 and the backports 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2 of 2026-11-10 fix the same flaw and five others (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The one that matters on workstations and CI runners is CVE-2026-111760: a long path that passes validation is written as .git and replaces a freshly cloned submodule's .git file with a symlink to a directory that holds attacker hooks or configuration, which GitHub says can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone (oss-security, 2026-11-11; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The maintainers believe it is only triggerable with --recurse-submodules and note that such a repository fails fsck, which does not protect downstream users, since an innocuous-looking .gitmodules pointing at it suffices (oss-security, 2026-11-11). GitHub Enterprise Server fixes are in 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4, and GitHub is coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the Copilot app with patched Git (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10); Git for Windows 2.56.1.windows.1 addresses the issue (Git for Windows, 2026-11-10). No source reports exploitation; GitLab documents a lab reproduction in which opening one merge request left a crash entry within a second and a half (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A self-managed GitLab CE or EE in the affected ranges that lets users create projects and merge requests, or any Git older than the fixed releases on a workstation, CI runner or service that clones or merges untrusted repositories; applications that bundle Git need their own update (GitLab, 2026-11-10; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10).
Detection
GitLab's rule fires when the error field of a Gitaly event contains merge-tree: signal: followed by anything other than killed or terminated, and a .gitattributes in the target branch that sets an unusually large conflict-marker-size supports a true positive; GitLab says a working attempt is silent, a clean result does not prove the flaw was not used, the rules rest on error wording captured on 19.4.1 only, and many installs do not ship the Gitaly and Sidekiq logs (GitLab, 2026-11-12). On build hosts, hook scripts or shells spawned by git during a recursive clone are the behavior CVE-2026-111760 produces.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade self-managed GitLab to a fixed release and, for a self-compiled install, rebuild both the Git in Gitaly and the Git at git.bin_path or move the distribution Git to 2.56.1 or later (GitLab, 2026-11-10); until then limit who can create projects and sign up, and on a hit treat the instance and every repository on that Gitaly node as compromised (GitLab, 2026-11-12). Servers that cannot upgrade yet can set conflict-marker-size=7 in each repository's info/attributes or turn off the merge checks for untrusted repositories (The Hacker News, 2026-11-11). Update Git on runners and workstations and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories until it is done.

NOTABLECVE-2026-123710 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-123710 and CVE-2026-110697, Red Hat Quay: an anonymous client can install its own registry signing key and read or overwrite every private image (CVSS 3.1 9.8), and a low-privilege account can steal other tenants' robot tokens (9.9); fixed in Quay 3.9.28 to 3.18.3, no fix for Quay 5 or the mirror registry, no exploitation reported

Red Hat's record for CVE-2026-123710 says an unauthenticated client of Red Hat Quay can obtain an anonymous registry token with an audience it chooses, present it to the service-key rotation endpoint and install its own approved signing key with no expiry (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). NCSC Switzerland summarises the impact as letting network attackers with anonymous or low-privileged access read, overwrite or poison private container images and steal registry credentials, compromising the software supply chain (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13). The condition is that the /keys endpoint is reachable by untrusted clients (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); anonymous access is on by default, and turning it off does not protect, because any valid Quay account can still exploit the flaw (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).

CVE-2026-110697 lets an attacker who creates a namespace containing an underscore match and retrieve robot accounts and their decrypted tokens from other tenants' namespaces; Red Hat says it needs no elevated privileges or victim interaction and that, where Quay is OpenShift's integrated registry, stolen robot credentials can inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).

Red Hat's page for the second flaw lists the fixed builds 3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 and 3.18.3 and says Quay.io is already fixed (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); its CSAF record for the first flaw links eight Quay errata, RHSA-2026:99019 and 99021 to 99027, as its fixes and lists Red Hat Quay 5 and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift 2 as affected with no fix available (Red Hat, 2026-11-13). NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A Red Hat Quay registry, standalone, deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift or as the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift, whose /keys endpoint untrusted clients can reach, and for the second flaw a multi-tenant registry where an account can create namespaces (Red Hat, 2026-11-13; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In Quay audit logs, service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events with a null expiration_date and approved service keys nobody recognises (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); for token theft, registry pulls or pushes that do not match expected robot-account usage (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). A planted signing key survives password resets and robot-token regeneration (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Update to the fixed release of your branch and, until then, restrict /keys at the proxy or load balancer to trusted internal components; a deleted rogue key is not durable before the fix, because the anonymous request can install a new one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). Where /keys was reachable, treat registry images as unverified until the keys are reviewed and, for the second flaw, restrict who can create namespaces with an underscore and rotate robot tokens of any namespace that collides with one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).

Microsoft's analysis describes RelayTrap, a rogue client built on the endpoint to deliver a payload to the technician who connects, and browser-cookie routines designed to push tools through the Shared Toolbox; ConnectWise says clients 26.6.5 and later block the transfer, and a second wave on 2026-11-13 hit 205 hosts at 41 organisations, one with a self-hosted RMM+, so every technician client now belongs on the action list.

A watcher on the endpoint enumerates the ScreenConnect client services and builds RelayTrap for each with the .NET C# compiler, and the toolkit's browser code searches Chrome, Edge, Opera and Opera GX profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH; a console-distribution component is designed to combine the cookie with the anti-forgery and access tokens, upload a payload, queue it through the Shared Toolbox and remove the uploaded item afterwards (Microsoft, 2026-11-13).
