threat12 Nov 04:05Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 · Trend Micro (TrendAI) · Symantec Threat Hunter Team (Broadcom)

02Trending vulnerabilities2 items

NOTABLENATOA2

Plone security fix of 2026-11-10: a chain of missing security declarations and opened modules lets an anonymous visitor run code on the server in every supported Plone version and back to 4.3; a working proof of concept exists, no CVE ids yet, no exploitation reported

The Plone and Zope security team says the fixes it released on 2026-11-10 close a chain of several issues that together let an anonymous visitor run code on the server, in all supported Plone versions (6.0, 6.1 and 6.2) and in older ones back to at least 4.3 (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The anonymous entry point is Products.CMFEditions: the conditional modifiers in portal_modifier had no security declarations, so an anonymous visitor could change a modifier's TALES condition and then run it, and the condition is also evaluated when an editor saves versioned content (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). Products.CMFPlone, Products.MimetypesRegistry and plone.batching opened whole modules to restricted code, which let TALES expressions and Python scripts escape the sandbox and reach modules such as os, and plone.restapi opened the json module (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The CMFEditions advisory rates its flaw 9.8 with no privileges required and states that a working proof of concept exists; the team says details are public and that with current AI tools it may not take long to turn them into a working exploit, and no source reports exploitation (Plone, 2026-11-10; Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

The fixed packages are CMFPlone 6.2.3, 6.1.6 and 6.0.16 with the helper package versions the announcement lists, or the hotfix Products.PloneHotfix20261110, which covers Plone 4.3 to 6.2, and all Zope instances must be restarted afterwards (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The team's pre-announcement of 2026-11-02 already gave the workaround, to block any URL containing portal_modifier at the web server at any path depth, which only helps if Zope's own port cannot be reached directly; the team advises keeping it after updating (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-02). After the fix, restricted code can import only the names Plone itself needs from the closed modules, so custom scripts that import others now get an Unauthorized error (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Plone site reachable by anonymous visitors, on a version below the fixed packages; no source states a non-default setting that the anonymous path needs, and Plone 5.2 and older are out of security support, with the fix released as an exception.
Detection
Web-server access logs for anonymous requests whose path contains portal_modifier; and the stored state, which survives the update: a changed modifier condition stays in the database, so as Manager open @@check-modifier-conditions on the site root, or read the hotfix's startup log line that reports modified versioning conditions, and treat the server as compromised if a condition is not recognised, although defaults have changed over time so a difference alone is not an attack (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update or install the hotfix and restart now on every internet-facing Plone site, keep the portal_modifier block in place, and run the modifier-condition check afterwards, because the fix does not remove a condition an anonymous request already stored.
vulnerability12 Nov 04:12Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Plone Security Team · Plone (GitHub Security Advisory, Products.CMFEditions)
NOTABLECVE-2026-119618updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-119618, Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70: a race in mod_http2 assign_headers() corrupts heap memory and leads to remote code execution on servers with HTTP/2 enabled; fixed in 2.4.71, Red Hat calls it unauthenticated and claims public exploit research, Axis OS version 6.50.5.10 and higher is affected with no fixed release yet, no exploitation reported

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71, released on 2026-11-11, fixes CVE-2026-119618, a race in mod_http2's assign_headers() that the project rates critical and says can lead to remote code execution, in versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11). The project publishes no CVSS score; Red Hat scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 and says it allows unauthenticated remote code execution, with a worker thread writing into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared lock-free allocator (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11). Red Hat states that only servers with HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) enabled through the Protocols directive are affected and that HTTP/1.1-only servers are not (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11); the project's own page is silent on that prerequisite (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11).

On exploitation the sources differ. Wiz wrote at its publication that no exploit was available and no exploitation in the wild was reported (Wiz, 2026-11-11), while Red Hat says public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled, without linking it (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11). A researcher has since posted a test setup that reports memory corruption and Apache child-process crashes on 2.4.70, and Wordfence says it does not demonstrate remote command execution (Wordfence, 2026-11-12). No source reports attacks, and the project's advisory carries no exploitation or workaround statement (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11).

The upstream fix is 2.4.71. The project lists standalone mod_h2 releases from GitHub, 2.0.8 through 2.0.42, as affected and names no fixed standalone release (Apache HTTP Server project, 2026-11-11). Red Hat shipped mod_http2 errata for RHEL 9 (mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1) and RHEL 10 (mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1) on 2026-11-11, rates them Important (Red Hat, 2026-11-11; Red Hat, 2026-11-11), says the packages allocate each HTTP/2 stream from a separate allocator, which makes exploitation substantially more complex, and lists RHEL 8 and earlier as not affected (Red Hat Product Security, 2026-11-11); Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine and SUSE Linux Enterprise 15 SP7 ship fixed packages (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-11-15; Ubuntu, 2026-11-12; Alpine Linux, 2026-11-13; SUSE, 2026-11-13). Axis says AXIS OS version 6.50.5.10 or higher is affected and has no fixed release yet, a service release for all affected tracks being planned within the next couple of weeks, and gives a workaround that sets System.HTTP2.AllowH2 and System.HTTP2.AllowH2c to no (Axis, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
An Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, or a distribution mod_http2 build without the vendor's fix, that has the mod_http2 module loaded and h2 or h2c in a Protocols directive for the server or a virtual host; the loaded modules and the Protocols directives of the configuration show it, and the distribution advisory, not the upstream version string, shows whether a backported fix is installed; AXIS OS version 6.50.5.10 and higher is affected (Axis, 2026-11-16).
Detection
Neither the project nor Red Hat publishes indicators of compromise; the researcher's test shows the corruption as httpd child-process crashes inside the allocator and HTTP/2 stream code (researcher repository, 2026-11-12), so watch for child crashes in the error log.
Defender takeaway
Update internet-facing servers that serve HTTP/2 to 2.4.71 or the distribution's fixed package and restart, and where no fix is available yet remove h2 and h2c from Protocols until it is (Wiz advises disabling HTTP/2 temporarily, Wiz, 2026-11-11), because Red Hat describes an unauthenticated path and a public exploit while the project describes neither.

eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block the eight ECDSA intermediates, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go)

First published 2026-10-21 · open finding →

Update12 Nov 2026 04:26 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

eMudhra's full incident report of 2026-11-10 says eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) were revoked on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation because their keys were handled in the memory of a Python script, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its policy; it had said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted, no source says the keys leaked, and the G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates.

eMudhra posted its full incident report in the Mozilla bug on 2026-11-10 (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). For the eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) it says the key integrity is intact, all signatures verifying, but that during re-import the private-key material was handled in the volatile memory of a Python process on the ceremony host, which is not consistent with its certification practice statement, so the RSA issuers are treated as not meeting it; it adds that logs cannot reliably establish or exclude how that material was handled (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). It identified this in early November after a root-program discussion, revoked the eight issuers on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation, not the compromise reason used for the ECDSA set, and had written on 2026-10-19 that the RSA issuers were not impacted (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-10-19). The G2C issuers were put into production in May 2026 and issued end-entity certificates, the last on 2026-11-03, after which issuance from them stopped; BleepingComputer reports that eMudhra says the affected customer certificates were replaced or migrated, and that the company has not detected malicious use of the keys (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-11). eMudhra also decided to exit public TLS, with all issuance from its emSign Root CA - G1 hierarchy to stop before 2026-11-16 and an independent review due 2026-12-04 (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10). No page read from Google, Microsoft, Apple, Mozilla or the incident tracker names the G2B or G2C issuers or says a vendor blocked them.

Polarion, Solid Edge, Calibre, Capital and four other software products are listed as not affected because Node.js is not present or predates Brotli (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-11-10).   • On every ScreenConnect instance your organisation or its IT providers run, disable the RMM+ extension immediately, verify it stays disabled and do not re-enable or reinstall it (on-premises instances by hand; ConnectWise removed it from cloud-hosted ones), review Run Command and Toolbox history and the instance audit logs for executions nobody started, including before 2026-11-11, and check managed endpoints for a second ScreenConnect client service; open no interactive session to a suspect host, use EDR live response or WinRM, because a session can trigger the toolkit to spread to the technician's workstation; update every technician host client to ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later, because a cloud-console update does not update them.
    FindingCVE-2026-127063→
  • Update Chrome to the current Stable build, 157.0.8103.78 or later (157.0.8103.50 is the first fixed build), and Extended Stable to 156.0.8078.100 or later on every managed endpoint, force the browser relaunch now, update Edge to 157.0.4341.46 or later and Edge for Android to 157.0.4341.53, and install the other Chromium-browser updates as soon as each vendor lists CVE-2026-125350 as fixed.
    FindingCVE-2026-125350→
  • Upgrade every FortiMail to 8.0.2, 7.6.7 or 7.4.9 (a 7.2 unit moves to a fixed release; 7.2.10 for CVE-2026-126150 is not released), every FortiAuthenticator to 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, every FortiOS to 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 or 7.2.14 (a 7.0 unit migrates), and every FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer on 8.0.0 or 8.0.1, 7.6, 7.4 or 7.2 to 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 or 7.2.13 (7.0 migrates), internet-facing units and FortiMail first, because the advisories describe unauthenticated code execution and account takeover and Fortinet warns that patch differences show attackers where the weakness sits; keep the FGFM and oftp ports and every administrative interface off untrusted networks.

Verification & coverage notes

Window: standard 26 h (gap to the previous fire 24.0 h). KEV sweep: no catalogue additions in the window and no ransomware-flag flips on covered entries. Held backlog row left untouched: zohe-hainaut-est (no source found, expiry 2026-11-17).

  • borderline-drop: PowerFolder cloud breach and /wopi/ server flaw, no CVE, no technical detail, no constituency deployment shown
  • borderline-drop: CNIL ten sanctions on French territorial authorities, generic hardening failings, no Swiss obligation change

Verification: four iterations. Iteration 1 found 29 findings (16 truth, 6 editorial, 7 advisory), iteration 2 found 19, iteration 3 found 9 (one new upstream fact: Huntress updated its ScreenConnect post with the RMM+ blank-access-key finding), and iteration 4 returned NEEDS_FIXES with truth 2 and editorial 0 and no F1 or F4, so decision rule 5 applied: the five findings were remediated, the gate re-run clean (58 pass, 0 warn, 0 fail), and the fire published on that early exit without a fifth pass. No double-CLEAN was reached; the two residual truth findings are fixed but unverified by a further cold pass, and the audit should give the ScreenConnect and Fortinet entries an independent read.

Operational notes: the jina reader pool is dead (every key HTTP 402), so pages that only the reader could serve were read by WebFetch or reported as unconfirmed. Research workers FU2 left six stray stub files at the filesystem root (/A_chrome_android.md, /A_chrome_android.err, /A_chrome_extended_156.md, /A_chrome_extended_156.err, /A_edge_security.md, /A_edge_security.err); the sandbox safety check denied deleting them and the run did not work around it, so the operator may remove them. They hold fetch scratch output only and are not part of the repo.

Gate note for the audit: check_run.py citation-cve matches an id against a skeleton that joins the id to the digits of the next bug number on Chrome Releases rows, so a clause naming CVE-2026-125346 on the Extended Stable page reads as a miss although the id is on the page; the Chrome entry avoids naming the id there. The three KEV additions the verifier listed for 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10 without entries (CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks, CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack, CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Webtop) were dispositioned as borderline-drops by the 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11 fires and are left for the audit sweep. Source health: seven records stay UNSOLVED. Fixed this run: ico-uk, safeonweb-be, netzwoche (recipes in sources_changed). Coverage gaps: connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport), sygnia (403), Siemens knowledge-base articles (login-gated), news-admin-ch, srf-news and swissinfo-ger (shallow reach through the listing recipes), the NCSC.ch BACS card recipe, ictjournal-ch, and rapid7's RSS (malformed).

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-11
item.description:
• Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 exploited: a crafted message file leaks authentication data; install the Office update. Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw (CVSS 3.1 6.5) that Microsoft marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed and that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10: a user who opens a crafted message file lets Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, which can disclose authentication information. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector; BleepingComputer reports that the disclosed credential is the user's NTLMv2 hash, and no source names the actor or the victims. →
  • Chrome zero-day CVE-2026-125350 exploited: update Chrome to 157.0.8103.50 and Edge to 157.0.4341.46 or later. Google's Stable-channel update of 2026-11-09 says an exploit for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in Chromium's XML component, exists in the wild; CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 and no source describes the attacks. The fix is in Stable 157.0.8103.50 (Linux) and 157.0.8103.50 or .51 (Windows, macOS) and in Extended Stable 156.0.8078.96, all of 2026-11-09, later Stable and Extended Stable builds of 2026-11-11 include it, and Microsoft's notes list the fix in Edge 157.0.4341.46 of 2026-11-09 and in Edge for Android 157.0.4341.53. →
  • Stolen Qubole vendor credentials assumed customers' idle AWS integration roles; a source-IP condition stops it. Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, reports that between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 an actor used IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with the data platform Qubole to assume customers' cross-account integration roles, each call carrying the correct External ID; most roles had otherwise been idle. Inside the affected accounts the actor listed resources, read Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration, tested harvested AWS, Entra ID and Okta credentials with TruffleHog and downloaded S3 data, in some cases whole buckets; no victim is named, the counts range from more than a dozen to dozens, and how the vendor identities were compromised is not known. →

Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Trending vulnerabilities 8Updates to prior coverage 8Action items 25

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

GhostFrame: Recorded Future's Insikt Group finds an ESXi post-exploitation framework (vmhostd-core implant, VM control panel, VMkatz credential theft) used by TAG-218, whose activity overlaps Settra ransomware and which targeted SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN appliances in the US and Europe

Insikt Group describes GhostFrame, a previously undocumented command-and-control and post-exploitation framework for compromised VMware ESXi hosts, which it saw used by TAG-218, a group "whose operations overlap with Settra ransomware" (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Operators must already hold root on the host: the implant, an ELF named vmhostd-core generated from a web operator panel, does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). It copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core, edits the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh and runs /sbin/auto-backup.sh to keep the change across reboots, masquerades as vmhostd, and about every five seconds disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly control that restricts execution of unsigned binaries, so an administrator who re-enables them is undone (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its command channel opens simultaneous TCP connections to one address on ports 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443, keeps the first that succeeds and retries after a random delay of 5 to 12 seconds, which Insikt notes is a network detection opportunity; the implant is mainly an in-memory shellcode loader (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10).

From the hypervisor the panel can list registered VMs, change power state, create or delete snapshots, enable VNC on a guest, run a SOCKS5 proxy for pivoting, intercept ESXi logins, and run the open-source VMkatz against VM memory snapshots, virtual disks or whole datastores which Insikt says may let an operator obtain NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets and NTDS.dit credentials without deploying malware inside each VM (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Insikt ties TAG-218's victim-facing servers to VPN-appliance targeting across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, "predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices", and says four of those organisations later appeared on the Settra leak site; it assesses that other financially motivated actors are highly likely to adopt the framework, which is an assessment, not an observation (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Unit 42 independently reports that after CVE-2026-0257 exploitation attackers pivot from the VPN gateway directly to the virtualization layer (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
ESXi hosts whose root credentials, SSH or shell, or vCenter are reachable after an edge compromise; no ESXi vulnerability is involved, so patching ESXi does not address it, and an estate that runs both a SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks or Fortinet VPN appliance and ESXi without isolated hypervisor management is in the pattern Insikt describes.
Detection
In ESXi file-integrity and shell-audit telemetry, changes to local.sh, a process masquerading as the host daemon or an unexpected executable under /opt, and repeated firewall-off and execInstalledOnly resets; in network telemetry, six near-simultaneous SYNs from the hypervisor management address to one destination on those ports, and any outbound command traffic from a hypervisor; in vCenter and ESXi logs, snapshot creation or deletion, VNC enablement and power-state changes outside change windows; in datastore telemetry, reads of VM memory-snapshot and virtual-disk files by an identity that is not the backup service.

Triage: administrators legitimately edit local.sh, create snapshots and use VNC; the discriminators are a firewall-off and execInstalledOnly loop, a /opt/vmhostd-core file or vmhostd process where the genuine daemon is vmware-hostd, and snapshot-file reads by a non-backup account.

Defender takeaway
Treat a VPN-appliance compromise as a possible hypervisor compromise and check the ESXi persistence files and the execInstalledOnly state before declaring the incident closed; restrict ESXi and vCenter management to dedicated administration hosts.
Correction15 Nov 2026 15:02 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditbody

Insikt Group gives the persistence file as /opt/vmhostd-core and says the implant presents its process as vmhostd, a name resembling the genuine vmware-hostd daemon; either the file or the process is the indicator it lists (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its reading of the VMkatz capability is hedged: the capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying credential-stealing malware inside each VM (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10).

threat11 Nov 03:41Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Recorded Future (Insikt Group) · Palo Alto Networks Unit 42
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Turla's Cereal toolset turns a compromised on-premises Exchange server into the command channel and mail collector at Kazakh and Romanian government bodies, with no attacker infrastructure and no new transport agent registered (ESET)

ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server on 2025-11-28 and on a Romanian government organisation's Exchange server compromised from 2025-12-23; in Romania the mail-collection module was configured to identify messages to or from NATO and EU institutional addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). ESET attributes Cereal to Turla with high confidence, on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarity to older Turla malware, and could not determine the initial access method, although it considers a vulnerability exploit possible because the servers are reachable from the internet (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

The command channel is the victim's own Exchange server. CerealNeuron runs on the compromised server and passively waits for requests on web paths made to look like Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic; a correctly encrypted request is treated as a command and a bad one gets a normal-looking Exchange error page, and ESET found no operator-controlled server and could not identify ingress addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). Each task runs as a small .NET assembly inside a CerealRunner (mailbox retrieval, Active Directory and WMI queries, LSA secrets extraction, file operations) (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealLoader, the only component written to disk in recognisable .NET form, abuses .NET VTable fixups so native code runs before managed code and is placed where trusted processes load it: the System32 wbem directory (ncobjapi.dll, wbemcomn.dll, loaded by WMI) and the .NET native image cache (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealBox, injected into EdgeTransport.exe, wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded, so "no new agent appears anywhere in Exchange's configuration"; it keeps messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match hard-coded sender, recipient, subject or attachment-name lists and stages them compressed and encrypted on disk for exfiltration through CerealNeuron (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any organisation that runs Microsoft Exchange on premises with a role reachable from the internet; ESET names no vulnerable version, so exposure is the deployment model.
Detection
File-integrity telemetry on the Exchange host for DLLs in the System32 wbem directory and .NET native image cache files that do not match the Microsoft originals; module telemetry for non-Microsoft assemblies loaded into EdgeTransport.exe while Get-TransportAgent lists nothing new; web-server logs for requests to the Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync look-alike paths from clients with no matching mailbox flow, whose encrypted bodies return a generic error page; and Exchange Web Services mailbox retrievals made from the server's own context. ReversingLabs adds live HTTP.sys listeners (netsh http show servicestate) and proxy, load-balancer and WAF logs for the look-alike paths, proxy DLLs that mimic system libraries in the service directories, and module loads in WmiPrvSE.exe (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). With no external C2 and no known entry vector, the check is a compromise assessment of every internet-facing Exchange server.

Triage: third-party anti-spam, data-loss-prevention and archiving products also inject into the transport service, but they are vendor-signed and appear in the transport-agent configuration, which CerealBox does not; the native image cache regenerates legitimately after .NET updates, so only a file that does not match the Microsoft binary is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat internet-facing Exchange servers as top-tier assets, baseline the wbem directory and the native image cache, and run the compromise assessment now, because network-only detection will not find a channel that rides the victim's own web paths.
Improvement20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsourcesbody

ReversingLabs correlated ESET's published loader samples and says the same files carry different vendor names, CerealLoader at ESET, BlankPage in Microsoft Defender and CerealMood in other engines, so a hunt on a single family name can miss matches; it says the work extends the artifacts defenders can search for and establishes no additional victims or initial-access method (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). Its hunting guidance (HTTP.sys listeners, proxy-DLL loaders such as version.dll and WTSAPI32.dll, and WmiPrvSE.exe module loads) is in the Detection line (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19).

CopperDragon: Check Point ties three China-nexus intrusion sets to one Sparrow-framework supplier, among them SilentDelivery watering holes on government, shipping, IT and research sites that show a fake Chrome certificate warning (Czech Republic, Germany and France in its telemetry)

Check Point Research's year-long investigation groups three intrusion sets under one malware-supply entity it calls CopperDragon, a possible "digital quartermaster" for China-nexus actors that use the cross-platform Sparrow framework (FamousSparrow and Earth Estries among them); Check Point itself cautions that the use of the same backdoor or C2 infrastructure "does not necessarily mean" the same actor ran two intrusions, so this is a hypothesis (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10).

SilentDelivery, active since early 2026 against Europe and Asia, is the set nearest the constituency. Compromised government, shipping, IT and research websites, one through cross-site scripting in an unsanitised input field, carry obfuscated JavaScript that fingerprints the visitor and replaces the page with a language-localised fake Google Chrome SSL warning urging a "Certificate Fix" utility; the MSI, served from compromised cloud storage buckets, installs the new SquadC backdoor or a SparrowDoor variant (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). SquadC can be set to run only while a browser process is alive, persists through a Run key named WindowsUpdateAssist, and offers file operations, command execution and screenshots. A second route is a spear-phishing RAR whose LNK abuses ftp.exe, with the same C2 (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). Positive Technologies independently documented the same fake-certificate chain, with victims in Taiwan, Germany, Indonesia and the Czech Republic (Positive Technologies, 2026-08-21).

The other two sets show what follows an intrusion. OceanGate in Asia starts from an exploited internet-facing Linux server and moves through trojanised ssh and sshd binaries that log passwords, a Linux backdoor that can load a kernel rootkit, FRP and Chisel tunnels, a hidden local administrator account and an LSA security-package credential interceptor; recent SparrowDoor builds embed the WinDivert driver to share a service port such as 443. DarkWire against Latin American telecom and government bodies uses DLL sideloading of uncommon executables, SoftEther VPN renamed to system-process names, DNS MX tunnelling and WMI lateral movement (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). No Swiss victim is named.

Exposure
Staff of public bodies, shipping, IT and research organisations who browse peer websites, web teams whose sites accept unsanitised input, and Windows endpoints that let a standard user run an MSI from a browser download.
Detection
In endpoint telemetry, a browser followed by msiexec running an installer named like a certificate repair utility and a new Run key value with an update-themed name; in module-load telemetry, DLL sideloading by rarely abused executables, and the WinDivert driver loaded by a process that is not a VPN or firewall product; in account telemetry, a new local administrator account; on Linux, ssh and sshd binaries that differ from the package-manager copy and frpc or chisel binaries; in DNS, MX-query volume from servers that send no mail.

Triage: WinDivert is legitimate in VPN and firewall products, so the signal is a parent that is a sideloaded DLL or backdoor rather than the vendor's signed service; SoftEther running under a system-process name such as vmtoolsd.exe is not legitimate; a genuine Chrome SSL warning is never cleared by installing an MSI.

Defender takeaway
Treat a browser page that offers a "certificate fix" installer as an incident trigger and stop standard users running MSI installers from a browser download; web teams of government and research sites should check for injected third-party script and input-handling flaws, because a compromised site becomes a delivery vehicle for its peers.

The SoftEther discriminator is the name, not the path: Check Point says the operators renamed SoftEther VPN to names such as vmtoolsd.exe and csrss.exe and deliberately placed their tools in existing system directories instead of creating new ones (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10), so a SoftEther binary or configuration under a system-process or VMware Tools name is the signal, wherever it sits.

Qubole: an attacker used IAM credentials from a vendor-associated AWS account to assume dormant cross-account integration roles in dozens of customer accounts, then harvested secrets and validated Entra ID and Okta client credentials (Wiz and Sentra, 14 to 26 October)

Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole, a big-data platform, between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 (Wiz, 2026-11-09). The actor used two Qubole IAM users to call sts:AssumeRole on the cross-account integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account; "every AssumeRole request we attributed to the threat actor included an External ID, and every one succeeded", most of the roles were otherwise not in use, and the traffic came from a rented hosting server and commercial VPN exits, not the AWS infrastructure where legitimate platform traffic originates (Wiz, 2026-11-09; Sentra, 2026-11-09).

Inside the affected accounts the actor enumerated resources, read Lambda function configuration, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, ran TruffleHog to test AWS access keys, Entra ID service-principal client secrets and Okta client credentials it found, and then downloaded S3 data opportunistically, in some cases whole buckets in one session (Wiz, 2026-11-09). Wiz found no tie to other reported activity and judges the targeting opportunistic; how the Qubole IAM users were compromised is not stated. Sentra writes that dozens of Qubole customers were impacted, and BleepingComputer could not find a public Qubole announcement (Sentra, 2026-11-09; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No Swiss or public-sector victim is named, but the exposure is shared by any account that gave a data or analytics vendor a cross-account role and left it in place.

Exposure
Any AWS account holding an IAM role whose trust policy lets a Qubole account, or any other vendor account, assume it, including roles left from integrations that ended; the roles' trust policies and last-used data show them, and Wiz publishes the vendor account identifier, the two principals and the attacker address ranges for a CloudTrail hunt back to 2026-10-01 (Wiz, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, AssumeRole events into integration roles whose calling identity is the vendor account but whose source address is not AWS infrastructure, and session names with a consistent attacker-chosen prefix; GetCallerIdentity calls from many keys within seconds and Entra ID or Okta sign-ins by service principals or clients right after, as the actor validates credentials; ListSecrets, GetSecretValue, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration reads in bursts. Object reads are absent from CloudTrail management events, so S3 data events or server access logs must be on, and Wiz says missing logs left responders unable to see what was read (Wiz, 2026-11-09).

Triage: legitimate vendor traffic comes from the vendor's own AWS infrastructure; the correct External ID does not discriminate, because it is logged in plaintext and often stored by the vendor, while a vendor role assumed from a consumer VPN or a hosting provider the vendor has never used is the high-signal case.

Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party trust relationships, delete the roles of ended integrations, narrow each trusted principal to the vendor's specific principal and add a source-address or endpoint condition, which Wiz says alone would have blocked every observed assumption; after an incident, revoke the issued role sessions and rotate every secret, parameter, Lambda variable and identity-provider credential the role could read.

CVE-2026-124194, Microsoft Outlook: opening a crafted message file makes Outlook reach an attacker-chosen network location without the usual warning and disclose authentication information; exploited as a zero-day, fixed in the November 2026 updates and listed by CISA (CVSS 3.1 6.5)

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw (CWE-356, the product does not warn the user of an unsafe action) scored CVSS 3.1 6.5, which the Security Update Guide marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted message file and convinces the user to open it, whereupon Outlook may connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, "potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user"; the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, so the file has to be opened (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 (CISA, 2026-11-10), and BleepingComputer counts it as the one actively exploited zero-day of this Patch Tuesday (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). The affected products are Outlook in Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2024 (fixed in 16.0.17932.21140) and Office LTSC 2021 (fixed in 16.0.14334.21048); Microsoft 365 Apps take the fix through the Office security-update channel (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10). BleepingComputer calls it an NTLM credential disclosure flaw: opening the attachment makes Windows connect to an attacker-controlled share and expose the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be captured and cracked offline (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No source names the actor or the victims.

Exposure
Every Outlook desktop below those builds; the build shows under File, Office Account, and the delivery path is mail or a download that carries a message file, which the user must open.
Detection
Outbound connections to non-corporate addresses over SMB (TCP 445), WebDAV or HTTPS from OUTLOOK.EXE or from the user's session shortly after a message-file attachment is opened, authentication events carrying the user's identity toward an external address, and mail-gateway logs for message-file attachments from unknown senders. Because the credential material may already have been captured before the patch, the check also covers the weeks before it. The disclosed material is the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be cracked offline or used to impersonate the user, so also watch for later logons by the account from unfamiliar hosts.

Triage: Outlook legitimately contacts SharePoint, OneDrive and corporate file servers; the discriminator is an external, non-corporate destination preceded by the opening of a message file.

Defender takeaway
Install the November Office update now rather than in the normal cycle, because the flaw is exploited and a patched machine still leaves earlier captured credentials valid; reset the accounts of users whose Outlook reached an external destination.

If patching must wait, clearing the Remote API checkbox needs no restart, and a request to the soap-axis1 confluenceservice-v2 servlet path should then answer HTTP 403. Atlassian says it "cannot confirm if your instances have been affected" and asks teams to check affected instances for compromise (Atlassian, 2026-11-09); no source reports exploitation of Confluence, and BSI CERT-Bund's bulletin rates the issue critical and its second revision notes that an exploit was added (translated from German) (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-10). A Data Center instance on any 9.x or earlier release, with 9.2.28 the only fixed version listed, whose Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting is ticked; the setting sits under General Configuration, Further Configuration.

Web access logs for requests to the soap-axis1 servlet path and the XML-RPC endpoint from unexpected sources, and child processes of the Confluence JVM that the application does not normally start; this is an inference from the attack mechanics, not a source statement.

Switch the Remote API off today and upgrade to 9.2.28, because the flaw is already exploited against another product's embedded Axis; because Atlassian asks for a compromise check, review the access logs of any instance that had the API enabled and was reachable from untrusted networks.

CVE-2026-85844 is an authentication bypass in Windows Kerberos: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted Kerberos authentication traffic and relays the resulting authentication to an affected domain controller, with no user interaction (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component that Exchange Server uses: an attacker emails a crafted attachment, Exchange indexes it automatically, so "the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment", and the code runs with the permissions of the processing service (Microsoft, 2026-11-10).

The other five are described more thinly: a double free in Windows DNS (CVE-2026-88218) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), an out-of-bounds read in Windows DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10) and a release of an invalid pointer in Windows iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), each reachable by an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints; an out-of-bounds write in the Windows LDAP service that gives code execution in its context through crafted LDAP calls (CVE-2026-119958) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10); and a heap overflow in SQL Server (CVE-2026-116945) that needs an attacker who controls a network endpoint an integration package connects to, with no credentials or user interaction when the package runs automatically (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). The fixes are the November cumulative updates per release, for example KB5131291 (Windows Server 2016), KB5131085 (Server 2019), KB5131090 (Server 2022) and KB5131080 or KB5131077 (Server 2025), and the November SQL Server updates, for example KB5129299 (2025 CU10) and KB5129300 (2022 CU27).

Exposure
Domain controllers (Kerberos, LDAP, DNS), DNS and DHCP servers, Exchange servers that receive mail from the internet, and SQL Server hosts that run Integration Services packages against endpoints an attacker could control; the installed cumulative update shows in the update history of each host.
Detection
No exploitation is reported, so detection is hardening-grade: crashes or restarts of the DNS Server, DHCP Server and LSASS processes on domain controllers, Kerberos or LDAP bursts from workstation networks toward domain controllers, content-indexing or transport worker crashes on Exchange after inbound mail with unusual attachments, and an inventory of which domain controllers and Exchange servers already carry the November update.
Defender takeaway
Put the November update on domain controllers and internet-facing Exchange servers first; Microsoft's records give an unauthenticated attacker a relay to a domain controller and a mail-borne path to code execution on Exchange, and the DNS, DHCP and iSCSI rows are reachable by an in-network attacker, so keep those services off untrusted segments until they are patched.

CVE-2026-133469, Vates Xen Orchestra (VSA-2026-062): a crafted empty-object login cookie bypasses authentication and is exploited to take over XCP-ng hosts; fixed in xo-server 5.213.1 and 5.211.2 (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 2026-11-10, rated Critical, for Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA), the web management plane for XCP-ng pools; the flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-133469, CVSS 3.1 9.8 (Vates, 2026-11-10; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23). Vates says a threat actor is actively exploiting the flaw, that an adversary can bypass authentication and act with Admin privilege, and that a compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full takeover of XCP-ng nodes as root (Vates, 2026-11-10). The mechanism, per Vates: the REST cookie parser turns an authenticationToken cookie of j:%7B%7D into an empty object, the REST authentication path hands that object to the token provider without requiring a string, the token lookup treats it as unfiltered and returns the first token, and the provider authenticates as that token's owner if the token has not expired; the authenticated token-listing route then returns reusable login token ids (Vates, 2026-11-10). The attacker needs network reach to the interface and an unexpired first token in the Xen Orchestra token store, and no credentials or user interaction; the attacker does not choose which token the lookup returns (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20).

Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2 (stable) and before 6.10.1 (latest) is affected, and the fixes are xo-server 5.211.2 on the stable channel and 5.213.1 on the latest channel; a source install must move to the latest master (Vates, 2026-11-10). The CVE record names the same fixed releases, 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, and states the flaw is actively exploited in the wild (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23); BleepingComputer named 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 as the fixed releases, which the CVE record contradicts (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Xen Orchestra or XOA instance below those versions whose web or REST port is reachable from an untrusted network; Vates' first mitigation is a dedicated management network, never the internet (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Detection
A successful exploit leaves no Xen Orchestra log, so the signal is on the wire or at a reverse proxy: HTTP requests whose authenticationToken cookie is an empty JSON object in the encoded or the literal form, and Vates warns that a rule written as a regular expression can be bypassed with other encodings (Vates, 2026-11-10). On the XCP-ng hosts Vates lists a VM that sends its serial console to a file, a VM with an unexpected name, cron files written by the actor and the dynamic-linker preload file, and says these cover only the known campaign, so their absence does not prove a clean host (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update now and take the interface off any untrusted network; for an instance that was exposed, treat the stack as possibly compromised, rotate every secret it held (backup remotes, the root and pool secrets, user and OTP secrets, mail-server passwords) and reinstall where compromise is confirmed (Vates, 2026-11-10).

GitHub, as numbering authority, published CVE-2026-133469 for this flaw on 2026-11-23 with CVSS 3.1 9.8; the record states that it is actively exploited in the wild and fixed in 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, the same releases Vates names, and lists xo-server before 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 as affected (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23). The project's own advisory, published on 2026-11-20, gives the root cause in the REST cookie parser and the token lookup, and the prerequisite: authentication succeeds only if the token returned first is unexpired and belongs to an existing user, and a successful request returns reusable login token ids (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20). The advisory includes a one-request proof of concept, so the technique is public (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20).

SonicWall's advisory of 2026-11-10 says SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled kept trusting the compromised eMudhra chains and re-signed them for clients; fixed in SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8), so a Gen7 unit on 7.3.4-7013 is still affected. Apple's macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 now block the certificates in the command-line tools, Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 from 2026-11-16, and Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9.

SonicWall's informational advisory SNWLID-2026-0021 of 2026-11-10, which has no CVE and no workaround, says SonicOS appliances with Client DPI-SSL enabled continued to trust certificate chains issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs because the firewall's local certificate store trusted the underlying roots, and that the firewall then re-signed traffic from the impacted servers with its local DPI-SSL CA certificate, preventing client browsers from rejecting connections signed by the untrusted intermediates (SonicWall, 2026-11-10; SonicWall advisory data, 2026-11-10). SonicWall removed the affected root certificates from the SonicOS certificate store and added blocking logic for the compromised chain. Affected are Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ 270 to TZ 670, NSa 2700 to 6700, NSsp 10700 to 15700) and Gen7 NSv up to 7.3.4-7013, fixed in 7.3.4-7015 and higher, and Gen8 hardware (TZ 80 to TZ 680, NSa 2800 to 5800) and Gen8 NSv up to 8.2.2-8015, fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher; a Gen7 firewall that took only 7.3.4-7013 is therefore still affected (SonicWall, 2026-11-10).

Apple revised its support page on 2026-11-10: from macOS 27.2.1 the command-line tools no longer accept the twelve intermediate certificates, and the two roots they chain to, with three more eMudhra roots, leave /etc/ssl/cert.pem; macOS 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 carry the same protection, and after updating the manual removal need not be repeated (Apple, 2026-11-10). The revised page no longer carries the block dates of its 2026-10-30 version, so the 2026-10-22 date of the tracker and BleepingComputer stands for Apple's block.

Microsoft's post carries an update of 2026-11-10: the remaining eMudhra roots leave Microsoft products starting 2026-11-16, the ten remaining roots leave the Windows trusted root list through the automatic certificate-trust update, Edge and WebView2 drop default trust for emSign Root CA - G1, C1, ECC Root CA and Root TLS CA - G1 on the same date, Azure Linux images follow that day, and the .NET container images and the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK follow upstream releases (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9 of 2026-11-10, which updates the products under investigation, impacted and not impacted (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-10).

PK Softech and the State Secretariat for Security Policy said on 2026-11-10 that no concrete ransom demand reached the supplier or the federal bodies, that the supplier never contacted the attackers, that the Confederation paid nothing and that there is still no indication of publication on the darkweb, which qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom.

PK Softech said on its homepage on 2026-11-10, "because of media speculation", that no concrete ransom demand has reached it and that it has at no time contacted the attackers; its investigation continues (PK Softech, 2026-11-10). A spokeswoman of the State Secretariat for Security Policy told Keystone-SDA the same day that the federal bodies handling the incident know of no concrete ransom demand addressed to them and that the Confederation paid no ransom, that, as she put it, a demand to the supplier was "not made concrete with an amount or deadline" (translated from German), and that the Secretariat still has no indication that data from the attack was published on the darkweb; Publica said it also received no demand, is not in contact with the hackers and does not know whether other organisations or individuals are being extorted, which the Federal Prosecutor's Office is investigating (watson.ch, 2026-11-10). This qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom: watson.ch's headline and lead say no demand reached the supplier or the Confederation, while the spokeswoman's wording leaves a non-specific demand to the supplier open, and neither the supplier nor the federal authorities confirm a concrete demand, and the Akira attribution and the data volume remain press-sourced.

BACS published its own public warning on 2026-11-10: it says Switzerland is affected and that the controllers also run in butchers, restaurants, pharmacies, doctors' practices, laboratories, logistics, industry and farms, many of whose operators do not know their plants are reachable from the internet, and it repeats that security updates for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family exist and that newer firmware enforces HTTPS.

BACS published a public warning on 2026-11-10, which repeats the earlier warning of the Cyber Security Hub advisory cited above; it says the attacks of recent weeks show that Switzerland is affected too and that it is repeating its warning because the systems are widespread among small and medium-sized businesses (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). Per BACS, attackers reach management interfaces that are directly reachable from the internet and then change temperatures, defrost cycles, alarm thresholds or notification settings remotely, which can spoil food, medicines and other temperature-sensitive goods; it names the end-of-life AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355, the current AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family when it runs outdated firmware, and Copeland and Dixell XWEB.

What is new is the wider population: BACS lists butchers and food producers, restaurants and hotels, pharmacies, doctors' practices and laboratories, logistics and warehouses, industry and farms among the users, many of which do not know their cooling plants are reachable from the internet or run by an external provider, and it repeats what the Hub advisory already said, that security updates fixing the known flaws are available for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family and that newer firmware activates additional protections and enforces encrypted HTTPS communication (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). It recommends identifying the controllers, those run by contractors included, installing vendor updates, restricting unsupported systems to trusted networks or a VPN, reaching them remotely only through one centrally managed access point with default passwords replaced, and replacing end-of-life products; it names no attacker, no exploited CVE and no count of Swiss victims.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on 2026-11-10 with seven CVE ids, which replaces the entry's statements that no fix, no CVE ids and no affected or fixed builds existed, and reports scanning activity associated with the public proof-of-concept code but no evidence of successful exploitation; on-premises servers must be upgraded and every Agent and Probe upgraded too.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, on 2026-11-10 as a critical security update; hosted servers are already upgraded, on-premises customers must upgrade their own servers, and every customer must upgrade Agents and Probes, Agents first as N-able recommends (N-able, 2026-11-10). Huntress lists seven CVE ids for the fixed flaws and relays N-able's status-page statement that it observed "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but no evidence that any customer environment was successfully exploited; Huntress has seen no exploitation in its partners' environments, and N-able's guidance is to keep on-premises servers offline until the upgrade is complete (Huntress, 2026-11-10). After the hotfix the built-in remote control is temporarily disabled and Take Control still works (N-able, 2026-11-10).

Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-11T0256Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 12 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Coverage window: standard, 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-10T0255Z-intel). Twelve new entries and eight changelog records; no deep dive, no critical. A heavy Patch Tuesday day (Microsoft, SAP, Adobe, Fortinet, Ivanti, Synology) plus six KEV additions drove most of it.

  • KEV sweep (kev-window.txt): CVE-2026-125350 (Chromium) and CVE-2026-124194 (Outlook) became new entries; CVE-2026-111560 (Barracuda, COVERED-STALE) moved to exploited through an update record on the existing entry; CVE-2026-116606 already covered. borderline-drop: CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks XXE; carrier and UC-supplier product with no stated constituency footprint, fix since 2026-08-19. borderline-drop: CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder; niche authenticated telecom webmail component, vendor CVSS 4.3, no European public-sector footprint. No RANSOMWARE rows.
  • Microsoft November Patch Tuesday: one entry for seven unauthenticated CVSS 9.8 rows in domain infrastructure and server roles (Kerberos relay to a DC and zero-click Exchange attachment indexing are the two whose mechanics force the timeline). borderline-drop: SharePoint CVE-2026-120002 (9.9, authenticated), Azure DevOps Server, VS Code, ASP.NET Core and the Edge Chromium rows (authenticated or user-driven), and further unauthenticated 9.8 rows in client-side or non-server components (DirectMusic, Media Foundation, Color Management, Xbox Live Networking Service) and cloud services (Entra Device Registration, Azure OpenAI, Azure Managed Grafana), which carry no mechanism beyond an in-network or crafted-packet prerequisite and are not server roles an on-premises estate patches; the entry says they exist.
  • borderline-drop: Roundcube 1.6.21 and 1.7.6 (17 fixes, no CVE ids, scores or exploitation); AXIS Camera Station CVE-2026-13312 (low-privilege prerequisite, no detail); Adobe Experience Manager APSB26-189 (authenticated 9.9); Red Hat Ruby errata and the Metasploit module for GitLab CVE-2026-97229 (no delta on a complete KEV-listed entry); Apple, Siemens WinCC and Cisco 1.11 inventory additions to the Brotli flaw (no exploitation against those products); React Server Components CVE-2026-126187, Rails Active Storage CVE-2026-126082, MongoDB, Arista EOS, rConfig, mailcow, GPUStack, the Polish CMS flaws, OpenSSL (all Low), Apache httpd 2.4.70, Firefox 160, Cisco ISE CVSS 4.3 and Exchange authenticated rows.
  • borderline-drop (S2, S3, S4): Vaud Grand Council interpellation 26_INT_155 (questions only; revisit after the Conseil d'Etat answers); CNIL ten sanctions on local authorities (French enforcement, generic control list); ENISA State of Cybersecurity in the Union 2026 (policy index, Switzerland not covered); Chur medical centre Gleis D and Medi Porta with Cloak's 87 GB claim (private provider, no vector, below the incident floor); Erowa (Büron LU) with Akira's claim (private manufacturer, no vector); UZ Brussel shared patient-record outage (hospital reports no indication of a cyberattack); five Japanese bulk-email SaaS breaches (no Swiss nexus, one secondary compile); Push Security AI-event lures with Kali365 and VoidProxy (delta on covered device-code themes, vendor pitch); iVerify Advanced Mobile Threat Report 2026 and Kaspersky Q3 statistics (vendor population statistics, no new technique); NoName057(16) doxing bounty portal (no Swiss nexus); iOS worse_query sandbox escape (no CVE, sideload precondition, no exploitation).
  • Backlog state/coverage_backlog.md: the single open row (ChimeraZ claim against the Belgian rescue zone Hainaut-Est) stays held, unchanged: S2 searched in French and English again and found no zone statement, Belgian press report or CCB notice; expiry 2026-11-17 stands.
  • Single-source items: Xen Orchestra VSA-2026-062 (Vates, first-hand for its own product; BleepingComputer is a restatement), Adobe Connect APSB26-191 (vendor bulletin), Ivanti EPM and Cloud Services Application (CNA records only, confidence medium), Turla Cereal (ESET) and GhostFrame (Insikt Group) as telemetry holders. Included with reduced confidence: Ivanti, because Ivanti's advisory pages are a script-built application that no transport read and the jina pool is empty; the entry says so.
  • Contradiction: BleepingComputer names Xen Orchestra releases 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 where Vates names 6.9.2 and 6.10.1; the entry uses Vates' numbers and the xo-server package numbers, which agree.
  • Registry: Check Point lists UAT-9244 as an actor separate from FamousSparrow while the registry carries it as an alias of actor:famoussparrow, and ESET's SparroWocky is Check Point's CopperDoor; no alias was merged or added, left for the audit. CopperDragon, SquadC and SilentDelivery are registered, SparrowDoor, SparrowShell and Melofee are not.
  • Candidate sources added: vates-security-advisories, vrt-nws, watson-ch-digital (each with its reason in sources_changed); S3's Cofense and Positive Technologies leads are not added (Positive Technologies publishes on Medium, vendor-site home to be found), and S1's Onapsis lead already exists as onapsis. Promoted to active: censys-advisories, cert-fr-cti (three contributing runs each).
  • Audit lead (S2): the ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 of 2026-09-22 has no matching entry in the store.
  • Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records were attempted. Coverage gaps: connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport), sygnia (403), ico-uk (403, ninth fire in a row), Ivanti and N-able advisory pages (script-built, read through ENISA EUVD and N-able's status release notes), Fortinet's RSS is capped at 50 items so more 2026-11-10 advisories may exist.
  • Mid-run stop-hook nudges to commit were acknowledged and ignored per the prompt: nothing was committed before Phase 6.
  • Verification loop: six independent cold passes (iteration 1 full ledger, 2 to 6 post-fix passes), findings falling from 32 (16 truth, 13 editorial) to 4 (0 truth, 1 editorial, 3 advisory); the loop ended on rule 5 (final truth + editorial ≤ 2 without F1 or F4), so the final NEEDS_FIXES verdict is an early exit, not a confirmed CLEAN, and its one editorial finding (an uncited console clause on the Adobe Connect entry) was fixed after the pass. Every finding and its remediation is in verification.iterations[]; per-iteration deltas are in work/<run-id>/deltas.iter*.md.
  • Follow-up research (iteration 1, F10): a scoped cti-research sub-agent (F10, 325 s) resolved the Cisco lead: the SD-WAN Controller and Secure Email Gateway advisories are revisions of advisories existing entries cover, and the Meraki advisory (first published 2026-10-07, revised 2026-11-09) is below the bar; no entry, findings in work/<run-id>/findings.F10.yaml. Recipe note for the audit: Cisco PSIRT's feed date is the last-updated date, so revisions of old advisories surface as new rows; read "First Published" on the advisory page.
  • Declined verifier suggestions, each with its reason in the iteration findings: priority high for the Vates and SAP entries (no CVE record and unconfirmed constituency exposure; unexploited), dropping the Confluence, Adobe Connect and Patch Tuesday entries, product keys on the Vates and Chrome entries (they would overlap other entries and raise the dedup warning), and removal of vendor-published implant, registry and file names from mechanism prose (Detection lines and actions describe behaviour).
  • Corrections made through verification: the Outlook entry now states the NTLMv2 hash disclosure; the Patch Tuesday entry scopes its seven rows to domain infrastructure and server roles and names the further 9.8 rows; eight updated entries were corrected in place with their records re-declared, among them eMudhra (Apple macOS 27.2.1 / 26.7.3 / 15.8.3, Microsoft's 2026-11-16 root removal, Cisco 1.9), the Linux kernel entry (Ubuntu fixed builds, scoped to the generic kernels) and Fortinet (FG-IR-26-265, CVE-2026-126251, added).

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-10
item.description:
• N-central: Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and blocks the Legacy API; 4EverAble2Shell exploited; upgrade Agents too. An independent researcher published proof-of-concept code on 2026-11-08 and 2026-11-09 for what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in N-able's N-central appliance, and a second disclosure on 2026-11-12 added 4EverAble2Shell, a chain through Apache Axis (CVE-2026-90436) that works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is on and is exploited on at least 21 production servers, and Agent2Shell, SYSTEM commands on managed Windows endpoints. Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26, 2026-11-10) fixed seven CVE ids and Hotfix 3 (build 2026.4.1.39, 2026-11-16) fixes 17 more, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate and blocks the Legacy API permanently, but N-able does not name either chain or say it is fixed; Huntress reports public proof-of-concept code for all 17 and no exploitation of them in its partners' environments. Every on-premises server and every Agent and Probe must be on Hotfix 3, including those already on Hotfix 2. →
  • BluePhishing: a consented rogue Entra agent blueprint gives tenant access; Entra users get blueprint rights in November. Proofpoint describes BluePhishing, a research proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID: a victim who consents to an attacker's multi-tenant agent blueprint gets a blueprint principal with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, and the attacker then creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions, which Microsoft's documentation says neither the Entra portal nor Microsoft Graph shows. Proofpoint has identified no in-the-wild activity, and Microsoft 365 message MC1506733 says default Entra users can create agent blueprints from 2026-11-04, in a rollout due to complete by late November, unless an administrator turns that right off. →
  • CISA lists IBM Aspera Faspex 5 admin takeover as exploited; patch to 5.0.19 PL1, IBM names no workaround. IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 fixes CVE-2026-123218 in Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19, an incorrect-authorization flaw that lets a user craft a specific message to bypass authorization and gain full administrative privileges (CVSS 3.1 9.8); the fix is 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images, and IBM lists no workaround. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation that it does not describe; IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation. →

  1. 01N-central: Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and blocks the Legacy API; 4EverAble2Shell exploited; upgrade Agents too. An independent researcher published proof-of-concept code on 2026-11-08 and 2026-11-09 for what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in N-able's N-central appliance, and a second disclosure on 2026-11-12 added 4EverAble2Shell, a chain through Apache Axis (CVE-2026-90436) that works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is on and is exploited on at least 21 production servers, and Agent2Shell, SYSTEM commands on managed Windows endpoints. Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26, 2026-11-10) fixed seven CVE ids and Hotfix 3 (build 2026.4.1.39, 2026-11-16) fixes 17 more, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate and blocks the Legacy API permanently, but N-able does not name either chain or say it is fixed; Huntress reports public proof-of-concept code for all 17 and no exploitation of them in its partners' environments. Every on-premises server and every Agent and Probe must be on Hotfix 3, including those already on Hotfix 2. →
  2. 02BluePhishing: a consented rogue Entra agent blueprint gives tenant access; Entra users get blueprint rights in November. Proofpoint describes BluePhishing, a research proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID: a victim who consents to an attacker's multi-tenant agent blueprint gets a blueprint principal with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, and the attacker then creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions, which Microsoft's documentation says neither the Entra portal nor Microsoft Graph shows. Proofpoint has identified no in-the-wild activity, and Microsoft 365 message MC1506733 says default Entra users can create agent blueprints from 2026-11-04, in a rollout due to complete by late November, unless an administrator turns that right off. →
  3. 03CISA lists IBM Aspera Faspex 5 admin takeover as exploited; patch to 5.0.19 PL1, IBM names no workaround. IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 fixes CVE-2026-123218 in Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19, an incorrect-authorization flaw that lets a user craft a specific message to bypass authorization and gain full administrative privileges (CVSS 3.1 9.8); the fix is 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images, and IBM lists no workaround. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation that it does not describe; IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation. →

HIGHCVE-2026-125883 +24exploitedupdatedNATOB2

N-able N-central: 33 alleged flaws published, and Hotfix 3 (build 2026.4.1.39, 2026-11-16) now fixes 17 more CVE ids and blocks the Legacy API permanently, which 4EverAble2Shell (Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436, exploited on at least 21 servers) and Agent2Shell need; N-able does not say either chain is fixed, and public proof-of-concept code exists for the 17

An independent researcher published what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in the N-central appliance, chaining into four exploits, and N-able took its hosted environments offline on 2026-11-09 (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

On 2026-11-10 N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, for which Huntress lists seven CVE ids (N-able, 2026-11-10; Huntress, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10).

On 2026-11-12 the researcher published a second set. 4EverAble2Shell is unauthenticated command execution as root that requires the Legacy API to be enabled, per BleepingComputer; it chains CVE-2026-90436, an Apache Axis 1.x deserialization flaw for which Apache does not expect a fix, with a root escalation in N-central's maintenance helper (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12; Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06; Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntback counts at least 21 servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, in North America, South Africa and Europe but not Switzerland, and Previdian's sensors recorded attempts at the chain (Huntback, 2026-11-12; Previdian, 2026-11-12). Agent2Shell is a set of more than ten issues in how the server talks to Windows Agents and Probes, two chains of which let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands as SYSTEM on managed endpoints; N-able confirmed it also requires the non-default Legacy API (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12; Huntress, 2026-11-13). N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled the Legacy API (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Hotfix 3 of 2026-11-16 fixes 17 more CVE ids, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate and blocks the Legacy API permanently, without naming 4EverAble2Shell or Agent2Shell or saying either is fixed (N-able, 2026-11-16); Huntress reports public proof-of-concept code for all 17 and no exploitation of them in its partners' environments (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
An on-premises N-central server, yours or an IT provider's, below build 2026.4.1.39, and for the second set any build up to Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API, off by default, is on and reachable (Huntress, 2026-11-13); an Agent or Probe not on Hotfix 3 can be impersonated (N-able, 2026-11-16). A compromised server reaches the systems N-central manages (Field Effect, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In N-central's authentication and audit logs from 2026-11-08 onward, unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and changes to stored credentials or API integrations; on managed endpoints, unscheduled software deployments, scripts and remote-control sessions (Huntress, 2026-11-09; Field Effect, 2026-11-09). For 4EverAble2Shell, Huntback names POST requests to the Axis endpoint /dms/services/ServerUI, a symlink at the N-central flag file path, a systemd unit or cron entry relaunching a miner and a hidden miner directory under /tmp or /var/tmp (Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntress's Agent2Shell indicators are static analysis only: SYSTEM PowerShell with an encoded command spawned by the Agent, where an Agent child PowerShell is common and the command is what matters (Huntress, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade on-premises servers to Hotfix 3, then every Agent and Probe, those already on Hotfix 2 included (N-able, 2026-11-16), and confirm the Legacy API is disabled and not internet-reachable, because Hotfix 2 did not stop 4EverAble2Shell, 19 of the 21 compromised servers already ran it (Huntback, 2026-11-12) and N-able does not say Hotfix 3 fixes it; treat a hit as a full compromise and rotate the administrator, service and integration credentials the platform holds where activity looks unauthorised (Field Effect, 2026-11-09). Ask each IT provider managing your endpoints through N-central whether it runs a server on premises and has upgraded it.

Huntress lists seven CVE ids for the fixed flaws and relays N-able's status-page statement that it observed "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but no evidence that any customer environment was successfully exploited; Huntress has seen no exploitation in its partners' environments, and N-able's guidance is to keep on-premises servers offline until the upgrade is complete (Huntress, 2026-11-10). The researcher's 2026-11-12 disclosure also includes Agent2Shell, which The Hacker News describes as more than ten zero-day flaws used to run commands as SYSTEM on managed Windows agents, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12). Update18 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3, build 2026.4.1.39, on 2026-11-16 as a critical security update that builds on and supersedes Hotfix 2; it fixes 17 further CVE ids, adds missing authentication and permission checks to server operations, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate with the server, adds validation to file publishing, path and XML import handling, and permanently blocks the legacy APIs (N-able, 2026-11-16). Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation, and all customers, hosted and on-premises, must upgrade every Agent and Probe to 2026.4.1 HF3 whether or not they already run Hotfix 2 (N-able, 2026-11-16).

The release notes name neither 4EverAble2Shell nor Agent2Shell nor the Apache Axis flaw and do not say they are fixed; what changes is the Legacy API, which N-able itself said both chains need and which is now blocked permanently (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17). Among the 17 ids, the release notes title CVE-2026-129272 "MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode", CVE-2026-129280 "ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks" and CVE-2026-129286 "SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE", and Huntress counts three critical, eight high and six medium scores, all assigned by N-able as CVE numbering authority (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Huntress reports that public proof-of-concept code for all 17 CVE ids appeared on the evening of 2026-11-16, shortly after the hotfix, says any unpatched server should be treated as exposed, and has not observed exploitation of them in its partners' environments (Huntress, 2026-11-17). Field Effect reports that technical details on 24 further N-central vulnerabilities were published and are reported to be addressed by Hotfix 3, a count that the 17 CVE ids in N-able's notes do not reconcile (Field Effect, 2026-11-09). Huntress advises confirming the Patch Management Engine is at 2.14.4.5829 or later, rotating secrets embedded in Automation Manager policies on a server that was exposed before patching, not relying on Take Control audit records from an unpatched server, and enforcing MFA on all N-central accounts (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

CISA added the Apache Axis flaw CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18 (CISA, 2026-11-18). N-able's own remediation update reads the agent-side risk more narrowly than Huntress: it says the Legacy API is off by default, and that exploiting agent impersonation needs an existing foothold on an endpoint and yields only the information an agent receives and the values an agent can set (N-able, 2026-11-13), while Huntress describes two Agent2Shell chains that let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands on managed Windows endpoints (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

CVE-2026-123218, IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 to 5.0.19: a crafted message bypasses authorization and gives full administrative rights, fixed in 5.0.19 PL1 with no workaround; CISA lists it as exploited two days after IBM's bulletin (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 says Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 contains CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect-authorization flaw (CWE-863) in which an authorized user can craft a specific message to bypass user authorization and gain full administrative privileges; IBM scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 with a vector that needs no privileges and no user interaction (IBM, 2026-11-07). The description speaks of an authorized user while the vector requires no privileges, and the bulletin does not resolve the difference. The fix is Faspex 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images and checking that the faspex-core container image is 5.0.19 (1ce4b13, Fix Pack 1); IBM lists no workaround or mitigation (IBM, 2026-11-07). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09, two days after IBM's bulletin, "based on evidence of active exploitation" that it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-09). IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation, and neither it nor CISA's listing gives an actor, a victim or the mechanism of the crafted message.

Exposure
An IBM Aspera Faspex 5 server at 5.0.19 or earlier (IBM lists the fix for Linux), above all one whose portal is reachable from the internet; the tag of the faspex-core container image shows the build (IBM, 2026-11-07).
Detection
Neither source names an indicator or describes the message, so the signal is the outcome: a non-administrator account that acquires administrator rights, new administrator accounts and API keys, and shares or packages created by accounts that did not previously have that access, in Faspex application and web logs. The fix does not undo a takeover that already happened, so the same review applies after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch Faspex 5 on Linux to 5.0.19 PL1 by patching the container images now, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and IBM offers no workaround (IBM, 2026-11-07; CISA, 2026-11-09); then review administrator accounts, API keys and shares created since the server was reachable.
