CVE-2026-76418, Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: a crafted request to the remote access SSL VPN reloads the device when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication; Cisco reports active exploitation and CISA lists it (CVSS 3.1 8.6)

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 describes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: an unauthenticated, remote attacker who sends a crafted request while connecting to the SSL VPN makes the device reload, and a successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026 and names no actor or victim (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 (CISA, 2026-10-29), and CERT-FR restates the advisory (ANSSI / CERT-FR, 2026-10-29). The stated impact is a reload and denial of service, scored CVSS 3.1 8.6 with availability as the only impact; no code execution or data access is described (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

The first fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104 (for 9.16 and earlier), 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11 (for 7.0 and earlier), 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco lists no workaround; its mitigation is to remove secondary authentication from the tunnel group, which lowers the security posture of the remote access VPN, or, where DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, to disable the tunnel group list with no tunnel-group-list enable (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco confirms that Secure FMC, Cloud-delivered Firewall, cdFMC and Secure Access are not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An ASA or FTD unit below the first fixed release of its branch whose running configuration has webvpn enabled on an interface and secondary-authentication-server-group on any tunnel group; the default tunnel group DefaultWEBVPNGroup counts even when the tunnel group list is disabled. On FTD, read the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting configuration in FMC or FDM (Devices > VPN > Remote Access) (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Neither Cisco nor CISA publishes an indicator. The mechanism points at device availability telemetry: unexpected reloads, HA failover flaps, uptime resets and crash files on units that terminate the remote access VPN, read against VPN authentication logs for connection attempts from external addresses that never complete a login.

Triage: a reload also follows upgrades, HA events and hardware faults; a reload that coincides with unauthenticated SSL VPN connection attempts from an external address is the pattern the stated mechanism produces.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade the units that terminate remote access SSL VPN with secondary authentication this week, perimeter units first; Cisco states denial of service as the only impact, so patching leaves no further step, and removing secondary authentication as a stop-gap trades an outage risk for a weaker VPN login.

privatim revises its cloud guidance for Swiss public bodies (Merkblatt v3.02, 2 October 2026): sensitive data stays under the body's own keys, SaaS from Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP is in most cases inadmissible for secrecy-bound data, and top management signs the residual risk

privatim, the conference of the Swiss data-protection authorities, dates version 3.02 of its guidance "Cloud-specific risks and measures" to 2 October 2026 (privatim, 2026-10-02); it replaces the version of 3 February 2022 (DCOD, 2026-10-27). For particularly sensitive personal data the public body must encrypt, the keys may be available only to it, and outsourcing such data, or data under a statutory duty of confidentiality, to SaaS from large international providers, with Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP named, is in most cases inadmissible because of the untenable risk (privatim, 2026-10-02). Keys may stay with the provider only where no untenable risk follows and the provider is bound by contract to use them only with the body's express consent and to log every access (privatim, 2026-10-02).

The body, or its top management, is to confirm in writing that it has understood the risks and accepts the residual risk, and data the cloud services generate about their users, such as telemetry and logging data, is to be treated with the same care and contract terms as the content data (privatim, 2026-10-02). The five risk areas are contract design, places of processing including foreign authority access, confidentiality with encryption and key management, user data, and sub-processors (privatim, 2026-10-02).

Defender takeaway
The guidance addresses public bodies subject to Swiss data-protection law; a body that runs or plans SaaS from the named providers for sensitive or secrecy-bound data is advised to keep its own encryption keys, to have top management sign the residual risk, and to hold provider telemetry and logs about its users to the same contract terms.

ANNUAL REPORT: Cisco Talos Incident Response trends Q3 2026: public administration tied with finance as the most targeted sector, help-desk vishing into remote-management tools, and ransomware operators uninstalling and killing EDR

Cisco Talos Incident Response reports that in Q3 2026 financial organisations made up 18 percent of its engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Phishing was the leading initial-access technique at 37 percent of engagements and exploitation of public-facing applications second at 33 percent; the phishing cases include numerous actors who phone the victim as the IT help desk to get remote access allowed through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Ransomware and pre-ransomware cases were 27 percent of engagements, with The Gentlemen, Qilin, Rhysida and the closed group Interlock among the families and a new variant, VYPR, that Talos calls operationally immature: it had no leak site when seen, reused leaked Conti-derived source code and exfiltrated over several days (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

The VYPR intrusion began with a vishing call that had the user start a Microsoft Quick Assist session; the actor then used RMM software that ran PowerShell to download and install an MSI from a remote address, with MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, an IP scanner and mstsc as tools, and disabled EDR with several vulnerable drivers (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Interlock operators repeatedly tried to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint, used PsExec and taskkill to end security services and integrity checkers, turned off Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared event logs (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Talos names insufficient logging (over 40 percent of engagements), weak credential and secret handling, and absent or incomplete MFA as the most common weaknesses, and recommends centralised logging with at least 90 days of retention (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
An organisation whose help desk or staff can be reached by phone and whose endpoints permit Quick Assist or an unapproved RMM agent; Talos names public administration among the most targeted sectors in its caseload.
Detection
In process-creation and software-install telemetry, an RMM or Quick Assist session started after an inbound call, followed by PowerShell run under the RMM agent that downloads an installer from an external address; in endpoint and service-control telemetry, attempts to uninstall the EDR agent, PsExec or taskkill ending security services, Defender real-time protection switched off, vulnerable kernel drivers loaded, and event logs cleared.
Defender takeaway
Treat a remote-support session that nobody at the help desk started as the vishing signal and inventory which RMM tools and Quick Assist are permitted on endpoints; alert on EDR uninstall and security-service termination as a ransomware precursor; and centralise logs with the 90-day minimum retention Talos recommends, because actors delete logs on the endpoint.

  • borderline-drop: Sophos GOLD OGRE and Aur0ra AI-agent intrusions; standard Active Directory chain run with AI agents, first reported by Gambit and CloudSEK in August; adds no new technique.
  • borderline-drop: Group-IB MadApe, SOCRadar n0n, Arctic Wolf Teams external-chat impersonation, Talos NIK C2, Cyble INJ3CTOR3 FreePBX, covered techniques or commodity capability with no victimology, vector or constituency exposure.
  • borderline-drop: OpenSourceMalware trojanized Claude Code extension, a single source that disclaims provenance; reopen on a vendor or second-source statement.
  • borderline-drop: EDK II PXE CVE-2026-97631, out-of-window: advisory 2026-10-22, firmware class, no exploitation.
  • borderline-drop: Binance theft (about 6.3 billion US dollars), global scale but nothing transferable beyond a preliminary "compromised engineer laptop"; reopen when the post-mortem names the vector.
  • borderline-drop: Polymarket and DebugBear script compromise, no Swiss or public-sector customer known; reopen if DebugBear names scope or a root cause.
  • Out-of-window items kept as developing stories (72 h window): the Silent Train report (2026-10-28), because it develops the KeyDrift story published on 2026-10-29.
  • Lookback: the privatim guidance (document 2026-10-02, announced 2026-10-13) entered through the dcod-ch lookback and is first coverage for the reader.
  • Coverage gaps: ox-security (article bodies 403 on every transport, lead-only); lab52 (feed SSL EOF, reader listing undated); resecurity (empty JavaScript shell on extract); golem-security (cookie wall, titles only); edoeb-ch-press (listing stale, sitemap recipe found); Juniper support portal, Progress and OpenText advisories (script shell or login wall).
  • Source health and recipes: S2 and S1 returned working recipes for ec-digital-strategy-newsroom (extract), edoeb-ch-press (sitemap), le-monde-info, github-advisory, enisa-euvd and ransomware-live; they are in the notes of those records. Three candidates added (privatim-ch, ncsc-nl-php2shell-tracker, infostealers-hudson-rock) and three promoted to active (veeam-kb-security, dream-research, safedep).
  • For the next audit: the GitLab, PAN-OS and Publica entries are 600 to 1,160 words in the main text although earlier records grew them; this run shortened the GitLab and Publica text but did not rewrite them to the 550-word bound.
  • Verification: four iterations; iterations 1 to 3 returned NEEDS_FIXES (23, 10 and 4 findings, all remediated or declined with a reason) and iteration 4, a post-fix pass over 111 of 241 claims plus the full text of all twelve entries, returned one editorial finding (the WordPress firewall wording), which was remediated before publication under the low-residual early exit (truth plus editorial 1). No CLEAN iteration ran, so this publication rests on the early exit, not on a confirmed double-CLEAN; the next quality audit should give these twelve entries an independent pass.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-29
item.description:
• Check Point gateways exploited (PHP2Shell, root escalation): Jumbo R81.20 t174, R82 t132, R82.10 t52, R82.20 t14. Check Point Research reports that from 2026-10-30 an attacker exploited unpatched Check Point gateways through the Mobile Access portal with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), escalated to root with CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS 7.8, a local flaw in the dynamic_server process that Check Point says was exploited against a couple of dozen customers), installed a persistent backdoor and in the first wave deleted files on a VMware ESXi host. The fix for both is in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator R81.20 take 174, R82 take 132, R82.10 take 52 and R82.20 take 14 or later, with none listed for R81.10 or R81, and the standalone PHP hotfix is not stated to cover CVE-2026-123039; sk1000302 itself carries no statement on exploitation. →
  • Talos: UAT-11473 implants KeyDrift in Cisco SD-WAN controllers through CVE-2026-20127 to collect data-plane keys. Cisco Talos reports that a cluster it calls UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, the peering authentication bypass in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator (CVSS 10.0, fixed releases since February 2026, no workaround), and then ran the KeyDrift implant inside the controller's control-plane process to collect session metadata and what Talos assesses to be data-plane IPsec keys. Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-28 to link Talos's post, says it is aware of limited exploitation, and Talos assesses with high confidence that the operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network. →
  • PHP2Shell: Trend Micro Apex, Mobile Security and Analyzer patches out, Analyzer 7.5 gets none; Quest KACE, NetApp fixed. Trend Micro posted Critical Patch build 7351 for Apex Central and build 20113 for Apex One Service Pack 1 on 2026-11-11, each upgrading PHP to 8.2.35 (the Apex One readme does not name the flaw), and its advisory, updated 2026-11-18, names both patches and lists critical patches 1020 for Deep Discovery Analyzer 7.7 and 1082 for 7.6 (none for 7.5, upgrade to 7.6) and for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector, while its Download Center carries a Mobile Security for Enterprise 9.8 SP5 patch dated 2026-11-17 that the advisory row has not caught up with; Quest says all KACE SMA and SDA versions are affected, with SMA 15.0 CU5 and 15.1 CU2 and the SDA 9.3 hotfix out and advice to block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until applied; and NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, with attacker access as the www user restricted to the PHP jail and hotfix builds from 9.12.1P20HF1 to 9.19.1P4. NetApp says it is aware of public discussion of the vulnerability and none of the three vendors reports an exploited case on its page, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited. →

Trend Micro posted Critical Patch build 7351 for Apex Central and build 20113 for Apex One Service Pack 1 on 2026-11-11, each upgrading PHP to 8.2.35 (the Apex One readme does not name the flaw), and its advisory, updated 2026-11-18, names both patches and lists critical patches 1020 for Deep Discovery Analyzer 7.7 and 1082 for 7.6 (none for 7.5, upgrade to 7.6) and for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector, while its Download Center carries a Mobile Security for Enterprise 9.8 SP5 patch dated 2026-11-17 that the advisory row has not caught up with; Quest says all KACE SMA and SDA versions are affected, with SMA 15.0 CU5 and 15.1 CU2 and the SDA 9.3 hotfix out and advice to block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until applied; and NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, with attacker access as the www user restricted to the PHP jail and hotfix builds from 9.12.1P20HF1 to 9.19.1P4. NetApp says it is aware of public discussion of the vulnerability and none of the three vendors reports an exploited case on its page, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 6Trending vulnerabilities 5Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 29

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures6 items

NOTABLECVE-2025-8088exploitedNATOB2

MDaemon mail server below 26.0.4 and Windows ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3: a crafted RAR emailed to any address runs code on the server through the bundled UnRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088, and ESET saw Russia-aligned attackers use it in Ukraine to deploy the HELLAGE and HELLTAG backdoors

ESET reports an active campaign in Ukraine in which Russia-aligned attackers exploited MDaemon mail servers and deployed two backdoor families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). MDaemon uses ClamAV to scan attachments of incoming mail; old ClamAV versions carry CVE-2025-8088, the WinRAR path-traversal flaw ESET uncovered last year, which ESET says was fixed in ClamAV's source on 27 July 2025 (the release notes below date the fixed ClamAV builds 2026-08-07), while MDaemon kept shipping an old libclamunrar.dll until MDaemon 26.0.4 of 2026-08-25 (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). The chain ESET describes: a crafted RAR archive is mailed to any address at a vulnerable server, MDaemon invokes ClamAV to scan it, and the exploit writes a malicious DLL to the server's file system with no user interaction, so the message carries no lure (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). CERT-UA names the backdoors: HELLAGE steals email messages and other data, talks to a hardcoded server and can deploy more malware, and HELLTAG takes commands, transfers files and does reconnaissance through a hardcoded Telegram bot; ESET cannot attribute the campaign to a known Russia-aligned actor (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

The exposure is wider than MDaemon. ClamAV's release notes of 2026-08-07 say it adopted the upstream UnRAR fix for CVE-2025-8088, which rejects path separators in NTFS alternate data stream names so that extraction cannot leave ClamAV's temporary scan directory on Windows, and that the issue affects ClamAV 0.101.0 through 1.5.3 with the fix in 1.4.6 and 1.5.4 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07). CISA has listed CVE-2025-8088 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2025-08-12 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An MDaemon server on Windows below 26.0.4 that accepts inbound mail (ESET Research, 2026-10-28), and any other Windows host that scans mail or files with ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07).
Detection
Because the attack needs no lure, the mail log shows an ordinary message with a RAR attachment. The telemetry that matters is file creation of a DLL by the ClamAV or mail-service scanning process outside ClamAV's temporary scan directory, inbound RAR attachments whose member names carry alternate-data-stream syntax with path separators, and the mail service process starting unexpected children or connecting to Telegram's bot interface; these follow from the described chain and are not an ESET detection list. An update does not remove a DLL or backdoor that was already written, so check the server after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch the mail scanning path first on any internet-facing Windows mail server, then look for unexpected DLLs and persistence and treat stored mail as exposed, since HELLAGE steals email (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

Builds on: 2026-06-10/year-old-winrar-flaw-cve-2025-8088-still-fuels-ukraine-intru · 2026-06-02/sekoia-consolidates-gamaredon-tooling-under-gammaphish-gamma · 2026-06-27/turla-s-stockstay-a-four-component-net-backdoor-for-diplomat

threat29 Oct 04:46Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: ESET Research · ESET Research (APT Activity Report, April to September 2026) · ClamAV · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
NOTABLENATOA2

Moldova's government digital services: attackers used flaws in services reachable without authentication to query about one million national identification numbers and extract data on about 750,000 of them between 19 and 23 October, and the Prime Minister says AI allegedly helped find the flaws

Moldova's Electronic Governance Agency (AGE) reported on 2026-10-27 that between 19 and 23 October attackers queried about one million national identification numbers (IDNPs) through state digital services and that, on preliminary estimates, data sets for about 750,000 of them were extracted; MOLDPRES had put the access requests at about 11 million on 2026-10-24 (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-24). AGE's technical explanation is that the attackers exploited vulnerabilities in services reachable without authentication and then used the data they obtained for further extractions; the first attacks hit an electronic service that logged the legal basis of processing incorrectly, which is why citizens saw entries for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue in the data-access history of the EVO app (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). Data that may be affected, not every category for every person, includes name, date and place of birth, first-degree relatives, insured status, family doctor, social benefits, pensions, disability, driving licence, photograph, vehicles and companies owned or run, IBAN, tax debts and payment history; AGE says card data is not held on the platform and it found no unauthorised change to state registers (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).

AGE stopped the extraction on 23 October at 11:30, reviewed 82 digital services and suspended the exposed ones, and its timeline says 82 public services and more than 30 information systems and administration panels were disconnected as a precaution on 23 October; it blocked further attempts on 25 and 27 October, and the Prime Minister's account is that 30 of the 82 services were disconnected (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). The Prime Minister says the incident is not isolated, that foreign state actors are being investigated and that the attackers automated the extraction, with the use of artificial intelligence allegedly facilitating the identification and exploitation of the vulnerabilities (MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). Moldova has not attributed the attack to any country or group (The Record, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A public e-service of a federal, cantonal or communal administration that returns person data for an identifier without authentication, or whose output feeds other registers, since AGE says the extraction chained from unauthenticated services into further data (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).
Detection
Citizens noticed the abuse because the data-access history in the EVO app showed processing for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue that they had not made, so a data-subject-visible access log is a detection channel (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). On the server side the relevant telemetry is per-service request volume and sequential or bulk identifier lookups from one source; the sources give no breakdown of the request pattern, so that is an inference from about 11 million requests against about one million numbers.
Defender takeaway
List the public services that answer for a person identifier without authentication and check what each one returns, whether it feeds other registers and whether its access log records the true purpose; rate limits and alerts on bulk lookups belong in front of every such service.

Builds on: 2026-08-29/swiss-cantons-eautoindex-vehicle-registry-data-harvesting

incident29 Oct 04:43Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Moldova Electronic Governance Agency · MOLDPRES · The Record
ROUTINENATOA2

Machelen (Belgium) municipality: its own timeline shows a foothold through misleading instructions on an external website on 2026-08-20, found 22 days later after a high-privilege user was reached, with personal data confirmed stolen and Rhysida now listing municipal and social-welfare files

Machelen's own timeline records that on 2026-08-20 attackers gained access to an internal laptop through misleading instructions on an external website, explored it extensively from 24 August to 1 September, and on 10 September had access to a user with high access rights and other IT systems; the municipality found the incident on 11 September, isolated all systems, reported to the Belgian CCB-CERT, restarted part of its systems from a backup of a safe date on 14 September and recorded the first evidence of leaked data on 17 September (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22). It confirms that personal data was leaked and says the scope is still being investigated (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22); the mayor had said on 14 September that no personal data appeared to be affected, and ITdaily reports that this proved wrong (ITdaily, 2026-09-23). Ransomware.live recorded on 2026-10-27 that Rhysida listed Machelen on its leak site, describing the listing as municipal and social-welfare file servers of about 1.3 million files, with client files that include passports and identity cards, nursing-home medical files and civil-status records, which are the group's own claims (Ransomware.live, 2026-10-27).

Detection
The timeline puts 22 days between first access and detection, with the first laptop explored from 24 August to 1 September; it names neither the website nor the commands, so the telemetry to review includes endpoint process creation after a user followed instructions on a web page and later use of a high-privilege account from that workstation, which is an inference from the timeline.
Defender takeaway
Treat a user who followed instructions from a website on a work laptop as a possible intrusion that can sit unseen for weeks; review high-privilege account activity from the user's workstation for the weeks after the event, not only the day it is reported.
incident29 Oct 04:44Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Municipality of Machelen (incident timeline) · Municipality of Machelen (FAQ on personal data) · ITdaily · Ransomware.live
HIGHCVE-2026-20127exploitedNATOB2

KeyDrift: Talos reports UAT-11473 exploiting CVE-2026-20127 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN controllers to run an implant inside the control-plane daemon that collects data-plane keys, with infrastructure overlapping Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network

Cisco Talos reports that UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass in the peering authentication of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28), and then installed a custom framework it calls KeyDrift (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). CISA has listed the flaw in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2026-02-25 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory (CVSS 10.0) says an unauthenticated remote attacker can log in as an internal high-privileged non-root user and reach NETCONF to change the SD-WAN fabric configuration, and that there is no workaround (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-28 to link Talos's post, says its PSIRT is aware of limited exploitation (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reported on 2026-10-28 that Volt Typhoon had exploited the flaw since late 2025 and after Cisco's February disclosure (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28), and Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473's operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

KeyDrift runs inside the control-plane daemon. The actor edits the runit launchers of sshd and of a look-alike aaamgr service and remounts /rootfs.rw executable: the sshd launcher starts a script that injects the PolyFlame library into every running vdaemon process by ptrace, and the aaamgr launcher runs a packed PolyFlame loader directly (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). PolyFlame is tasked in-band over the control-plane traffic and offers a command, file-write and file-read backdoor and an intermediate command relay; Talos recovered no hardcoded address, port or domain (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). A second component, LittleFilch, hooks SSL_read in vdaemon and collects peer system addresses and 32-byte values Talos assesses to be OMP-distributed IPsec data-plane keys, writing them RSA-encrypted to /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Talos lists observed targeting as space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research, calls the activity historical and does not say how many controllers were affected (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Every Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator regardless of configuration, on-premises or in Cisco's hosted clouds, on a release below the first fixed one in the advisory's table; Cisco says controllers with ports exposed to the internet are at risk (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
On the controller's authentication log, Cisco says to audit /var/log/auth.log for accepted public-key logins of the vmanage-admin account from addresses that are not among the configured System IPs, and to validate control-connection peering events, those of peer type vmanage first, against maintenance windows and asset inventory (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). On the host, Talos names modified runit run scripts that remount the overlay root executable and start a background script, an aaamgr service that runs a compiled, packed ELF, extra libraries mapped into vdaemon with ptrace activity against it and encrypted staging files under /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Cisco asks for admin-tech files and a TAC case when compromise is suspected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Triage: an aaamgr service that runs as a compiled ELF is the discriminator, because the legitimate component is a Python package and does not normally appear that way (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed releases and restrict the control components' management ports, then treat any controller that was internet-reachable on a vulnerable release as a compromise-assessment target, because Lumen dates exploitation of the flaw to late 2025, before Cisco's February disclosure, and the implant runs in the process that handles the fabric's control sessions.

Builds on: 2026-06-06/cve-2026-20245-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager-actively-exploi

threat29 Oct 04:40Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Cisco Talos · Cisco PSIRT · Lumen Black Lotus Labs · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
NOTABLENATOB2

testmetest: an npm worm in the Miasma and Shai-Hulud family now starts when an application imports the package, so install with --ignore-scripts no longer protects, and JFrog finds 42 third-party GitHub repositories already armed with its publisher

SafeDep counts 19 npm packages from the same operator between 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-27, eight of them published through four npm accounts, that carry a worm sharing code with the June Miasma worm and adding the token-revocation wiper of Mini Shai-Hulud; SafeDep has not confirmed the lineage, and JFrog says its evidence does not establish that the original Miasma operators are responsible (SafeDep, 2026-10-27; JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26). The install trigger has changed twice: first a command expansion in a binding.gyp file, with no install script; then a postinstall script that loads a native addon which decodes and starts the worm; and, since SafeDep's update of 27 October, an addon that runs when an application imports the package, so a hardening step that disables install scripts does not stop it (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).

The payload exits on CIS locales and in known analysis sandboxes. It steals SSH keys, registry and Git credentials, .env files, browser logins, AI-tool, cloud, Vault and Kubernetes secrets and GitHub Actions secrets read from runner memory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). It exfiltrates by committing encrypted data, with the victim's encrypted GitHub token, to a new public repository in the victim's own account, injects a GitLab CI job that requests npm and PyPI OIDC tokens, adds its loader to the victim's npm packages and publishes new patch versions, republishes to PyPI and RubyGems, commits a fake CodeQL workflow and AI-agent configuration files that infect the host again, and copies itself over SSH to the hosts in known_hosts (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). A persistence service checks the stolen GitHub token every 45 seconds for 48 hours and on an authentication failure deletes the home directory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). JFrog found 42 armed third-party GitHub repositories of 11 legitimate owners with hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, and says the payload blobs were large enough to evade GitHub's search and API paths (JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26).

Exposure
Any developer endpoint, build agent or CI runner that installed or imported one of the operator's packages, and any GitHub or GitLab account whose token such a host held (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Detection
In package metadata, a binding.gyp whose sources field runs node in a package with no C or C++ sources, a postinstall that requires a .node file and discards errors beside a large high-entropy file, and prebuilt addons with no native source; on endpoints and CI runners, a node process that downloads or finds and runs the Bun runtime and a child node process started from a temporary path named after its process ID; in GitHub and GitLab audit logs, a new public repository in a developer's own account with a generic project description, commits with a fixed automated-sync message, commits that add AI-assistant configuration files (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .vscode tasks, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), an injected CI job that requests OIDC tokens, and unexpected patch releases of your own packages (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Defender takeaway
An install that ran with scripts disabled is not clean once the package has been imported; for an affected host SafeDep's order is to disconnect it, remove persistence first, rotate all credentials, check the accounts for the repositories and commits above and reinstall the operating system (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). Because the wiper is triggered by the token's revocation, the host is isolated and cleaned before the GitHub token is revoked.

Builds on: 2026-05-20/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-53-tags

threat29 Oct 04:47Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: SafeDep (living post, updated 2026-10-27) · JFrog Security Research
NOTABLENATOB2

Huntress: phished MDM enrolments in Hexnode and Rippling give attackers a management path that brings ScreenConnect back after it has been removed

Huntress reports several recent incidents in which attackers used legitimate mobile-device-management platforms, not flaws in them, as a trusted management path, naming Hexnode and Rippling as the two it saw and noting the list is not definitive (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the first case, proposal-themed emails led a user to download an MSI named like a DocuSign installer that installed Hexnode components (gateway, agent and PostgreSQL components); ScreenConnect followed shortly after and connected to an attacker relay, the managed-service provider removed it, and it came back several hours later to the same relay while the Hexnode client was still installed (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the second, a receptionist clicked a link in an email about tax planning that led to a fake Teams calendar page; about a minute later a Rippling enrolment registry key appeared, the agent was downloaded into a SYSTEM profile path and installed with SYSTEM rights, and about 35 minutes after that the attacker used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A managed Windows endpoint whose user can run an installer or follow an enrolment link, in an organisation without an inventory of its authorised MDM tenants, agents and RMM instances (Huntress, 2026-10-28).
Detection
The chain Huntress describes as a stronger signal is social engineering, then a new MDM enrolment, then an RMM installation, then outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay, correlated across identity, MDM, endpoint and network telemetry; in endpoint telemetry that is an MSI run from a browser download folder that installs an MDM agent, an enrolment registry key on a device nobody enrolled, a new SYSTEM-level agent in a vendor directory shortly after a click, and an RMM installed by that agent (Huntress, 2026-10-28). A repeat of the same RMM relay after the RMM was removed, as in the Hexnode case, points to a remaining MDM client as a possible source (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Triage: a corporate enrolment started by IT looks similar in process telemetry; the discriminators are a tenant that is not in the authorised inventory, a trigger that is an emailed link or a user-run installer instead of IT's enrolment workflow, and an RMM install within minutes (an inference from Huntress's two cases).

Defender takeaway
Treat an unexpected MDM enrolment as a security event and keep an inventory of authorised tenants; after removing a rogue RMM, unenrol the device from the unauthorised tenant, disable accounts the attacker created, revoke sessions and tokens, reset credentials and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed, as Huntress advises (Huntress, 2026-10-28).
threat29 Oct 04:45Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Huntress

02Trending vulnerabilities5 items

HIGHCVE-2026-109618 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-123039, Check Point Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls: PHP2Shell on the Mobile Access and VPN web interfaces, chained with a local root escalation, is exploited against unpatched gateways (implant, ESXi wiper); the fix is in Jumbo takes R81.20 take 174, R82 take 132, R82.10 take 52 and R82.20 take 14

Check Point's advisory sk1000302 says that under certain circumstances the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both scored CVSS 9.2, may allow remote code execution through firewall web interfaces; affected are Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls that use Mobile Access Portal (not Spark), Remote Access VPN with SSL Network Extender (not Spark) or with SAML realm authentication, the Identity Awareness captive portal, the UserCheck portal or Zero Phishing, on R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20 and on Spark R81.10.x and R82.00.x, and end-of-support lines are also listed (Check Point, 2026-11-12). The standalone hotfix of 2026-10-23 implements the PHP 7.4 fix and needs a reboot (Check Point, 2026-10-29); the sk now says the fix is included in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator R82.20 take 14, R82.10 take 52, R82 take 132 and R81.20 take 174, names Spark fixes from builds B998002843 and B996005005, and keeps the R81.10 hotfix (Check Point, 2026-11-12). Until then, Check Point's mitigation is a cp-httpd.conf block denying multipart Content-Type requests, removed before the hotfix (Check Point, 2026-10-29).

Check Point Research reports that from 2026-10-30, about a week after the fix, an attacker exploited unpatched gateways through Mobile Access portals with PHP2Shell and escalated to root with CVE-2026-123039: the first wave targeted Israeli organisations and included destructive activity against some, and a wider wave on 2026-11-02 targeted organisations in several countries (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12). CVE-2026-123039 is a local escalation: the root dynamic_server process runs whatever command it receives on a world-writable local socket without authenticating the caller, and Check Point says it observed an active exploit against a couple of dozen customers (Check Point, 2026-11-12). After root the attacker placed PHP web shells in the directory the Mobile Access portal uses for its login pages and the TSGA implant, a root-run passive backdoor that Check Point says provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection and firewall-log tampering; it ran a scanner, moved by SSH to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper there (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12). The standalone PHP hotfix text names only the two PHP CVEs (Check Point, 2026-10-29), and sk1000362 lists no Jumbo take for R81.10 or R81, so protection there is not stated (Check Point, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
For the PHP flaws, a gateway on a listed release with at least one of the six portal or VPN features in use (Check Point, 2026-11-12); for CVE-2026-123039, a Force gateway, management or log server, Multi-Domain server or Maestro on R81 to R82.20 below those Jumbo takes (Check Point, 2026-11-12).
Detection
The vulnerable daemon logs every command it receives to /var/log/dynamicCli.log, and Check Point says any command that does not use the legitimate Clish wrapper may indicate a command executed as root and requires investigation (Check Point, 2026-11-12); Check Point Research also describes the web-shell, listener and SSH-to-ESXi behavior above (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12).
Defender takeaway
Install the Jumbo take that carries both fixes on gateways and on management and log servers, apply the cp-httpd.conf mitigation and stop dynamic_server where it has to wait (Check Point, 2026-11-12; Check Point, 2026-11-12), and treat a gateway that was exposed and unpatched since 2026-10-30 as needing a compromise check, because a hotfix is not stated to remove an implant already installed, which is an inference from the persistence Check Point Research describes (Check Point Research, 2026-11-12).

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, PHP2Shell in management servers and storage: Trend Micro released critical patches for Apex Central and Apex One server on 2026-11-11, Mobile Security for Enterprise on 2026-11-17 and Deep Discovery Analyzer by 2026-11-18, Quest KACE SMA and SDA have fixes and should block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until patched, and NetApp ONTAP 9 is affected by CVE-2026-109618 only, inside the PHP jail

Trend Micro's Download Center dates Critical Patch build 7351 for Apex Central and Critical Patch build 20113 for Apex One Service Pack 1 to 2026-11-11 (Trend Micro Download Center, 2026-11-11; Trend Micro Download Center, 2026-11-11). Both patches upgrade the bundled PHP module to 8.2.35, and only the Apex Central readme names PHP2Shell (Trend Micro, 2026-11-05; Trend Micro, 2026-11-09). The customer advisory KA-0024802, updated 2026-11-18, lists the Apex Central patch as CP B7351 and the Apex One server patch as CP B20113, critical patches 1020 for the Deep Discovery Analyzer 7.7 OS image and 1082 for 7.6 with none planned for 7.5 (upgrade to 7.6), and critical patches for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector (Trend Micro, 2026-11-18). Its Mobile Security for Enterprise row still reads impacted with a critical patch ETA of 17 November, while the Download Center lists Mobile Security for Enterprise 9.8 SP5 Critical Patch 10 dated 2026-11-17 (Trend Micro Download Center, 2026-11-17), whose readme says it includes the official fixes for both flaws (Trend Micro, 2026-11-17). Trend Micro says it has not seen successful exploitation in its products or services (Trend Micro, 2026-11-18).

Quest's knowledge-base article says all versions of the KACE Systems Management Appliance (SMA) and Systems Deployment Appliance (SDA) are affected and that CVE-2026-115560 does not affect them; KACE SMA 15.0 CU5 (15.0.378) and 15.1 CU2 (15.1.177) with PHP 8.4.27 were published on 2026-10-23, the cumulative updates 15.0 Patch 4 and 15.1 Patch 1 do not contain the fix, and the SDA 9.3 hotfix 9.3.312 with PHP 8.3.36 followed (Quest Software, 2026-10-29). Until an appliance is updated Quest says to block all public internet access and, because a potentially exploitable communication path remains after the agent tunnel on port 52230 is established, to block inbound web traffic including ports 80, 443 and 52230 (Quest Software, 2026-10-29).

NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, scored CVSS 4.0 9.2, where an unauthenticated attacker could potentially gain access as the www user but would be restricted to the PHP jail, and lists hotfix builds from 9.12.1P20HF1 to 9.19.1P4, 9.17.1P12, 9.15.1P21 and 9.18.1P9 among them (NetApp, 2026-11-18). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26, although none of the three vendors reports an exploited case (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A Trend Micro Apex Central, Apex One, Mobile Security for Enterprise or Deep Discovery Analyzer server whose console or web endpoints a hostile network can reach; any KACE SMA or SDA, whose web ports and agent port 52230 are named; any ONTAP 9 cluster whose web services are reachable and that runs a release other than the fixed builds (Trend Micro, 2026-11-02; Quest Software, 2026-10-29; NetApp Knowledge Base, 2026-10-26).
Detection
None of the three vendors publishes an indicator. For a management server or appliance that was reachable before its fix, the telemetry to review is shells and downloads started by its web service and outbound connections the server initiates; this is an inference, since the pages do not describe the attack.
Defender takeaway
Install the Trend Micro patches now (Apex Central, Apex One, Mobile Security for Enterprise, Deep Discovery Analyzer) and keep the Trend Micro, KACE and ONTAP management interfaces off untrusted networks until each is fixed; Trend Micro asks customers to restrict the impacted consoles to trusted addresses (Trend Micro, 2026-11-12).

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, F5 BIG-IP: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the Configuration utility of every module and the APM and SSL Orchestrator access profiles on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0, and F5's cumulative critical releases 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4 carry the fix

F5's release notes for BIG-IP 17.1.3.7, 21.1.0.4 and 17.5.1.11, each updated on 2026-10-24, list K000163821 as the reference for the fix of the PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and describe each build as a critical release whose only new changes are PHP vulnerability fixes and which is cumulative and includes earlier hardened and critical releases (F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24). NCSC-NL records F5 as confirming that BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 are vulnerable through the Configuration utility control plane in all modules and, for APM and SSL Orchestrator, through the access-profile data plane, and that earlier affected releases stay vulnerable until updated (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26; nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A BIG-IP on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 or 21.1.0 whose Configuration utility is reachable from a network the attacker can reach, or that publishes an APM or SSL Orchestrator access profile (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26).
Detection
F5's article on exploitation and mitigations could not be read and no indicator is published in the sources found. The telemetry to review on an exposed system is access to the Configuration utility and the access-profile web paths from untrusted sources, and shells or downloads started by the web service; this is an inference, not an F5 statement.
Defender takeaway
Move to the cumulative critical release of your train and read K000163821 in a browser for F5's own mitigation list; until then keep the Configuration utility off untrusted networks, and treat an APM or SSL Orchestrator system that was exposed and unpatched as needing a compromise check.

WatchGuard Fireware OS 2026.4, 12.12.4 and 12.5.22: seven of 17 fixed Fireware OS flaws are scored 9.0 or higher, among them unauthenticated memory-corruption and missing-authentication rows in the Access Portal, the SIP proxy and the FireCluster sync daemon; WatchGuard knows of no exploitation

WatchGuard's advisory listing of 2026-10-27 opens with 18 rows, 17 for Fireware OS and one for Mobile VPN with SSL Client for Windows, and seven of the 17 are scored 9.0 or higher (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). The fixes are in Fireware OS 2026.4, 12.12.4 and, for T15 and T35 models, 12.5.22. Three of the seven need no authentication but a specific feature. CVE-2026-93866 (9.2) is an integer overflow in the WebSocket handling of the Access Portal that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker write beyond the bounds of a heap buffer while the Access Portal is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93857 (9.2) is a stack buffer overflow in the SIP proxy that gives remote code execution when a SIP proxy is configured on the Firebox (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93865 (9.2) is missing authentication in the FireCluster synchronization daemon: a remote unauthenticated attacker invokes privileged administrative actions with a crafted request to the FireCluster management IP when clustering is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

The other four need a network position. CVE-2026-112709 and CVE-2026-112710 (9.2 each) are heap overflows in the authentication service that give denial of service and possibly code execution to an attacker who controls or intercepts traffic to the configured Active Directory server and returns a crafted response (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103594 (9.5) is a stack overflow in WireGuard configuration processing for a man-in-the-middle with TLS-decrypted access between a Firebox that acts as a FireCloud Gateway and WatchGuard Cloud (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103593 (9.1) is a stack overflow in the logging service that gives root code execution to a network-adjacent attacker who impersonates or intercepts traffic to the log server with a crafted certificate, in FIPS mode (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). Six rows affect Fireware OS 2025.1 up to before 2026.4 and 12.0 up to before 12.12.4, T15 and T35 up to before 12.5.22, the WireGuard row starts at 2026.2 and 12.12, and each page states that WatchGuard is not aware of exploitation in the wild (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Firebox on a Fireware OS release inside those ranges with at least one of the listed features: the Access Portal, a SIP proxy policy, FireCluster membership, an Active Directory authentication server, the FireCloud Gateway role, or FIPS mode with an external log server; the three unauthenticated rows are reachable by any host that can reach the Access Portal, the SIP proxy policy or the cluster management address (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).
Detection
WatchGuard publishes no indicator and no workaround. For the three unauthenticated rows, connections to the cluster management address from hosts that are not cluster peers, WebSocket upgrade requests to the Access Portal from unexpected sources, SIP traffic from outside expected carriers, and restarts of the portal, SIP or sync services on the Firebox are the telemetry to review; this is an inference from the stated mechanisms.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed release on appliances with the Access Portal, a SIP proxy or clustering first; where an upgrade has to wait, turn off a feature that is not used and keep the cluster management address off untrusted segments.

CVE-2026-108142, Veeam Backup & Replication: an unauthenticated authorization bypass on the CDP Coordinator Service of 13.x backup servers (CVSS 4.0 9.1), fixed in 13.1.2 and 13.0.3, with a Backup for Microsoft 365 SQL injection to code execution and a Veeam ONE MFA bypass fixed the same day

Veeam published three advisories on 2026-10-27. In Backup & Replication, CVE-2026-108142 (CVSS 4.0 9.1, critical) lets an unauthenticated attacker bypass authorization on the CDP Coordinator Service of Windows-based Backup & Replication and of the Veeam Software Appliance; it affects 13.1.1.18 and all earlier 13.1 builds and 13.0.2.29 and all earlier 13.0 builds, is fixed in 13.1.2 (build 13.1.2.57) and 13.0.3 (build 13.0.3.63), and does not affect 12.x (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). The same advisory fixes two medium path-traversal flaws that need the Restore Operator role plus control over the contents of a backed-up NAS share and that write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server, and a local privilege escalation in Veeam Agent for Linux version 13.1.1.4 and earlier that applies only to agents managed by a Backup & Replication server (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 8.5.0.1014 and earlier carry CVE-2026-106076 (9.0, critical): an authenticated organization-transfer peer injects SQL into the source server's configuration database, which gives cross-tenant read and write of configuration data and remote code execution as the PostgreSQL service account; the fix is 8.6 (build 8.6.0.1102), as it is for CVE-2026-106077 (8.3), which lets a user with the Backup for Microsoft 365 Administrator role read arbitrary files on the backup server as LocalSystem; two further flaws, an unauthenticated REST API authentication bypass with a forged federation token (6.9) and an installer file-write (4.3), need 8.6 Patch 1 (build 8.6.0.5011) (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27). Veeam ONE 13.1.0.7233 and earlier let an attacker with valid Administrator credentials disable multi-factor authentication globally before completing MFA verification (8.5, high; fixed in 13.1 P1, build 13.1.0.7940) (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27).

NCSC Switzerland relayed the Backup & Replication and Veeam ONE advisories on 2026-10-28, lists the exploitation status as unknown with the vendor reporting no evidence of active exploitation, and gives the prerequisite for the critical flaw as network access to the backup server's CDP Coordinator Service (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-28). heise adds that backup servers are a favourite target of ransomware groups (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-10-28), and Veeam itself says attackers will likely try to reverse-engineer a disclosed patch to exploit unpatched deployments (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Veeam Backup & Replication or Veeam Software Appliance on a 13.x build below 13.1.2 or 13.0.3 whose CDP Coordinator Service accepts connections from a network the attacker can reach; 12.x is out of scope (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 version 8 below 8.6 Patch 1 (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27) and Veeam ONE 13.1 below Patch 1 (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27) are the other affected builds.
Detection
Veeam publishes no indicator. The telemetry that bears on this flaw is authentication and authorization events and service-account activity on the backup server, and new or changed backup jobs, repositories, stored credentials and restore operators; this is an inference from the described flaw, not a Veeam statement. For Veeam ONE, an MFA setting switched off followed by an Administrator sign-in is the sequence the flaw describes.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed builds on every backup server first, since backup infrastructure is what ransomware groups try to reach before encrypting, and keep backup servers off networks that untrusted hosts can reach; where a backup server was reachable and unpatched, review its jobs, repositories and credentials for changes nobody made.

The earlier statement that no source ties a named CVE to a production compromise is replaced, an action for appliances that embed PHP is added, the URWB fix date in the vendor list is corrected from March 2027 to November 2026 (advisory version 1.9), and the PAN-OS hotfix status is updated to nineteen of twenty released (advisory of 2026-10-29). Removed from the text: the sentence on the release time, Karimi's two-source-address-clusters and PHPSESSID remarks in the main text (the 2026-10-27 section keeps his reliability caveat), VulnCheck's failed web-shell attempt in the main text (the Detection line keeps it), the lab log-path remark and most of Sansec's note on its CVE attribution (kept as a short clause); the 'no source ties a named CVE' statement of 2026-10-27 is dated, and the evidence record for Karimi's clusters remark is dropped.

CISA's catalog entry of 2026-10-28 for the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 says it can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Dream Research reports a chain that takes these flaws to root on appliances: a custom, non-public PHP2Shell build for the management web server of one large vendor's firewall software, which runs PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit, gave code execution as the nobody user, and the kernel flaw lifted it to root in one HTTP request in under 15 minutes (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). Dream found the build tuned to eleven firmware versions, nine exploitable, with offsets from the vendor's own PHP library, the deployment-specific calibration CrowdStrike expects a reliable exploit to need (an inference) (Dream Research, 2026-10-27; CrowdStrike, 2026-10-23). From about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls of that vendor it narrowed to 240, rooted 24 and left a PHP webshell on each, and from the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) built a persistent outbound SSH tunnel, rooted the organization's firewall management server through it and began an attack on its Active Directory; Dream could not tell whether that attack succeeded, does not name the vendor, calls the campaign apparently Chinese and AI-assisted and does not attribute it to a named actor (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). The targets were firewalls whose management interfaces were reachable from the internet (Dream Research, 2026-10-27).

Palo Alto Networks' advisory as read on 2026-10-29 lists all PAN-OS hotfixes as released except 11.1.7-h12, due on 2026-10-30 (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-29).

Dream Research describes a chain of this kind from artifacts its tooling recovered: a custom, non-public PHP2Shell build, tailored to the PAN-OS management web server, which runs PHP 8.0.30, gives code execution as the nobody user, and the Fragnesia exploit then overwrites /etc/pam.d/su in the page cache so that su root succeeds without a password; Dream says SELinux confines the web server's domain from modifying system files and that the whole chain runs in one HTTP request in under 15 minutes (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). From about 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls that it found through a search engine, the attacker narrowed to 240 in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, rooted 24 and planted a PHP webshell on each; on the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) it set up an outbound SSH tunnel kept up by a systemd service and an rc.local entry, rooted the organization's firewall management server through the tunnel, decrypted the LDAP service-account password with root access and sprayed passwords against a domain that had no lockout threshold (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). Dream says the recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration but could not tell whether the password spray succeeded, calls the campaign apparently Chinese and AI-assisted and does not attribute it to a named actor (Dream Research, 2026-10-27).

Coverage gaps: connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport; the new application's identifiers on the Trust Center page are unreadable here); ec-digital-strategy-newsroom (403 on every transport, fourth run); ox-security (feed lists dated items but every article body is 403); previdian (listing feed 403, one featured CVE only); resecurity (empty JavaScript shell); golem-security (cookie wall); F5 K000163821 (my.f5.com is a JavaScript shell on every reader, so F5's exposure, mitigation and exploitation wording is unread); Juniper support portal (JavaScript shells); Broadcom per-product PHP2Shell pages (login-gated); the Cisco advisory's Snort rule links were not re-read after version 1.9; Palo Alto's PAN-OS hotfix status was re-read before the commit (19 of 20 released, only 11.1.7-h12 still carries an estimated date, 2026-10-30), so that build is the one to re-read at the next fire.

TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01DeadTag: expired tag domains send visitors to iPhone exploit kits; opening the page is enough on vulnerable iOS. Report URI and iVerify report that an operator they call DeadTag buys the expired domains of old analytics and advertising tags that thousands of websites still load, so every page that carries the tag runs the operator's script, and sells the visitors on; Report URI counts more than 660 re-registered domains. For chosen iPhone visitors one chain ends at a page that serves the Coruna kit to iOS 13 to 17.2.1 and a modified DarkSword kit to iOS 18.4 to 18.7, both of which attack the browser itself, so that opening the page compromises a vulnerable device and steals keychain passwords and crypto-wallet data. →
  2. 02PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356): Magento upload flaw attacked since March, fixed in July, CISA lists it as exploited. Sansec reports that PolyShell, the unauthenticated file upload in the Magento and Adobe Commerce REST API that Adobe tracks as CVE-2026-48356, has been attacked since 2026-03-19, with a mass wave on 2026-03-30 that put a JavaScript loader on 471 stores in one hour. Adobe's bulletin APSB26-73 of 2026-07-14 names the 2026-jul builds as the fix and still says Adobe knows of no exploits, while Sansec says Magento 2.4.9 carried a fix on 2026-05-12; CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-27. A store that ran an unpatched build may carry a webshell that the update does not remove. →
  3. 03HPE ClearPass 6.14, 6.12 and 6.11 are affected by PHP2Shell; a hotfix patch exists for each train. HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05171, released on 2026-10-22 and revised on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-29, lists ClearPass Policy Manager 6.14.0 and earlier and 6.11.15 and earlier as affected by the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each scored CVSS 3.1 9.8, adds the 6.12 train in its machine-readable record, and names a hotfix patch for 6.14.1, 6.12.8 and 6.11.16. HPE asks customers to consider removing guest portals and all management interfaces from public access until the affected instances are upgraded; the bulletin says nothing about exploitation of ClearPass, although CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 2Trending vulnerabilities 3Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 15

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures2 items

NOTABLENATOB2

DeadTag: re-registered domains of defunct analytics and advertising tags redirect visitors of thousands of sites, among them to a page that serves the Coruna and DarkSword iPhone exploit kits, which compromise a vulnerable device when the page opens

Report URI and iVerify describe a campaign they name DeadTag: attackers buy the expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that thousands of websites still load, so every page that still carries the tag runs the operator's script without the site owner changing or noticing anything, and the operator sells the visitors those tags bring in (Report URI, 2026-10-22). Report URI has identified more than 660 re-registered domains still embedded on thousands of sites and cautiously estimates 135 million visits a month (Report URI, 2026-10-22). The script is about 2 KB, does nothing for search engines, scanners and other bots, asks the operator's server what to do with each visitor and redirects the chosen ones, and Report URI found that the operator stopped answering when it probed from data-centre addresses or returned too often from residential ones; destinations include scam pages, a fake VPN pop-up and, for iPhones, a page that serves two exploit kits (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

One chain ends at a fake prediction-market page that picks the kit by the visitor's iOS version, Coruna for iOS 13 to 17.2.1 and a modified "P7" variant of DarkSword for iOS 18.4 to 18.7; both attack the browser itself, so opening the page is enough to compromise a vulnerable device, and the spyware they install steals keychain passwords, crypto-wallet app data and device and account information and reports to one server; Report URI notes that Coruna and DarkSword are separate exploit kits that have been seen in different campaigns, and that here both send their stolen data to the same server, which it reads as one operator running both (Report URI, 2026-10-22). iVerify reads DeadTag as mostly focused on European domains rather than .com (iVerify, 2026-10-21), and saw the P7 variant reach an employee's device at a customer organisation through a malicious Instagram ad while the employee was scrolling in the app (iVerify, 2026-10-21). The kit operator does not rely on DeadTag alone: Report URI found DarkSword loaders on hundreds of online shops on one e-commerce platform, PrestaShop (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any public website that still loads a script from a third-party domain whose provider no longer operates it, where the browser fetches nothing useful and the page looks normal, and any iPhone on iOS 13 to 17.2.1 or 18.4 to 18.7 that opens such a page (Report URI, 2026-10-22).
Detection
Inventory the external script references of each public site and flag any whose domain has been re-registered or no longer belongs to its provider; Report URI recommends script monitoring that shows when a new script or domain appears on a page, and a Content Security Policy that controls which domains a site may load code from (Report URI, 2026-10-22). A security scanner usually sees only an empty response from the malicious script, because the operator answers only selected visitors.
Defender takeaway
Remove dead third-party tags from every site you run, enforce a Content Security Policy and keep iPhones on the current iOS, with Lockdown Mode for people who may be targeted; for an iPhone that may have opened an affected page, Report URI advises restarting it, changing the passwords stored in its keychain and moving crypto assets to a new wallet (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

threat28 Oct 03:54Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Report URI (Scott Helme) · iVerify Threat Intelligence Team
ROUTINENATOC3

ARA-Region Lyss-Limpachtal (canton Bern, communal wastewater-treatment association): SafePay has put about 49 GB into the darknet, which Risikomonitor's analysis, relayed by Inside IT, finds holds personal records, bank statements, weak passwords and a third party's monitoring credentials; the association declines to comment

The tracker DeXpose recorded on 2026-09-15 that SafePay had claimed an attack on ARA Lyss, the wastewater-treatment association at ara-lyss.ch, posting that the full leak would be published soon unless a company representative made contact (DeXpose, 2026-09-15). Inside IT reported on 2026-10-27 that SafePay has put the stolen data into the darknet, about 49 GB in the case of the Bernese association ARA-Region Lyss-Limpachtal, that the security firm Risikomonitor analysed it, and that the association's management declined to comment (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). Risikomonitor's analysis, relayed by Inside IT and not verified independently, finds about 3,200 e-mail addresses and data on more than 1,200 identifiable persons; user folders and a data store with content up to March 2026 that hold 255 password hits, 195 of them very weak; bank statements and a transaction list with more than 100 payments by private persons with name and address; the full login data to the monitoring portals of the photovoltaic plants of another company's customers, stored on the same server; and a 2015 applicant list with birth dates, civil status, former employer and interview notes that was never deleted (Inside IT, 2026-10-27).

BACS told Inside IT that SafePay, which relies on double extortion, is among the more active ransomware groups in Switzerland and, together with The Gentlemen, the third most active in 2026 after Akira and Payload, that it has no clear focus on Switzerland, and that it was first observed there in May 2025 (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). No source says how the attackers got in or that data was encrypted at the association.

Defender takeaway
A communal body or association should look for credentials, bank statements and applicant files on its own file servers before an attacker does: Risikomonitor found 255 password hits in files, another company's portal logins and a 2015 applicant list that had never been deleted, and those are what a published dump gives fraudsters (Inside IT, 2026-10-27).

Sources: Inside IT (article with Risikomonitor's analysis) · DeXpose (leak-site tracker, claim record)

02Trending vulnerabilities3 items

NOTABLECVE-2026-48356exploitedNATOB2

CVE-2026-48356 (PolyShell), Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source: an unauthenticated file upload attacked since March 2026, fixed for supported lines in July, and listed by CISA as exploited on 2026-10-27

Sansec named the flaw PolyShell: a missing validation in Magento's REST API that lets unauthenticated attackers upload executable files to a store, using a polyglot (code disguised as an image) to pass the image check (Sansec, 2026-03-17). It reports that its Shield service has blocked exploitation attempts against 79.5% of the Magento stores it protects since 2026-03-16, with first attacks observed on 2026-03-19, and that the vulnerable code has existed since the first Magento 2 release (Sansec, 2026-03-17). On 2026-03-30 a mass wave uploaded webshells, spread backdoor scripts across several directories and injected a JavaScript loader into the CMS pages of 471 stores within one hour (Sansec, 2026-03-30).

Sansec dates a fix in Magento 2.4.9 to 2026-05-12, without a backport to the supported 2.4.8 and 2.4.7 lines, and the backport to those lines to 2026-07-14, in bulletin APSB26-73 (Sansec, 2026-03-17). That bulletin rates the flaw Critical at CVSS 3.1 9.6, lists 2.4.9 among the affected versions, names the 2026-jul builds, 2.4.9-2026-jul included, as the fix for Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source, and still says Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild (Adobe, 2026-07-14). CISA added CVE-2026-48356 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-27 on evidence of active exploitation and gives no detail (CISA, 2026-10-27; CISA KEV, 2026-10-27). Sansec's research of 2026-10-24 shows the operator behind the March wave still active: its newest loader domain, registered on 2026-10-06, sits in the CMS blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which already carried an earlier loader, and one of them, on Magento 2.4.7-p1, still lacks APSB26-73 and holds PolyShell webshells disguised as images (Sansec, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Every Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce store without the 2026-jul fix, 2.4.9 included (Adobe, 2026-07-14); the anonymous guest-cart item routes need no credentials, and the upload becomes code execution on stock nginx for the oldest 2.x lines, on any non-stock nginx that hands every .php file to the PHP handler, and on Magento before 2.3.5 running on Apache without the engine switch set for that directory (Sansec, 2026-03-17).
Detection
Sansec calls any .php, .phtml or .phar file in the custom-options upload directory a strong indicator of compromise, and the uploaded file stays on disk even where execution is blocked (Sansec, 2026-03-17); also look for requests that add items to guest carts with embedded file data from unfamiliar sources (Sansec, 2026-03-17), script tags in the CMS block table and administrator accounts nobody created (Sansec, 2026-10-24).
Defender takeaway
Install the fix now, and treat a store that ran an unpatched build while internet-reachable since March as possibly compromised until its upload directory, CMS blocks and administrator accounts are checked, because an uploaded file stays on disk even where execution is blocked (Sansec, 2026-03-17), so the fix does not remove a shell already written (an inference), and deleting a loader script does not remove the access behind it (Sansec, 2026-10-24).

vulnerability28 Oct 03:54Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Sansec (PolyShell advisory) · Sansec (mass PolyShell attack wave) · Sansec (CMS block loader campaign) · Adobe (security bulletin APSB26-73) · CISA (alert, CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.27)
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, HPE Networking ClearPass Policy Manager: bulletin HPESBNW05171 lists the 6.14, 6.12 and 6.11 trains as affected by the PHP2Shell flaws and names a hotfix patch for each (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05171, released on 2026-10-22 and revised on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-29, covers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the PHP flaws behind PHP2Shell, in ClearPass Policy Manager and scores each CVSS 3.1 9.8 with network access, no privileges and no user interaction (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). Its affected-products note lists ClearPass 6.14.0 and earlier in the 6.14 release train and 6.11.15 and earlier in the 6.11 train, while its machine-readable record also lists the 6.12 train and gives 6.14.1, 6.11.16 and 6.12.8 as the boundaries; the bulletin does not reconcile the two (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The fix is a hotfix patch for each train, 6.14.1, 6.12.8 (added in revision 3, which HPE says "exceptionally" includes 6.12.8) and 6.11.16, downloadable from the HPE Networking Support Portal; versions past end of maintenance are presumed affected and are not covered, and HPE has not assessed versions past end of support, which it says should be considered potentially impacted (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).

HPE recommends confining the CLI and web management interfaces to a dedicated layer 2 segment or VLAN, or controlling them with firewall policy at layer 3 and above, and asks customers to consider removing guest portals and all management interfaces from public access until the affected ClearPass instances have been upgraded (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). Other HPE Networking products and software versions it does not list are not known to be affected, and for Mist products the bulletin points to a Juniper reference advisory (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-27); the bulletin itself says nothing about exploitation of ClearPass (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Every ClearPass Policy Manager on the 6.14, 6.12 or 6.11 train without the hotfix patch; the guest portal and the management interfaces are the surfaces HPE asks to take off public access (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).
Detection
HPE gives no indicator and no post-patch check; CISA's PHP alert advises monitoring for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools (CISA, 2026-10-21), which on a ClearPass node would be processes started by the web worker account (an inference, since HPE does not describe how ClearPass runs PHP).
Defender takeaway
Install the hotfix patch for 6.14.1, 6.12.8 or 6.11.16 on every node now, the remediation HPE's bulletin names, and take any guest portal or management interface reachable from untrusted networks off public access, as HPE asks (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).
Update30 Oct 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

HPE's revision 3 of bulletin HPESBNW05171, dated 2026-10-29, updates its affected and resolution sections to exceptionally include ClearPass 6.12.8 (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). A ClearPass 6.12.8 hotfix patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 is now named beside the 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 patches, downloadable from the HPE Networking Support Portal (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The affected-products note of this revision reads 6.14.0 and earlier in the 6.14 train and 6.11.15 and earlier in the 6.11 train, while its machine-readable record gives 6.14.1, 6.11.16 and 6.12.8 as boundaries, and the wording of revision 2 that named 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 as versions providing some level of mitigation is no longer in the bulletin (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The bulletin still says nothing about exploitation of ClearPass.

Sources: HPE Networking (CSAF advisory HPESBNW05171, revision 2, superseded at this URL by revision 3) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.27) · CISA (alert, Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching) · HPE Networking (CSAF advisory HPESBNW05171, revision 3)
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Cisco Expressway, Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul, Duo Access Gateway and ISE Portal Builder: Cisco's final PHP2Shell advisory names Expressway 15.5.21 and Duo Access Gateway 3.2.0 as the fixes and knows of no malicious use against its products

Cisco's advisory cisco-sa-php-october26-Jj384Daq, published on 2026-10-21 and final at version 1.11 on 2026-11-06, lists Expressway, Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul, Duo Access Gateway and ISE Portal Builder as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the PHP flaws behind PHP2Shell (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). Expressway Series and Expressway Select Series (bug CSCwx37062) have fixed release 15.5.21 and a workaround described in the bug record; Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul and Unified Industrial Wireless Software (bug CSCwx37073) have fixed release 26.2.1.9, available since 2026-11-06, and a workaround, and there the attacker must be authenticated as an administrator, which lowers the CVSS 3.1 score to 6.6; Duo Access Gateway is fixed in 3.2.0; and ISE Portal Builder has a fix deployed with no customer action required (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). The advisory gives no affected-version ranges and no workaround steps; its bug records carry platform-specific information, workarounds and fixed releases, and a product it does not list is, in Cisco's review, not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Cisco says it is aware that a public announcement is available and knows of no malicious use of the flaws against any Cisco product (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-27). For Expressway the PHP fix is 15.5.21 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28), while the release Cisco names for the unauthenticated root command execution on clustered units, CVE-2026-76466, is X15.5.20 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Every Expressway Series and Expressway Select unit and every Duo Access Gateway not on a release Cisco lists as fixed (15.5.21 and 3.2.0), since Cisco gives no affected-version ranges; the advisory names no version-check command and no component that runs the PHP; its bug records CSCwx37062 and CSCwx37073 carry platform-specific information (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Cisco publishes no indicator and reports no attack on its products, but lists Snort rules 67359 and 67360 as action links for the advisory (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); beyond that, CISA's PHP alert advises monitoring for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools (CISA, 2026-10-21), which on these products would be processes started by the web worker account (an inference, since Cisco does not describe how they run PHP).
Defender takeaway
Move Expressway to 15.5.21 and Duo Access Gateway to 3.2.0, the fixed releases the table names (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); an Expressway already upgraded to X15.5.20 for the clustered-device flaw (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21) is not named as fixed in the PHP table, which lists only 15.5.21 (an inference from the table, not a Cisco statement), so apply the bug record's workaround until 15.5.21 is installed (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul and Unified Industrial Wireless Software move to 26.2.1.9, available since 2026-11-06.
Update29 Oct 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-10-29T0255Z-intelsummaryupdated_atcvessourcesevidencebody

Cisco published version 1.9 of the advisory on 2026-10-28 to update the fix availability date for Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul and Unified Industrial Wireless Software: release 27.1.1 is now listed for November 2026 instead of March 2027, and the workaround in bug CSCwx37073 remains the control until it ships (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). The other rows are unchanged, and Cisco still knows of no malicious use against its products (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
